Traditionally, business process management concentrated on organized, task-based processes, but the rise in importance of intellectual work brings semi-organized processes into prominence. Current approaches for modeling business processes relying on in-depth knowledge often utilize restrictive logic based on sets, but case-based methods, such as FBDN and BOC, incorporate flexible relationships between cases through similarity measures, making them suitable for handling semi-organized processes. However, both methods have a common limitation when dealing with processes involving strict data constraints by employing set-based logic. This limitation is addressed by introducing an innovative technique where the notion of inclusion is replaced by the concept of non-empty intersection. The technique is further developed into two case-based methods for modeling business processes: FBDD and BOCD, which leverage the principles of description logics to incorporate data constraints in semi-organized processes effectively. The proposed methods demonstrate superior performance compared to existing approaches, as confirmed by practical examples and experimental results. The accompanying documentation provides a detailed mathematical justification for these techniques. The FBDN model is refined into FBDD, and the BOC model is enhanced into BOCD. The enhancements involve addressing the issue of non-empty intersections and developing methods for identifying and combining relevant cases. The techniques for handling data constraints, including both the initial and enhanced approaches, are examined. The FBDD and BOCD methods are evaluated using real-world scenarios, and their results are presented. The FBDD and BOCD methods are then compared with alternative approaches for business process management. The comparison is based on predefined criteria, and the results are discussed. The FBDD and BOCD methods are utilized to solve actual problems, and their effectiveness is demonstrated. The technical report is divided into 11 sections as follows. Section 1 introduces the concept of semi-organized processes and their importance. Section 2 provides an in-depth review of business process management. Section 3 explores the role of case-based reasoning in business processes. Sections 4 and 5 delve into the FBDN and BOC models, respectively. Sections 6 and 7 introduce the enhanced models FBDD and BOCD, respectively. Section 8 evaluates the proposed models. Section 9 demonstrates the application of the proposed models. Section 10 discusses the potential future research. Section 11 concludes the technical report. The technical report is accompanied by additional material as follows. Document ID. Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) data streams retrieved from geostationary satellites.

model. Nevertheless, leveraging satellite data streams alone impedes the model

constructed, enabling the prediction of AOD values and their future temporal
evolution. Moreover, the proposed framework enables the visualization and
prediction of wildfire aerosols dispersion maps. Extensive experiments have
verified the proposed approach as a deep generative model, outperforming other
competitive methods available in the literature. Consequently, this deep model
can utilize widespread satellite data effectively to predict AOD and aerosols
spatial and temporal distributions. Hence, the developed model has promising
applications for environmental monitoring and pollution prediction. The work
presented here has been enabled by research software tool, PyRCL, making the
Randall-Charlson model and its reductions accessible to a broad research community. Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we studied how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual and group differences, and our analysis suggests that multisite studies are feasible when utilizing large sample sizes. Our data showed that combining resting-state data from different sites using Internal Alignment or External Alignment did not significantly alter connectivity measures or our ability to accurately predict cognitive tasks. Notably, we observed that External Alignment may offer better overall performance compared to Internal Alignment. With regard to multisite research, our results indicate that site effects can be considered random effects, and that group differences can be accurately detected when the sample size is sufficiently large. In terms of prediction accuracy, our findings indicate that a combination of functional and anatomical brain information can lead to accurate predictions of cognitive performance, and that models incorporating both functional and anatomical features tend to perform better than models built with the same features but using only functional or anatomical data. Recent breakthroughs in NLP for code-mixed texts have been largely fueled by the introduction of wordpiece tokenization and learning-based language models. Researchers have developed various language models for code-mixed texts, but due to the diverse nature of language use, a unified model cannot be effective. To address this challenge, we present the Switching Point Embedding (SPE) technique, an innovative solution that dynamic and position-dependent token and token-piece embeddings can be learned for any given language pair. We utilize SPE in a model called SPE-LM and evaluate its efficacy on two popular code-mixed datasets, FMILIMED and IITK-AMI. We compare the performance of SPE-LM with established language models, including LM+PE, LM+RP, LM+ES, LM+MS, LM+FinPE, LM+MS-PE, LM+RRPE, LM+RRPPE, and LM+RRPPE-MS. The results indicate that SPE-LM significantly outperforms other models in terms of accuracy, error rate, sentence length, and word length. Furthermore, we analyze various speech characteristics, including speech rate, pause time, and phrase structure, to develop a relative positional encoding (RPE) table. We then incorporate RPE into SPE-LM to enhance its performance, resulting in an even higher accuracy rate. To facilitate widespread adoption, we open-source SPE-LM and make it available for download at public GitHub repository. Fisher introduced the concept of average effect to describe the magnitude of a gene's influence on a complex trait. This concept is calculated as the average covariance between a gene and the trait after removing all other variables. We demonstrate that this measure is equivalent to a partial path coefficient in a directed acyclic graph representing a causal relationship between a gene and a complex trait. Fisher's average effect can be thought of as the average causal influence of a gene on the trait, and is useful for understanding the role of genetic factors in complex diseases and traits. In particular, we show that this measure can be used to estimate the magnitude of a gene's influence on a trait, and to identify genes that have a significant impact following statistical analysis. We also discuss how this measure can be used in conjunction with a statistical test, such as the ridge regression MAGMA tool, to accurately identify genes that have a significant causal effect on a complex trait in cases where there is strong confounding of the relationship between the gene, the trait, and environmental factors. Examples are provided using data from the PGC ADHD TWAILF family study, and further analysis can be found in the accompanying supplement. Based on our understanding of the causal relationship between genes and complex traits, we propose that precise language be used to distinguish between the technical concept of a gene's influence and the actual biological effect, and suggest alternative phrases such as 'causal influence,' 'genetic contribution,' or 'biological effect' to describe a gene's impact on a complex trait. We believe that precise language in scientific communication is essential to convey our understanding of the complex relationships between genes, environment, and disease. Furthermore, incorporating the concept of a partial path coefficient in statistical analyses can facilitate a deeper understanding of the underlying biology of complex diseases and traits. By representing Fisher's average effect as a partial path coefficient in a causal network, we can visualize and estimate the magnitude of a gene's influence on a complex trait, and this measure can be used to build a causal framework of the relationships between genes, environment, and disease. This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback control system, which generates periodic references based on a critically damped model of walking. We've demonstrated that incorporating feedback from sensors and adjustable models allows us to adapt to changing real-world conditions such as terrain inclines, uncertainties in models, and external disturbances. This approach has been successfully tested in a series of 27 simulations, producing satisfactory results in all cases. Furthermore, simulations showed that incorporating thruster assistance can lead to increased efficiency, robustness, and walking speeds. Specifically, under certain conditions, walking assisted by thrusters can be up to 30% more efficient than unassisted walking, and up to 50% faster than unassisted walking on flat terrain. However, these benefits come with increased computational costs compared to unassisted walking, but are comparable to previously published research on unassisted walking models. The development of faster and more efficient feedback control systems and actuators will enable these benefits to be translated into real-world performance improvements. This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering. By applying surfel reprojection constraints, this method optimizes both keyframe positions and map features within the database. A step-by-step camera relocalization process is then applied to determine 6-DoF camera poses by leveraging the constructed visual database. Moreover, this method exploits machine-learned descriptors to achieve enhanced performance, especially under difficult conditions, without necessitating any manual annotation during the database creation. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in geometric relocalization, yielding superior results under diverse scenarios. Code and dataset will be jointly provided for reproduction of these results.

To better assess the Emergency Department's admission process, we analyzed average response curves for treatment duration. Extending the time for treatment is considered an effective strategy for improving admissions; however, this method's effectiveness varies depending on the current treatment duration. A mathematical representation of this concept was developed and tested using real data from two hospitals. Using the hospitals' treatment duration data, we created an average response curve model to confirm that shorter initial treatment times are often associated with longer ultimate treatment durations. A key model parameter representing the rate at which treatment durations reach their equilibrium was also identified. The model's findings suggested that implementing the admissions strategy might not always be an efficient use of resources, as it could potentially worsen the overall treatment duration. Further research is necessary to determine the model's full potential for optimizing the Emergency Department's admissions process. The real data sets used for this analysis are publicly available for use in future studies. They include the data from Bellevue Hospital Center and Elmhurst Hospital Center, both of which were provided by NYU Langone Medical Center. Any interested parties seeking access to the data can submit an inquiry to Harvard Dataverse with the reference code nyu-erd-data-20191002. The data will be readily available for use in the specified repository. The mathematical representation used in this study was based on a model developed by Martin Forer, as described in his 2017 paper titled "Average Response Curves for Treatment Time in the Emergency Department, http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jmpe.2017.09.003." Forer's full paper can be accessed via the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics Publications database with the reference code 2017JMPEman001. Research has examined the correlations of charges in particle interactions within Pb-Pb collisions, specifically looking at whether evidence of the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) exists in the collision data collected at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The study considered all charged particles within specific pseudorapidity and transverse momentum ranges, with particular emphasis on peripheral collisions. A signal related to CME was observed in specific correlator calculations and found to intensify with increasing collision peripherality. The surge in online fundraising (or "crowdfunding") has created a substantial need to understand the crowd dynamics that influence its success. Donations are not merely rational financial transactions but also reflect intangible crowd behaviors that signal a project's worthiness. We investigated these crowd signals in both general online and platform-specific contexts through a combined qualitative and quantitative analysis of textual feedback from donors. Our study uncovered a range of positive emotions (joy, hope, excitement) and a project's ability to evoke empathy as common crowd signals that indicate a project's potential for success. We also identified distinct characteristics of the feedback posted by donors, which suggested that the nature of these crowd signals varies across different platforms. Ultimately, our research provided key insights for developers on how to design systems that effectively harness the power of crowd behaviors to facilitate successful fundraising. The findings were shared with the developers of Fundly, the platform on which the data was collected, and have since influenced its redesign. Moreover, our research offered a framework for analyzing the relationship between system design, user interaction, and crowd behavior that can be applied to the study of other crowdfunding platforms. Machine learning (ML) based detection of network attacks has shown effectiveness when tailored to a single organisation's network, but combining data from multiple sources is challenging due to compatibility issues. A possible solution is to employ federated learning, a distributed ML technique that enables multiple organisations to collaboratively train a model without exchanging data. Our proposed framework leverages federated learning for training a cyber threat intelligence (CTI) based intrusion detection system, allowing several organisations to share threat information while keeping their individual datasets private. We assessed the efficacy of this approach by comparing it to a non-distributed training method using integrated data, and observed similar accuracy in detecting Rsync and Proces execution attacks using a CNN based model. Additionally, the model achieved comparable performance to traditional ML methods on detecting DoS, Bot, Scalability, and Sql Injection attacks using a federated learning approach with support vector machine. These findings indicate that federated learning can be an effective solution for training ML models based on shared threat intelligence while maintaining data privacy. We expect this technique to become increasingly important as organisations strive to develop and improve their cyber security systems while minimising data exchange risks. The sequential arrangement of tasks is a fundamental problem in planning for single robotic arms, whereas managing multiple robotic arms presents a expanded version of this issue, requiring consideration of inter-arm correlations, like those arising from grasping objects between different clusters in a workspace. The Expanded Sequential Task Arrangement problem (ESTA) encompasses these additional constraints, and we propose introducing the Cluster Task Arrangement Algorithm (CTAA) to enhance ESTA's efficiency and scalability. CTAA is based on a clustering technique that groups task dependencies and starts with an initial solution, which we then refine using a local search method. The algorithm's effectiveness is validated through simulations utilizing scenarios with up to 20 tasks and various numbers of robotic arms. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that CTAA yields solutions comparable to the optimal arrangement in terms of overall task sequence quality, and this improvement is particularly pronounced in scenarios with inter-arm correlations. Furthermore, CTAA shows strong scalability, with a average linear relationship between its runtime and problem complexity. The algorithm's performance is further bolstered by its ability to produce high-quality task arrangements in real-time, making it suitable for practical applications. The proposed CTAA represents a promising solution for solving ESTA efficiently and accurately within realistic time constraints. We investigated the potential for integrating MOSFETs into a full 300mm CMOS process with multiple layers to investigate MOSFET performance beyond typical transistor functionality. To evaluate MOSFET performance as a single channel entity, we developed a device architecture that incorporates a body tie and a body contact, allowing for operation in a non-self-healing mode. Characterization involved leveraging a full CMOS toolset to examine MOSFET behavior. Measurements showed a 450 V breakdown voltage, accompanied by a low on-resistance of 1$\Omega$/sq and a high mobility of 2000 cm$^2$/V s. This work lays the foundation for advanced MOSFET technology in CMOS processes.

In complex networks, a phenomenon occurs where different clusters of oscillators, comprised of distinct systems, synchronize with their own distinct rhythms. When each cluster contains identical models, synchronized within that group, but oscillators from different groups are uncorrelated, this phenomenon is known as group synchronization. Typically, strict conditions need to be met to achieve synchronization, but research has revealed that slight discrepancies in parameters or connections do not necessarily preclude it. Through advanced analysis, it is now possible to identify stable conditions for group synchronization, including the impact of within-group connections, which can be unidirectional or bidirectional. By comparing various parameter configurations, it has been found that group synchronization is often more robust with bidirectional connections within groups. This discovery holds important practical implications for both real-world applications and theoretical modeling, where adjustments to systems can be predicted to improve their ability to synchronize and recover from disruptions. These predictions can be made using a novel approach, identifying specific metrics and indicators that were previously unseen. Ultimately, a framework has been established for maintaining stable group synchronization in complex networks with interconnected components. Specifically, when intragroup connections are strong and unidirectional, a threshold is reached where further additions can actually decrease group stability. This counterintuitive effect is likened to a tipping point and potentially exploited in systems where synchronization is desired, such as neural interfaces, where a switch from unidirectional to bidirectional connections could improve synchronization quality. Research has also extended beyond static networks to dynamic systems, where group synchronization is shown to occur even when parameters within a group are mismatched, and a measure of stability is developed for these scenarios. Notably, a distinct feature is observed where group synchronization transitions from one stable state to another. This work presents the first known research combining advanced analytical methods to explore the complex and intriguing phenomenon of group synchronization in interconnected systems. Specifically, a framework is established for maintaining stable group synchronization in complex networks with bidirectional components, and group synchronization is successfully extended to systems with parameter mismatches. Ultimately, a deeper understanding is gained into the complex dynamics of group synchronization and the role of intragroup connections. Research has also revealed previously unknown features, including correlations between group stability and connection patterns, and potentially exploitable effects, such as a group synchronization 'tipping point'. These findings could be applied in numerous areas, such as neural interfaces, where a better understanding of group synchronization could improve performance and enable new functionalities. Additionally, these findings could be used to control and switch between different states of group synchronization in electronic circuits and other technological systems.

Our study examines the existence of domain-level source diversity bias in video search outcomes by utilizing a virtual agent-based method. The approach entails comparing the outputs of five prominent search engines, comprising four Western and one non-Western search engines, for both English and Russian language queries. The research reveals significant variation in source diversity according to language, with English search queries yielding more diverse results. Additionally, the analysis discovers that the video-sharing platform YouTube dominates the top search outputs for all Western search engines, excluding Google. Interestingly, the sampled Google search results lack video content from its main competitors, including Vimeo and Dailymotion, implying a possible ranking bias towards Google-owned services. These findings underscore the need for further investigations into owned-data bias within Google's search outcomes. Based on our analysis, we propose a methodical approach for auditing diversity bias in video search results by analyzing the outputs of multiple search engines, alongside a comprehensive set of queries spanning a broad spectrum of topics. The audit can help identify and overcome internal and external data biases, thereby enhancing the overall quality of video search. A possible future application of this auditing approach could contribute to developing more inclusive video recommendations, free from source diversity and owned-data biases. The study's source code is publicly available on GitHub at the link provided.

Additionally, we provide a way to identify this curve using the curve's discriminant and a value from its minimal polynomial, demonstrating that the curve's uniqueness is linked to properties involving 13th roots of unity and the behavior of a specific polynomial over possible Galois extensions of rational numbers. This work ultimately leads to a method of determining whether a particular elliptic curve, defined over a cubic field, has a point on it that corresponds to a 13th root of unity in that curve. If such a point exists, we provide a way to compute it directly. Finally, we investigate how this relationship could apply to curves defined by other fields that are also cubic in nature but have fields that are not rational. Specifically, we examine whether a particular curve, defined by the fifth root of two, has a point on it that corresponds to a 13th root of unity in that curve and provide a way to compute such a point directly. This result could be extended to other curves, defined by other fields that are cubic in nature but not rational. Consequently, we prove that there is only one curve, up to uniqueness, defined by the fifth root of two that has a point on it that corresponds to a 13th root of unity in that curve. Finally, we investigated whether a particular curve, defined by the quadratic root of three, has a point on it that corresponds to a 13th root of unity in that curve and provide a way to compute such a point directly. This result could be extended to other curves, defined by other fields that are cubic in nature but not rational. Consequently, we proved that there is only one curve, up to uniqueness, defined by the quadratic root of three that has a point on it that corresponds to a 13th root of unity in that curve. Random access methods used in contemporary wireless networks can generate unanticipated dependencies between uncoordinated signal interference experienced by devices, potentially hindering performance and causing blackouts. This study aims to uncover the benefits of a particular diversity technique known as random access diversity, which capitalizes on the correlated nature of interference experienced by devices in wireless networks. A thorough analysis of interference correlation properties is provided, along with a mathematical framework for evaluating the impact of random access diversity on wireless networks. This analysis reveals that random access diversity can enhance a baseband transmission rate by up to a factor of $4\eta$, where $\eta$ represents the proportion of interference correlation within a network. This result is validated through practical experiments conducted using LoRaWAN, demonstrating that random access diversity can improve packet reception success by as much as $36\%$ in a particular scenario. Furthermore, theoretical estimates show that random access diversity can outperform traditional diversity techniques by up to a factor of $0.4/\sqrt{\eta}$ when $\eta$ approaches its maximum value of $1$. These findings indicate that random access diversity can provide superior performance benefits in high-interference scenarios. Nonetheless, the development of efficient protocols capable of harnessing random access diversity remains complicated by a lack of existing research in this area, presenting an opportunity for future investigation and development. Consequently, this paper contributes a novel approach for mitigating interference in wireless networks through the creation of a simple, random access diversity-based algorithm, along with a mathematical proof demonstrating its superiority over traditional diversity techniques. Notably, this approach remains applicable in a variety of real-world scenarios where devices may experience brief signal disruptions, broadening its potential practical applications. Ultimately, this paper delves into the fundamental limitations of diverse wireless access techniques, providing insight into their capabilities and limitations in uncoordinated and allied wireless networks. Additionally, this study identifies potential avenues for future research in diverse wireless access techniques, including the development of novel protocols capable of harnessing random access diversity. Moreover, this paper presents a comprehensive summary of existing research in diverse wireless access techniques, including an exhaustive list of various diversity techniques, along with their underlying causes and examples. Additionally, this study provides an in-depth analysis of the various testing methods employed to evaluate the performance of diverse wireless access techniques. Lastly, this paper identifies potential gaps in the current research on diverse wireless access techniques, presenting potential avenues for future investigation and development. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using the same loss function, failing to acknowledge the distinct characteristics of these labels. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on labeling nodes with the greatest informative value, which effectively represents their surrounding neighborhood through mutual information maximization. To counterbalance the risks of pseudo-label noise, we also introduce a robust pseudo-label filtering mechanism, thoroughly assessing the consistency of filtered pseudo-labels before selecting them for training. Furthermore, InfoGNN separates the pseudo-label loss into different components for pseudo-labels and actual labels to ensure precise supervision. Through thorough evaluations on 7 graph datasets, InfoGNN has proven to outperform existing state-of-the-art methods. For instance, it achieves 100% accuracy on Cora, an accuracy improvement of 11.8% over Baseline, and even surpasses double the baseline accuracy on Citeseer, PubMed-NILM, PubMed, and PubMed-RR with improved accuracies of 7.8%, 4.2%, 2.2%, and 10.6% respectively. Thus, InfoGNN has proven to be a highly effective pseudo-labeling framework. Its innovative approaches to informative pseudo-labeling may also contribute to the development of new graph neural networks in the future. The source code is available at https://github.com/Chen-550/InfoGNN.

A new method using energy harvesting (EH) enables devices to sustain their power consumption by converting available radio signals into usable energy. This has the potential to increase energy efficiency in wireless networks by utilizing techniques such as simultaneous wireless information and energy transfer (SWIPT). To achieve this, our proposed framework combines the utility functions of the devices with the objective of maximizing the system's overall sum utility. This is achieved through a multi-stage process involving two techniques: SWIPT mode detection using an iterative generalized successive convex approximation (GSCA) algorithm and resource allocation using a low complexity two-stage weighted multi-objective Bandyopadhyay algorithm. This allows us to optimize the trade-off between energy transfer and information transmission. Numerical results demonstrate that our approach can significantly boost sum utility compared to current standards and scale efficiently with growing network sizes. This provides a useful framework for wireless network designers to allocate resources effectively and increase energy harvesting efficiency. This in turn enables the deployment of more resilient and efficient next-generation wireless networks. To evaluate the performance of our approach, we conducted extensive simulations based on real-world scenarios using actual device utility functions which are often non-convex, thereby preventing the use of standard convex optimization techniques. To address this limitation, our GSCA algorithm detects the SWIPT mode by iteratively optimizing a convex surrogate function of the original problem. This allows us to jointly optimize the radio frequency (RF) power for information transmission and the directional energy transfer power using a standard convex optimization algorithm. This provides a simple and efficient solution to a complex multi-objective problem, thereby ensuring low overhead and fast convergence. To allocate resources, our two-stage WMO-Bandyopadhyay algorithm first determines the overall power allocation using a standard convex optimization algorithm. This is then followed by a low complexity iterative process that jointly optimizes the EH modes, information transmission powers, and directional energy transfer powers. This allows us to efficiently optimize the system's overall sum utility in the presence of multiple interfering devices. To evaluate the performance of our approach, we conducted extensive simulations based on various real-world scenarios. Results demonstrate that our approach offers significant improvements over current standards and scale efficiently with growing network sizes. This provides a useful benchmark for wireless network designers to deploy more resilient and efficient next-generation wireless networks. This in turn enables the deployment of more energy-efficient wireless networks. This research investigates the dynamics of a robot that tracks a moving wall in a foreign environment, examining how the robot's pursuit is affected by sensory limitations. Unlike previous studies on wall following bacteria, which assumed perfect sensing capabilities, our model reveals that sensory constraints can lead to chaotic behavior. Interestingly, as the quality of sensing improves, the system undergoes a series of complex phase transitions, starting with chaotic dynamics, followed by the emergence of periodic orbits and finally settling into coherent, synchronized motion among the robots. To better understand these phenomena, we employed a combination of analytical methods, including scaling theory and semigroup theory, as well as extensive numerical simulations. Moreover, our analysis was supplemented by a simple model that reduces the complex dynamics of the system into a manageable, effectively one-dimensional problem, allowing for a deeper exploration of the underlying physics. Ultimately, our study provides new insights into how the intricate behaviors of small living organisms can arise from their individual physiological limitations. Additionally, our research offers potential avenues for manipulating the micro-machines of biology, such as bacteria, to exhibit diverse patterns of life. Lastly, our work also serves as a suitable case study for tackling challenging problems in biological physics by employing innovative mathematical analyses. Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. Smoke produced by laser ablation in such procedures obstructs the surgeon's visibility, highlighting the need for smoke removal to ensure a clear view. To apply smoke removal techniques effectively, it's essential to accurately detect and assess the level of smoke presence. Although existing smoke detection methods show promise, they are hampered by difficulties in balancing true positives and false positives. To overcome these limitations, we explore the image enhancement approach, which can benefit smoke detection by visually improving low-quality input images, thereby facilitating better performance in this context. However, conventional image enhancement methods are often used as input for classification tasks, but don't consider the interdependence of detection reliability and false positives. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that incorporates the use of image enhancement as a distinct detection strategy, independent of classification methods. By leveraging domain-specific insights, we develop an image enhancement method capable of amplifying relevant features and suppressing irrelevant ones. Additionally, we employ a weighted fusion strategy to combine the outcomes of different image enhancement techniques in an optimal manner. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, we conduct extensive experiments on the smoke image enhancement dataset, SIED. The results demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance compared to alternative methods, showcasing its potential for practical application in smoke detection and removal for laparoscopic surgery. We've established a specific type of ordered relational topological space known as orthomodular spaces. Our method for creating these spaces involves combining a particular kind of frame, introduced by Hartonas, with a topology in a manner similar to the approach taken by Goldblatt in topological logic. We then demonstrate that the set of orthomodular lattices, along with their order-preserving homomorphisms, forms a category that is equivalent to the category of orthomodular spaces. This equivalence is a generalization of a previously established duality theorem for classical lattices, as well as a duality theorem for distributive lattices proposed by Bimbó. We further examine the relationship between orthomodular lattices and their corresponding frames, showing that the set of frames for a given lattice is bi-homomorphically embeddable in the set of its orthomodular expansions. This expansion concept, introduced by Hardegree, represents a unifying framework for various substructural logics. The results presented here provide a foundation for further exploration of the relationship between orthomodular lattice theory and the theory of orthomodular spaces, offering insights into the intrinsic duality between these two frameworks. This research also brings a topological space perspective to the study of orthomodular lattices, enabling new methods to be applied to this area of study. In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, the termination criterion often presents challenges. This article proposes an innovation in IPMs by developing a novel convergence criterion that directly utilizes the residual norm's relationship with the primal-dual optimal complementarity gap. This advancement enables the use of standard generalized minimum residual (GMR) and flexible GMR (FGMR) Krylov solvers without requiring a preconditioner. Furthermore, a GMR variant that addresses null-space issues is presented and demonstrated to perform well, especially when an equivalent or better level of precision is achieved in fewer iterations than the conventional GMR approach. Computational data also indicates that the proposed GMR solver often surpasses the preconditioned conjugate gradient squared (PCGS) method in terms of efficiency and effectiveness. Notably, when paired with the proposed null-space GMR (NSGMR) method, the inner iterations can be substantially reduced, leading to a notable enhancement of the overall computational efficiency and robustness of the code. Specifically, code enhancements based on early inner iteration termination and adaptive inner loop resizing have been incorporated into the interior-point solver IPOPT, resulting in substantial performance improvements, particularly for large-scale optimization problems. These optimizations have been thoroughly tested against a diverse set of 442 test cases. IPOPT's premier solver has been replaced with the NSGMR variant, which has proven to be superior in virtually all instances of these test cases. Detailed comparisons with other contemporary IPMs have also been conducted to solidify the premise that the interior-point optimizer's revised foundation is exceptionally superior to other leading methods. Specifically, it has been demonstrated that the interior-point optimizer outperforms CONDOR, CPLEX, and SNOPT in nearly all cases across 442 test problems. These notable results were facilitated by several key contributions, including the interior-point optimizer's primal block row strategy, the primal-dual kernel, and the revised solver selection mechanism. These foundational elements have been effectively integrated into the interior-point optimizer, resulting in a substantial enhancement of its performance, robustness, and flexibility. The principle underlying the renormalization group bears a strong analogy to gradient flow, especially in scalar field theory where the RG and gradient flows share a direct connection through the ERG formalism. To generalize this connection in Yang--Mills theory while maintaining gauge invariance, we propose an ERG equation based on a similarity principle and further extend it to lattice gauge theory from the continuum theory context. We verify that our ERG equation replicates key aspects of the Horowitz--Polchinski theorem, revealing a direct correlation between the ERG equation and the equation of gradient flow in the classical regime. We also demonstrate that the numerical solution of the ERG equation exhibits a form of 'universal line' where the RG and gradient flows meet, and we discuss how the ERG equation can be used to define an improved action that incorporates a form of decoupling to high momenta. Due to its gauge invariant structure, the ERG approach may offer a valuable alternative to other methods for simulating Yang--Mills theory and quantum gravity. In the latter case, the incorporation of matter fields presents technical challenges related to the 'non-abelian gauge dependence of the Fock space', which may be addressed through a form of decoupling, thereby enabling an RG-like description of the gravitational force as a free field. Given that our proposal is rooted in the concept of renormalization group, we hope that this idea stimulates innovative approaches to simulating quantum systems based on the RG principle. In particular, we hope that the community comes together to tackle the associated theoretical and technical difficulties!

Over the past decade, significant advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) technology have positioned it as a key tool for tackling environmental challenges, primarily by enhancing the efficiency of environmental protection and ecological conservation efforts. However, the development and implementation of AI systems, which are core to these efforts, give rise to unforeseen and concealed environmental implications. The literature thus far fails to provide a comprehensive analysis of the potential environmental consequences of AI technology itself. To address this knowledge gap, our study aims to systematically examine and categorize the existing research on the environmental impacts of AI systems, focusing on their sources, effects, and interactions with the environment. Through in-depth stakeholder engagement, we also seek to identify prospective areas of research and develop a general framework that can be applied across various AI technology domains to reveal and mitigate any adverse environmental effects during the design phase itself. The research highlights the scarcity of current studies on the environmental impacts of AI technology and identifies several areas, including cardiovascular risk, data quality, AI training, and social media, that warrant further investigation. The findings also point to potential research opportunities across 11 identified categories and suggest four overarching areas for future research, including the environmental impacts of AI technology on future generations, AI data storage, AI technology waste, and climate change. The research ultimately contributes to the development of a comprehensive theoretical structure that can be utilized to study the environmental impacts of AI systems and suggests strategies for reducing the adverse effects of AI technology through a reduce, reuse, recycle approach. The strategies involve reducing energy consumption, reusing AI knowledge through transfer learning, and promoting the adoption of sustainable lifestyle patterns via AI-powered recommendations. The research holds key implications for theory and practice, potentially addressing the concern that the benefits of AI technology, particularly in environmental protection, may be compromised by its negative environmental impacts if the adverse effects are not mitigated during the design phase itself. This proof-of-concept investigation demontstrates that the integration of asynchronous audio-visual information can accurately determine the moment of an object fall within a few tens of milliseconds. This precise timing is capable of differentiating between occluded object drops near their point of release, a capability that binocular vision alone is unable to achieve. Techniques such as multi-scale temporal fusion, data augmentation, and loss functions are exploited to enhance the efficiency of a neural network in capturing the combined audio-visual cues. Consequently, a notable 95% accuracy rate is achieved for localizing object drops. Ultimately, the ground-based findings of this study hold promising signs for the effective application of this method in advanced robotic systems. By comparing our data to existing research, we also created a comprehensive pressure-temperature phase diagram that sheds new light on the origin of shear thickening. Unlike other polymers, our data suggests that shear thickening occurs in a much broader concentration range and is more susceptible to changes in pressure. Based on our analysis, we presented a simplified model that explains shear thickening as a result of temporary polymer networks that collapse and impede the flow of the fluid as it accelerates. This model not only explains our observations but also connects to other mechanical properties of the fluids. Interestingly, our data takes on a more intricate form at high pressures, which indicates that shear thickening becomes more complex and multi-faceted as the pressure increases. We proposed that shear thickening consists of two distinct mechanisms, one of which involves the flexible polymer chains interacting with the solvent. Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a task called program synthesis. A novel framework for generating code based on flow charts is presented, where a deep neural network called GRCNN is trained to accurately interpret these visual specifications by identifying their graphical structures. By being trained end-to-end, GRCNN is capable of simultaneously predicting node and edge details in flow charts. The framework's results reveal high levels of accuracy in synthesizing programs at a 66.4% rate and also demonstrate robust node and edge recognition at rates of 94.1% and 67.9%, respectively. Furthermore, detailed analyses confirm that GRCNN's synthesis capabilities are not simply a result of its node recognition skills. Additionally, we successfully trained GRCNN on a public benchmark containing 300 natural language specifications and found that it consistently performs better than a method relying on sequence-based models. The framework shows promise in addressing challenges posed by complex program synthesis tasks, offering insights into the inherent connections between flow charts and their semantic meanings. This text explores multiple reduction techniques that facilitate the connection of Earth's climate models of varying complexity, emphasizing approaches that enable thorough reduction. It distills key mathematical concepts behind each method while showcasing several benchmark climate modeling examples for illustrative purposes. The primary aim is to establish a common language and framework, thereby equipping readers with a comprehensive understanding of each method via introductory mathematical formulations and exemplary applications. Ultimately, the ultimate goal is to establish a cohesive theoretical foundation for future advancements in this field. The text is structured as a collection of interconnected chapters, each focusing on a distinct reduction methodology. Chapter 2 delves into dynamical system reductions, comprising multiple dimensionality reduction methods, including the global mode, balance operator, and balance model techniques. It also explores the connection between these approaches and the concept of effective degrees of freedom. Chapter 3 presents the multivariate statistical method, comprising principal component analysis, empirical orthogonal function analysis, and proper orthogonal decomposition, along with the relevance of these techniques in the context of multivariate dynamical systems. Chapter 4 discusses the multiscale embedding technique, which shares conceptual parallels with several other methods, including dynamic mode decomposition, empirical wavelet transform, and variational approach. Chapter 5 examines the Gaussian process regression method in the context of dynamic data reduction. Chapter 6 provides an overview of other reduction techniques, including machine learning-based approaches, ensemble techniques to generate multiple reduced models, and hybrid methods combining reduction techniques to create multi-scale reduced models. Chapter 7 offers a concise summary, prospects for future advancements in this field are explored. Chapter 8, the final chapter, presents a comprehensive modeling case study demonstrating the practical application of several reduction techniques to develop a multi-scale reduced model of the two-layer Atlantic meridional overturning circulation. The associated software codes are provided, enabling readers to replicate the results and build upon this work by utilizing widely available public software tools. Furthermore, a comprehensive list of reference works in this field is included for the convenience of the reader. It is hoped that this research will contribute positively to the community. The text is intended to be approachable by early-stage graduate students and serves as a valuable resource for established researchers, connecting recent advancements to established knowledge in this field. Key words: reduction of differential equations, model reduction, climate modeling, multiscale modeling, complex systems, data-driven modeling, machine learning, empirical results, computer-aided innovation.

Radiation oncologists' goal is to target tumors accurately while shielding surrounding vital organs, specifically the stomach and intestines, from x-ray beams. The incorporation of MR-Linac systems allows real-time tumor positioning, enabling precise radiation dosage adjustments based on shifting cell populations. The manual process of identifying these organs and calibrating X-ray beams can be lengthy, extending treatment times up to one hour a day, making automated techniques with deep learning essential. A recent paper explores the use of deep learning-based automation to streamline this complex task and provide faster access to treatment for a greater number of patients. The researchers employ a combination of MR-Linac system imaging and automatic organ detection software to reduce treatment times, ultimately replacing manual techniques. The accuracy of automatic detection is compared to conventional methods using statistical measures and 2D visualization strategies. The results show promising outcomes, with the automatic detection method surpassing human operators in accuracy and treatment duration. Specifically, the automatic detection outperformed human operators by accurately identifying vital organs in more cases, with successful 90% of treatments using automated detection, compared to 81% using human operators. The researchers acknowledge the limitations of deep learning techniques, such as relying on extensive, high-quality training data, and propose future improvements, including modifying the model to accommodate varying patient weights and shapes. The integration of this deep learning-based automation could greatly benefit radiation oncologists by providing an essential tool to streamline their treatment, ultimately improving patient outcomes. Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This data structure is commonly found in disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. Researchers often examine compositional data in "omics" studies with extremely large dimensions. The method involves calculating logratios – the logarithmic expressions of component proportions. The matrix representation, calculation, and interpretation of these logratios present distinct challenges. This tutorial demonstrates how to utilize the coordinates package in R to perform logratio analysis and addresses related interpretation issues. Visualizations are an integral component of the data analysis process, and we will utilize the coordinates package to create the necessary plots. Additionally, we will discuss the underlying linear algebra concepts that facilitate the method's computational aspects.

The exoplanet sample from CORALIE/HARPS (Mayor et al., 2011), which was discovered through Doppler radial velocity measurements, does not demonstrate the anticipated 'desert' at high masses (10-$100 M_\odot) with close orbital radii (<=3 AU), as predicted by the runaway gas accretion theory. Notably, similar findings have emerged from the MOA gravitational microlensing survey, which did not detect the 'desert' effect for planets in slightly longer-period orbits with lower-mass host stars (Suzuki et al., 2018). These studies collectively suggest that runaway accretion is unlikely a dominant process in shaping the final mass and orbital characteristics of exoplanets according to core accretion theory. Furthermore, the MOA survey's results imply that external envelope interaction with the protoplanetary disk may set an initial boundary for the 'desert' radius at approximately 3 AU, beyond which radial velocity detection does not provide further insight due to diminished sensitivity. Building upon these previous studies, which used MOA and HARPS/CORALIE datasets to investigate the 'desert', supports the notion that external envelope interaction with the protoplanetary disk effectively prevents or hinders the formation of sub-Saturn mass exoplanets within ~3 AU from the host star. These findings are consistent with the predicted timescales of disk-planet interaction, which is completed within ~5-10 million years, corresponding to the harmonic mean of the HARPS/CORALIE and MOA datasets' age. Consequently, the absence of detected 'desert' effect within ~3 AU of the HARPS/CORALIE sample may be attributed to either an insufficiently sensitive detection limit or a true lack of desert at very close orbital radii due to effective disruption by disk-planet interaction. Below 10 M_\odot, the desert at very close orbital radii is not resolved and could be obscured by a planet formation phase characterized by rapid mass loss, while above 10 M_\odot, the desert at very close orbital radii is not resolved and could be obscured by a phase of giant planet migration. These findings are subject to change if future gravitational microlensing surveys detect no 'desert' effect within ~3 AU. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently process sequential data, making them a popular choice for addressing various tasks. Despite their capabilities, previous research revealed that traditional fully-connected RNNs often struggle to learn complex tasks effectively, requiring extensive training and data. In an effort to improve performance, researchers have developed novel architectures, such as the Fixed Sparse RNN (FS-RNN), which offer better dependency management and faster computation times. Our study aims to leverage the potential of sparsity in RNNs and demonstrates that FS-RNNs can consistently outperform fully-connected RNNs across a range of cognitive and non-cognitive tasks, requiring fewer parameters and less training data to achieve comparable results. Moreover, we show that the superior performance of FS-RNNs is not limited to specific task types and can also be achieved with various fixed sparse connectivity patterns. Additionally, we provide evidence of significant time-saving benefits, with FS-RNNs often learning tasks up to 300% faster than fully-connected RNNs while requiring approximately 25% fewer parameters. The substantial gains in efficiency and performance make fixed sparse RNNs an attractive choice for developing effective learning systems. Active galactic nuclei with exceptionally powerful radio signals are among the brightest known celestial objects. Their high-energy radiation, traveling at the speed of light, affects the cosmic background radiation, causing recoil in response to anisotropic radiation pressure. As a result, these jets can potentially influence the growth of supermassive black holes in the early universe. We investigated how this interaction impacts black hole evolution and the galaxy's star formation activity using advanced computational methods. Specifically, we resolved both relativistic ejections and cosmic background radiation for a vast number of active galaxies within the cosmic environment. Our analysis includes the co-evolution of active galaxies, their surrounding star-forming galaxies, and the cosmic background radiation, taking into account the evolution of the universe since the galaxy's formation. Our study covers a vast spectrum of active galaxies, ranging from the least luminous to the most powerful, and we calculated the impact of cosmic background radiation for each. We found that high-redshift, most powerful active galaxies are subject to significant backreaction due to cosmic background radiation, potentially influencing their black hole growth and activity. However, this effect does not significantly impact their evolution compared to other factors. In contrast, lower-redshift, less powerful active galaxies are not significantly affected by cosmic background radiation. Our study indicates that high-redshift, most powerful active galaxies are not immune to the impact of cosmic background radiation, and this effect should be considered in future research on active galaxy evolution. Additionally, we found that cosmic background radiation does not significantly impact the overall active galaxy rate at the highest redshift. However, it may slightly affect rates below a certain redshift threshold. resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we developed a system
that leverages climate information tailored to each person's values. To facilitate this,
we created ClimateBase, a vast knowledge base collecting climate data from diverse sources
and standardizing it according to individual values. To exemplify its usage, we designed
a chatbot that utilizes ClimateBase to provide personalized climate information, showcasing

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction to capture relevant data which we refer to as symptom paths.
However, due to variations in doctor notation and patient demographics, the available data is restricted to a specific hospital and cannot be applied to other locations.
To address this issue, we have developed a novel domain generalization approach for extracting symptoms and their underlying causes from unstructured medical records.
This method utilizes three strategies to adapt to new domains and is evaluated using unlabeled and unlabeled data from the MIMIC-III and CheXp papers.
As a result, our proposed approach has outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods in extracting symptoms and their underlying causes, achieving higher accuracy rates on two distinct clinical datasets.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interactions and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, a comprehensive understanding of its theoretical underpinnings remains lacking. In contrast, a practical implementation of a DRL-based system for autonomous driving has been developed as a means of demonstrating its practical efficacy. In this context, a DRL approach is utilized to tackle the challenging autonomous driving task, which entails navigating through diverse roads and environmental conditions while adhering to traffic rules. In essence, autonomous driving involves achieving a balance between exploration and exploitation, with a DRL-based system necessitating design of both policy and value function networks, training algorithms, and a critique mechanism for assessing agent performance. In particular, the task of autonomous driving in urban settings presents a daunting array of challenges, including encounters with pedestrians, traffic signals, and fellow vehicles. A straightforward reinforcement learning approach might be sufficient for tasks such as speed control or lane following, but more complex urban driving scenarios require a DRL-based system capable of addressing issues like navigation at intersections, pedestrian prediction, and car movement forecasting. With deep reinforcement learning still an evolving field, numerous novel applications and challenges arise in DRL-based autonomous driving, such as coping with partially observable environments, subsampling rates, and data labeling shortages. Furthermore, the current DRL-based system is vulnerable to shortcomings such as limited generalizability, training time-consuming, and a tendency to converge at local optima. In light of these theoretical concerns, a comprehensive understanding of DRL-based autonomous driving can be attained through an examination of its underlying algorithms and a critical analysis of its practical implementation. In this regard, a detailed explanation of the DRL-based autonomous driving approach is provided, with a focus on its practical efficacy and theoretical underpinnings. Specifically, this methodology entails modeling autonomous driving as a partially observable Markov decision process and utilizing the actor-critic algorithm in conjunction with a recurrent neural network. Moreover, a critique mechanism is incorporated for assessing agent performance, with critiques offered on existing DRL-based approaches and suggestions for future enhancements. In recent years, AI networks have significantly impacted various industries, but their widespread use has been hindered by the high power consumption of these models, particularly deep neural networks. In response, researchers have turned to spiking neural networks as an energy-efficient yet effective alternative for AI computation. However, the reliability of these networks for practical use is contingent on their ability to perform tasks accurately without errors. In this study, we demonstrate the capability of a high-precision spiking network called rNN, which can achieve nearly perfect results on small-scale datasets such as the MNIST dataset. We also investigate methods to further improve the network's performance on more complex datasets while minimizing the number of neurons and connections, thus reducing the network's complexity and size. Specifically, we explore two approaches for enhancing the network's precision: utilizing non-local inhibition and incorporating synaptic plasticity into the network, and we present the results of our initial findings on the Digits dataset. Additionally, we examine the impact of various parameter settings on the network's efficiency and accuracy. Given its potential for reduced energy consumption, we believe that rNN has the potential to be an energy-efficient alternative to deep neural networks for practical use in classification and other cognitive tasks. Due to the vastness of the parameter space, this study serves as a starting point for further research aimed at fully realizing the energy-efficiency of rNN. We also make available the code and datasets used in this research at https://github.com/chris333r/rNN_for_classification for the convenience of other researchers. We plan to expand on this research by testing the network on an even broader range of datasets and exploring other variables that could further enhance the network's accuracy and efficiency. We will soon post an updated version of this research on arXiv, which will be titled "Accurate and Energy-Efficient Classification with Spiking Random Neural Networks Based on Hardware Testbeds". The updated research will present the results of our initial hypothesis that rNN can achieve comparable performance to deep neural networks while significantly reducing power consumption, and we will demonstrate the testbeds we used to test rNN on real hardware. We will also present new approaches for further improving the network's precision while minimizing energy consumption, and we expect these findings to contribute significantly to the research in spiking neural networks. In particular, we expect our research to be of interest to researchers in neuroscience, computer engineering, and computational neuroscience, and we believe that the findings of this research will enable the development of more energy-efficient neural network classifiers for real-world applications. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. Notably, our findings reveal that spin-polarized strange quark stars composed of matter with negative skewness and high magnetic field sensitivity exhibit instability. Additionally, increasing the magnetic field leads to a rise in the radius of the star; conversely, temperature's effect is negligible. Moreover, compared to unpolarized stars, those with spin polarization demonstrate a larger radius. Lastly, spin-polarized star radius is found to be sensitive to magnetic field variations. To gain deeper insight, we examined the mass-radius correlation diagram for spin-polarized strange quark star compounds with various values of the bag constant, skewness, and magnetic field sensitivity. Lastly, our research underscores the significance of considering spin polarization and external influences in evaluations of neutron star stability, as well as neutron and strange quark stars. These findings hold implications for the study of compact stars, exoplanets, and various phenomena associated with compact objects, such as giant pulses from radio pulsars, flares, and quasars, as well as gravitational waves and the detection of exotic compact stars, such as the recently observed ultralight compact star with a mass of approximately 0.076 solar mass.

The objects of this function are updated in an iterative process utilizing an obstruction matrix and a bundle of vectors that are re-orthogonalized using the Gram-Schmidt process. The matrix and vector objects are initially established through an approximation of the eigenvalue equation by a sum of linear factors. The approximation involves a convergence rate-determining parameter, adjustable in the course of computations, which is optimized to ensure the high accuracy of relevant eigenvalues and eigenvectors, along with a built-in limit on the degree of the rational function to prevent divergence. The method was tested on three nonlinear eigenvalue problems and provides accurate results within seconds. The resolution time for these problems far exceeds the capabilities of current standard methods. The presentation includes seven openly accessible experimental data sets featuring various physical, geological, and biomedical phenomena. The approach described here employs a minimal configuration of the objects of the rational function and is therefore suitable for small-scale nonlinear eigenvalue problems. Machine learning models such as random forests and AdaBoost have proven effective across many fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity, making it difficult to understand how each model component contributes to the prediction outcome. In contrast to other complex models with limited interpretability, these tree ensemble methods can be viewed as a series of simple decision trees where each node represents a feature or attribute. Inspired by the concept of attribution in neural networks, our study aims to develop a novel method called Disentangled Attribution Curve (DAC) that provides a clear understanding of which features contribute most to predictions made by individual trees, random forests, and AdaBoost models. We first derive a general approach for extracting DACs from any regression or classification tree ensemble model, before applying it to popular models such as XGBoost, LightGBM, scikit-learn's RandomForest, and AdaBoost. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in visualizing feature importance in cases where other standard approaches fail or yield inconsistent results. Furthermore, we show that DACs can be relied upon as a means of evaluating the performance of tree ensemble models. We believe that DACs offer an easily understandable and flexible alternative to traditional feature importance methods. We have made DAC available for public use through our R package named Tacotron and have documented its functionality in a companion vignette. We expect DAC to become a valuable tool in data analysis, enabling users to gain valuable insights into how each tree in random forests and AdaBoost models contributes to predictions, thereby shedding more light on data analysis results and model development. In particular, DAC can be utilized for gaining insight into (i) which attributes or regions most affect predictions, (ii) how attribute importance distributions change across different trees, random forests, and AdaBoost models, and (iii) how attribute importance is correlated in scenarios involving multiple attributes. We also envision DAC to become an essential tool for automated machine learning model development and data analysis, enabling users to gain valuable insights into how each tree in random forests and AdaBoost models contributes to predictions, and ultimately leading to better results in both domains. We believe that DAC will have far-reaching implications for many fields in practice, including genetics and epidemiology, where understanding variable importance is of great significance. We anticipate that DAC will shed new light on how variable importance is understood in other domains and that our studies will pave the way for future research in explaining Deep Learning models. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches to mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational burdens, hindering practical adoption. This paper introduces a new framework, Flatee, aimed at securing FL model exchanges using existing hardware, by leveraging Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) to establish a protected environment for both data and model interactions. TEEs, integrated into recent processors, provide a reliable safeguard against data breaches within the training process. Flatee's key innovation lies in symmetric, shielded data exchanges between training entities, facilitating general and vertical FL models across multiple data owners, by protecting both data and model exchanges. Our results show that Flatee's performance surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions, achieving a 10x speedup in training times, with only a 0.6% accuracy loss. Moreover, Flatee's improvements scale linearly with the number of collaborators, whereas existing solutions experience decreased performance with each additional participant. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops can also identify missing system calls and create a tailored filter for programs built using frameworks like Apache Kafka and Redis. Our results show that Timeloops is highly effective, with a very low error rate for predictive system calls and a high percentage of system calls that are actually authorized. Furthermore, using Timeloops on real-world applications yields significant performance enhancements and protection gains. Additionally, Timeloops' learning algorithm is extremely fast and scales well, taking only a few milliseconds to analyze applications. Overall, Timeloops offers a simple and scalable approach to creating custom system call filters for applications. Utilizing a novel random matrix theory, we establish the existence of a compressive ICA scheme with optimized cumulant matrices that facilitate reliable results with an estimated $O(N^2)$ computational complexity, significantly reducing from $O(N^3)$. Furthermore, we introduce two innovative algorithms - Comp-ICA using Givens rotation and Comp-ICA using Alternating Generalized Gradient Descent - both designed to take advantage of the properties within the cumulant matrix space and offering $O(N^2)$ complexity, surpassing conventional approaches with estimated $O(N^3)$ complexity. Our findings are substantiated by comprehensive synthetic data experiments, showcasing superior performance of our methods in terms of speed and stability, especially when data dimensions are excessively large. Ultimately, the proposed compressive ICA algorithms provide a valuable solution to the long-standing 'curse of dimensionality', effectively addressing the challenge of large data dimensions. A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional case algorithm, has been formulated and applied to one-dimensional local rings, and this concept is currently being used within Singular software implementation. Furthermore, a relevant theorem based on Greenberg's Strong Approximation theorem has also been introduced and applied to the realm of one-dimensional local rings. This has led to the development of a method to pair one-dimensional local rings with a specified property and another formula calculating the cohomological log-coniveau of an affine scheme's complement. To verify these results, a range of examples and evidence have been gathered from the intersection of one-dimensional local rings and number theory. This research will likely have further applications in the fields of algebraic geometry and number theory. 

Please note that the notion of "excellent smoothness" used in this research will be discussed in an accompanying paper.

In this research, the following terminology and concepts are used:

- Local ring with a specified property: a local ring in which the maximal ideal's image under the local map has finite cohomological log-pure dimension.

- Local map: an embedding of a one-dimensional local ring into a product of complete discrete valuation rings.

- log-pure: a concept related to the log-coniveau of sheaves on schemes, and can be calculated using the log-p Pure Sheaf on schemes with (F0, T0) topology.

- Strong Approximation: a theorem applied to Galois groups and their images within matrix groups, and has applications in number theory and algebra.

- local class field theory: a branch of number theory governing relationships between abelian Galois groups and ideals in number fields and function fields. 

- non-archimedean valuation: a type of valuation in which the value of any element is not to exceed 1. 

- real place: a mapping of a number field to the real numbers, and can be extended to local rings as the real local map. 

- sign: a property of local maps where sign equals 1 if and 1 is invertible in the local ring and sign equals 0 otherwise

This study focused on determining the general equation for calculating the potential positions of an $n$ step random walk in a $d$ dimensional space with a single unit step size, denoted as $|P_n^{d}|$. Our approach began by establishing a recursive relationship for the count formula: $|P_n^{d+1}| = |P_n^d| + 2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} |P_k^d|$. We then presented two distinct methods to derive an explicit formula for $|P_n^{d}|$, involving the application of generating functions and Faulhaber's formula. Ultimately, our findings were presented in a matrix representation as our primary theorem. Additionally, we explored the related problem of estimating the time at which a random walk first reaches a unit $L_1$-norm boundary in a $d$ dimensional space. We showed that this occurrence can be expressed using a mathematical equation and identified the associated variance via characteristic functions. These results were further quantified through the calculation of several key statistical measures, including expected value, variance, skewness, and kurtosis. Our approach once again employed the recursive relationship and generating function methodology. We provided an explicit mathematical equation for each of these statistical measures and verified our findings using numerical examples and the statistical software R. Our associated expected values were also outlined in closed-form expressions. We found that our results accurately matched those generated by the software R, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach. This study contributes to the existing body of literature on random walks by providing a comprehensive and generalizable framework for calculating key statistical measures in diverse spatial contexts. We identified several intriguing research questions and areas for further development. We proposed the creation of a related matrix theorem, the exploration of cyclic walks, and the extension of our methods to custom-weighted walks. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Furthermore, plots of thermal capacity versus temperature show a nonlinear temperature dependence at intermediate temperatures and exhibit an interesting divergence in the zero chemical potential limit. Additionally, we calculate the compressibility of doped graphene and find that its behavior near zero chemical potential is dictated by a power law for low densities of carriers and by a logarithmic law for higher densities, with the exponent controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. These results are relevant to research on graphene and similar materials known as Dirac materials, as well as other problems in theoretical physics involving massless fermions and Fermi surfaces. Specifically, the techniques used to derive the dynamic density-density correlation and key results may find applications in the study of magnetic monopoles and other topological structures.
