This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type, focusing on the properties of the weight spaces with respect to the Cartan algebra $\frak h$. It is shown that for Lie algebras of the Weyl type, a weight module that is completely $\frak h$-free can be decomposed into a direct sum of one-dimensional weight modules. Notably, this result is representative of a broader class of Lie algebras and is linked to the existence of non-trivial one-parameter groups within the algebras. An example demonstrates that the broader class of Lie algebras is not confined to those of the Weyl type; it is also seen in certain solenoidal algebras with a one-parameter group structure. Conversely, it is established that for an abelian Lie algebra $\frak g$, a module that is completely $\frak g$-free can be decomposed into a direct sum of one-dimensional weight modules. Additionally, some specific conditions under which simple weight modules are completely $\frak h$-free are outlined, along with an examination of the characteristics of the tensor product of two weight modules that are completely $\frak h$-free. Finally, certain specific types of weight modules connected to the Lie algebras of differential operators on a circle are examined, focusing on the properties of the weight spaces with respect to the Cartan algebra $\frak h$. It is shown that for these types of Lie algebras, a weight module that is completely $\frak h$-free can be decomposed into a direct sum of one-dimensional weight modules. Notably, this result is representative of the class of finite-dimensional Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Various examples are also provided to illustrate the properties and characteristics of the weight modules in question. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset. 
The objective of this project is to make a positive impact through data science by supplying
relevant stakeholders with easy-to-understand visualizations and actionable insights gained
from social media monitoring. The proposed approach can be utilized as a baseline model for
automated sentiment analysis on short texts. Moreover, it demonstrates the effectiveness
of utilizing multiple diverse datasets in training models for sentiment analysis. Lastly, it is
an illustration of the utility of data science in addressing real-world problems that are
relevant, soluble, and of practical importance. The code used for this project is openly
accessible at https://github.com/SajadSajad/LSTM_Tweet_Sentiment_Analysis. The datasets
utilized can be found at https://github.com/SajadSajad/Tweet_Sentiment_Datasets. The
pre-trained models, and the derived models, are available at https://github.com/SajadSajad/Tweet_Sentiment_Models. The sentiment analysis tool is at https://sajad-sentiment-analysis.herokuapp.com/. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role specifications as a framework for guiding the development of open-domain
dialogue systems. This framework enables the systematic incorporation of
characteristics such as persona, style, or politeness into a chat system.
Additionally, our work explores the utilization of large language models in
open-domain dialogue development, marking a departure from existing approaches
that often rely on custom training data and models. Specifically, our results
demonstrate the efficacy of leveraging a single large language model like
Lang-8 to provide a rich set of open-domain dialogue features. Detailed
evaluations and analyses are provided to substantiate these findings. Moreover,
our code and data are openly sourced on GitHub at https://github.com/HostCross/RSDODS.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game framework with a neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence system that facilitates causal reasoning. This integrated strategy involves a novel word-building language that can dynamically create semantic symbols based on common patterns in text data and extracts relevant information from messages to emerge with context-specific meanings. To efficiently convey this meaning, a neuro-symbolic causal inference engine is used to identify and prioritize relevant message elements. A signaling game model is then implemented to optimize the emergent semantic symbol's performance by controlling the transmission of context and message content through a sequential process. Simulation results demonstrate that this communication system offers a significant reduction in data transfer and latency compared to other systems. Additionally, the emergent semantic symbol is shown to provide better memory efficiency and latency performance compared to traditional symbol options. This communication system offers a versatile solution that can be applied to diverse semantic communication applications with various performance requirements. Furthermore, the word-building language and its pattern-based symbol creation approach can serve as a universal language for various semantic communication use cases. Moreover, this integrated strategy can be applied to develop various applications with distinct performance needs, and its principles can be further expanded to support novel features and functions. The Natural Language Processing area has received an increase in attention due to the data-rich environment, allowing advanced modeling capabilities. Models like Language Model, Maximum Likelihood Estimation, and N-gram Model have been widely used and studied in the past. In this research, we examine the effectiveness of combining Naive Bayes and Latent Variable models for Word Prediction, leveraging the benefits of both. The proposed model integrates the statistical power of Naive Bayes models with the explanatory capabilities of Latent Variable models. Moreover, the combined model mitigates the drawbacks of Naive Bayes models, such as overfitting, by incorporating regularization. Moreover, the model allows for the extraction of semantic characteristics from word data, providing insights into the hidden structure of the data. Experimental evaluations on various datasets demonstrate the substantial improvement in the predictive performance of the hybrid model compared to Naive Bayes models, especially in datasets with rare word occurrences. The model's semantic feature extraction capabilities facilitate the understanding of data semantics, revealing interesting results. The hybrid model, termed HB-NB-LV, has been implemented in R and made available on GitHub for public access. The model's R script can be accessed at the following URL: https://github.com/saifalipk/HB-NB-LV/tree/main/HB\_NB\_LV. Further information about the model is documented in the PDF report attached. The model has been evaluated on datasets from different domains, including English text data and Arabic text data. The results demonstrate the hybrid model's ability to improve predictive performance while uncovering hidden semantic properties and reducing overfitting. The model's combination of statistical and latent variable models capabilities makes it an innovative solution for Word Prediction. The accompanying R code and PDF documents provide a comprehensive guide to the model's implementation and use. The model's predictive performance and semantic feature extraction capabilities are showcased in Section 5 of the PDF report. In particular, the hybrid model HB-NB-LV surpasses Naive Bayes models in Word Prediction, especially for rare words. Moreover, the model's latent variables capture semantic characteristics of words, revealing common patterns and reducing overfitting. This research presents an extensive evaluation of the hybrid model's effectiveness. The model's performance and semantic feature extraction capabilities are highlighted in Figure 1 of the PDF report. In summary, the hybrid model HB-NB-LV integrates the statistical power of Naive Bayes models with the explanatory capabilities of Latent Variable models, allowing for the extraction of semantic characteristics from word data and reducing overfitting.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Recent examples include NextItemRank and NARM have demonstrated superior performance in various benchmarks. Inspired by past research in Embedding-based methods and Neural Matrix Factorization, we introduce Candidate Rank Embedding (CARE), a novel concept that enhances BSRE models such as NextItemRank and NARM by incorporating a unique position embedding. By doing so, we found that the initial and recurrent embeddings play distinct roles and found that the inclusion of position embedding facilitates the model to focus on items in different ranks and improves its item selection. Moreover, we found that the proposed CARE enhances the performance of state-of-the-art baselines in two realistic datasets. Notably, we observed that the improvement is more pronounced in the NARM model. We also studied the model's interpretability by analyzing its embedded dimensions and conducted a series of ablation studies to validate the efficacy of the model. Interestingly, we found that the model's performance declines when the item rank is unknown and the recommendations are posed as a choice rather than a sequential task. The code for this research is available on GitHub for public access.

We have thoroughly evaluated our framework by replicating and verifying three renowned laboratory test cases, which demonstrate diverse fracture patterns models. This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: first, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and second, designing efficient strategies to reassemble the swarm from any given configuration (formation restoration). A vast array of methods exists for solving the first problem, but the second remains understudied. To address this gap, this paper contributes a restored formation structure inspired by the centroid-based point set registration technique used in surveying. Upon initial formation restoration, collision avoidance reformation is tackled using a locally expanded version of the restored formation structure. Two variants of this approach – with and without momentum – are tested and compared to conventional methods, including the boid algorithm and optimal formation reformation. Comprehensive simulations in diverse environments validate the efficacy of our approach. To ensure generalizability, this research was conducted without using real-world data. A significant contribution of this work is that it addresses the underexplored area of forming restoration and provides a new framework for solving this complex problem. Moreover, it demonstrates that certain existing methods, including boid, may be inefficiently general and applicable only in specific scenarios. Additionally, it shows that temporarily dispersing the swarm may not always be necessary for collision avoidance. Finally, it highlights the potential of forming restoration structures in addressing this challenge. Code and additional information are available for reproduction of the results. Research has been conducted to identify potential areas for improvement. A key finding is that existing tools may be inadequate for solving this complex problem. New research could be conducted by considering the use of more advanced machine learning techniques for forming restoration. Another potential area for further research is the development of more sophisticated forming restoration structures, such as those inspired by the regulation of bird flocks. It could also be explored whether momentum-based reformation is applicable to other areas beyond collision avoidance. Additionally, it could be investigated whether forming restoration structures can be utilized in other domains, including but not limited to drone swarms, such as regulating the movement of swimming fish. It is hypothesized that boid and other existing methods may be inadequate for solving this problem because they are not aware of their surroundings. New research could be conducted by utilizing data from environmental studies using techniques such as reinforcement learning to inform this problem. Also, it could be explored through protein structure prediction using structures like Protean Form. In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints. Our study contributes to expanding the applicability of optimal control principles for stochastic differential equations with an emphasis on the use of fractional Brownian motion, marking a significant advancement in this field. Due to the complexity of fractional Brownian motion, our investigation is primarily based on existing research and does not aim to provide novel probabilistic inequalities or measure-theoretic results. Nevertheless, this contribution maintains the necessary level of detail and referential consistency with existing literature, including books by Nualart, Liang and Li, and Carmona, Driver, and Touzi. Furthermore, the appendix contains supplementary information, including a brief overview of the fractional White noise calculus, Cutraru and Scheinkmann's result on differentiating functions of measures, and an application of the maximum principle to a delayed consumption optimization problem, which involves solving a system of stochastic Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations. These supplementary materials ensure the paper remains self-contained and facilitates the seamless integration of the presented results into the existing research paradigm. Lastly, our study is significant because it enables the optimal control of delayed linear-quadratic problems, which can be critically interpreted as modeling the optimal behavior of delay-constrained agents under the presence of time-fractals. This represents a significant advancement over the traditional Markovian paradigm, which would otherwise fail to deliver valid solutions due to the issue's inherent computationally hardness. This study is expected to contribute to various real-world problems, such as controlling delayed linear-quadratic problems, consumption optimization, and applications in finance and biology. In particular, the model of consumption optimization from a cash flow, which is examined in Section 5, has significant implications in modeling an farmer's behavior, who may experience delays in receiving news about crop yields. Similarly, linear-quadratic problems under delay constraints offer a suitable model for tuning a linear system with time-fractals, which is a common occurrence in various technological contexts. We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking two well-known limit cases, each associated with the absence or presence of elliptic parameters. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant lens index problems. This involves employing a novel approach to normalize eigenfunction templates, which requires precise diophantine analysis. As a result, we gain access to the spectral structure, allowing for the study of spectral phases and zeta function regularization in the context of elliptic parameters. Moreover, we've identified a distinct regime in parameter space where the Dirac operator's spectrum exhibits a non-self-adjoint zero-energy mode, characterized by a set of necessary and sufficient conditions, highly sensitive to the choice of elliptic parameters. This zero-energy mode is associated with a second-order difference equation with piecewise-constant coefficients, which can be generalized to the absence of elliptic parameters, showcasing intriguing behaviors. Additionally, we've derived key applications regarding the operator's transmission and reflection properties within a scattering theory framework based on imaginary time techniques. These findings generalize known results from the uncoupled case to the coupled case, specifically regarding transmission at zero energy and the entire spectrum in the absence of elliptic parameters. Lastly, we've constructed three-dimensional finite-band potential models, each corresponding to a non-self-adjoint Dirac operator in three-dimensional spaces (in the absence of elliptic parameters) or corresponding to elliptic parameters, which can be obtained through the projection of four-dimensional finite-band potentials onto a three-dimensional subspace. These models allow for the extension of our analysis to a three-dimensional setting. To showcase the diversity of our models, we've provided two concrete examples - a Dirac operator in a three-dimensional compact domain with a non-self-adjoint zero-energy spectrum and a Dirac operator in a three-dimensional manifold with an intrinsic elliptic parameter. This article presents a comprehensive summary of our recent research outcomes. For additional details, we refer the interested reader to our previous publications. RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative analytical framework for 2-Tier heterogeneous vehicular networks incorporating RSUs, vehicle relays, and vehicle UEs. Building on this model, we analyze outperforming relaying techniques, optimize user speeds, develop an innovative relay placement method, and explore the impact of parameter variation on the network. Our results show that by utilizing vehicle relays, the network can overcome poor signal weakness and increase coverage range, ultimately reducing the network's access latency and increasing its overall capacity. Moreover, by targeting the most disadvantaged users with relay assistance, the network can further increase these users' overall data transfer rates. These outstanding features make vehicular networks an extremely appealing option. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/hadijolodar/VANET-phd.git. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics. However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. One key factor has enabled other information platforms to surpass Wikipedia's scope and quality: the ability to label content electronically. In contrast, Wikipedia relies on manually collected data, which hampers its growth and development in this regard. This study explores the possibility of using Wikipedia's rich data on editing behaviors to label content electronically. By analyzing patterns in revision histories, we develop methods to identify patterns characterizing high and low quality articles. Leveraging these patterns, we show that Wikipedia's existing data can be employed to train machine learning models that predict high quality articles with 90% accuracy using features based on the distribution of editing behaviors. Furthermore, pre-labeled articles can be used to update the model through transfer learning, enhancing its performance and confirming that editing behaviors hold the key to differentiating high and low quality articles. Finally, this study outlines a plan for automatically labeling articles across the entire knowledge base, potentially freeing up editors to concentrate on articles that need in-depth updates and improvements. Overall, this research demonstrates how Wikipedia can harness its data on editing behaviors to develop new approaches to content evaluation and curation. It is now positioned to explore automatic labeling, a long-term goal that aligns with the knowledge base's established values, including reliance on human judgment and article neutrality. In the short term, this study is expected to improve data collection methods, including algorithms already in use, by employing Wikipedia's rich data in a more targeted manner. In the intermediate term, this research is anticipated to lead to the development of new tools and interfaces enabling editors to work more efficiently and effectively. Specifically, patterns in revision histories can be leveraged to provide quantitative data on article quality, enabling editors to make data-driven decisions in article discussions and umbrella tasks. Moreover, data collection tools can be informed by analysis of editing behaviors, thereby incorporating the perspectives and experiences of editors. Ultimately, this research is expected to contribute to the ongoing evolution of the knowledge base into a more dynamic, living platform that is even more reliable and useful to readers and visitors. In particular, patterns in revision histories can be used to surface articles that require in-depth updates and improvements, including those currently labeled as low quality. Furthermore, editors can utilize analysis of these patterns to inform articles in progress and enhance their content. By labeling articles electronically, Wikipedia can accelerate its growth and development

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its decision boundary and its nearest neighbor class, which is shown to be linked to the corresponding softmax model's entropy. This concept is extended to non-parametric models, where the distance between the original data and its corresponding softmax model is estimated through support vector machines. This study proposes a new distance metric for non-parametric models, which is shown to be connected to the model's loss function. Two main techniques are introduced to leverage this connection: (1) extracting the original data from the network's boundary points and (2) using query adversarial networks to create new data classes. These methods are further tested for their efficiency in handling limited training data and for their compatibility with pseudo-labeling. The study evaluates the effectiveness of these methods in zero-shot knowledge distillation and shows that it outperforms other current knowledge distillation methods. The source code for this research study is available at: https://github.com/0bue/decisions-based-kd. Two datasets are used in this research: CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet. The study tests its methods on different network architectures, including the mobileNetV2, ResNet-18, SeNet-44, DenseNet-121, and LeNet1 networks. The research study also assesses its methods on data that has been encrypted using advanced encryption methods, such as PATE. The study trains models under three different scenarios: full training, semi-supervised training, and zero-shot training. The study's techniques for knowledge distillation are highly adaptable and can be applied across a wide range of networks and training scenarios. Furthermore, we effectively translate geometric concepts such as free differential actions, symplectic moments, and Poisson actions into algebraic terms, ultimately demonstrating the equivalence of the noncommutative torus with a discrete group $\Gamma$ to a commutative torus with nontrivial discrete $\Gamma$-action. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced by learning from expert guidance, yet obtaining expert demonstrations is often costly and impractical. This research proposes a novel method, called conditional imitation learning, that enables the learning of expert policies without requiring actual demonstrations. We identify an implicit set of feasible actions taken by experts, making the learning process possible under a restricted yet achievable framework. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing it favorably to established models in a simulated robotic task. Specifically, we show that our conditional imitation learning method enables the transfer of policies across diverse states and observation spaces, surpassing the performance of traditional imitation learning, which is confined to replicating demonstrated trajectories. With the ability to learn from implicit expert input, our method holds significant potential for improving systems that interact with expert feedback in the form of binary evaluations or ranking lists. This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the assumption that annotated information is available for several frames. We have developed an algorithm that uses a novel network to create a continuous, detailed reconstruction of hand-object interactions throughout a sequence of frames. This reconstruction is possible thanks to a novel variant of the VAE that incorporates the continuity of temporal sequences and spatial continuity in RGB cameras, combined with spatial invariant information from depth sensors, all while maintaining efficient inference capabilities. Additionally, we have developed a metric to evaluate the accuracy of 3D hand pose estimation even in the absence of reliable ground truth information for challenging sequences involving complex hand gestures. This metric demonstrates the superior performance of our algorithm over alternative approaches that rely solely on kinematics and object relationships in frequent hand interaction scenarios. Finally, our algorithm's superior reconstruction performance has been confirmed through evaluations of both qualitative and quantitative nature. This confirmation is a direct result of our algorithm's ability to produce accurate continuous reconstructions of hand-object interactions, demonstrating generalizability on novel unseen datasets and scenarios, and providing clear and interpretable visual representations of its outputs. The source code for this project has been made publicly available at https://github.com/epaoule/hand_object_interactions. A novel, markerless system utilizes real-world depth camera data and robot-specific information to calculate the positions and orientations of the end-effector and key interactive points without relying on external markers. A training-friendly, probabilistic method generates accurate 3D object pose estimates by analyzing depth images in the context of pre-established object models. Meanwhile, a novel interactive sampling framework efficiently identifies and prioritizes relevant historical robot pose data for calibration, and a calibration algorithm utilizes these poses to calculate accurate transformation matrices between the robot coordinate system and the original object mesh coordinates. Our system was successfully tested using a Universal Robots arm and a depth camera on various objects, achieving average pose estimation errors of approximately 2cm and achieving accurate calibration with as few as three interactive points. All generated code can be accessed at https://github.com/brl-bots/ml-robot-calibration. A pre-trained model can be downloaded at https://brl-bots.github.io/ml-robot-calibration/model.zip. Essential hardware can be sourced through Neuron Robotics at https://neuron-robotics.com. Our work aims to bridge the gap between raw sensor data and established collision-avoidance systems, enabling accurate and marker-less collision avoidance, interaction, and more. In the future, we plan to integrate this system with existing Braintree Lab Robot platforms and further expand to integrate with other popular robot systems, ultimately facilitating a wide range of robot-based research across various domains. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2]. Examples illustrate the diversity of k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities, demonstrating that certain key characteristics do not apply to k-Du Bois singularities of codimension two. A new classification of k-Du Bois singularities for hypersurfaces in dimensions two and three has been developed, incorporating an alternative proof of the k-rationality criterion in dimension three, a result previously established by [FL2]. This work further extends k-rationality criteria in dimension three to singularities of T*P^1 holomorphic projections. Additionally, a classification of k-Du Bois singularities for surfaces with Q-Cartier divisor line bundles is presented. This includes an identification of the k-rational singularities, a 1-dimensional generalization of [FL2]'s findings, and a new proof that k-rationality in dimension two implies vanishing Chow groups in degree two. Examples illustrate that this implication may not hold universally. This research further delves into the properties of k-Du Bois singularities for surfaces with Q-divisor line bundles, demonstrating that vanishing Chow groups exhibit certain duality properties and that k-rational singularities can be characterized by vanishing cycles. Specifically, for surfaces with Q-divisor line bundles, k-rational singularities are shown to be equivalent to singularities with vanishing middle cohomology groups. We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance measurements and quantum Monte Carlo simulations using the experimentally determined parameters are employed to determine the critical parameters of the system. The anisotropy of the critical temperatures is found to be proportional to the corresponding exchange couplings, thereby validating the BKT theory's predictions. This research presents a novel way to manipulate the critical properties of a system using external field-induced anisotropy, thereby showing the potential of BKT physics in producing an observable effect in a near future quantum device. Lastly, the research outlines the necessary requirements for achieving this effect, specifically a moderate exchange coupling and a significant anisotropic factor. Given the aforementioned conditions, a similar BKT effect could potentially be observed in the spin system of a carbon nanocone, which consists of a nearly isotropic 3D BKT system with a large exchange coupling of around 9 Kelvin and strong anisotropy due to field-induced shape effects. However, the 3D BKT regime in carbon nanocones might be obscured by large impurity-induced spin freeze-out effects, which would require cooling to a superconducting state below around 7 Kelvin to overcome. Therefore, the exchange of variables between the two systems presented in this research offers new avenues for exploring BKT physics in a wide array of quantum devices and materials. Lastly, achieving the best possible device performance would depend on exchanging the 3D BKT regime in carbon nanocones, where the critical temperatures would be determined by the exchange coupling and anisotropic factor of the respective spin system. The latter would result in a critical temperature of around 6.4 Kelvin for carbon nanocones. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant dataset consisting of nearly 600,000 coeval stars. Utilizing an extragalactic environment represented by $K$2, scientists analyzed the stellar objects across a magnitude range of 11.1 < $g$ < 18.2. Notably, about 70% of these stellar objects are dual-line objects, with a significant 50% belonging to A-F spectral types. This data also helped scientists create atmospheric radial velocity templates, which in turn enabled them to assess radial velocity measurement precision and signal-to-noise ratio. Ultimately, this research laid the groundwork for radial velocity follow-up studies on a large, diverse population of stars. This includes 1787 blue large linear stars and 1078 binary star candidates. Additionally, through a low-resolution spectroscopic survey with 3700 Angstroms coverage, scientists identified approximately 8000 narrow-line active stars, utilizing the DASH method which is limited to lines with 600 Angstroms coverage. Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to these faults to create high-throughput random numbers. We validate the practicality of TuRaN through SPICE simulations on diverse process nodes and assess its reliability through real-world experiments conducted on two commercial FPGA boards. Furthermore, we demonstrate the high quality of the random numbers produced by TuRaN using the NIST standard randomness tests and note its exceptional performance with respect to throughput, energy consumption, and latency. Additionally, we show that TuRaN's undervolting feature yields significant reductions in both the thermal voltage and the SRAM failure rate. The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context. Following the established procedure for deriving the sign factor from the angular momentum properties for any spin value, we demonstrate that the parity operator's contribution to the sign factor is significant, revealing that the permutation sign is directly linked to the wavefunction's parity for any spin type. Consequently, the Pauli exclusion principle can be attributed to the exclusion of states with odd parity for bosons. Moreover, fermions are distinguished by their ability to occupy states with either even or odd parity, whereas fermions in one-dimensional systems exhibit an effective exclusion of states with odd parity due to constraints imposed by the momentum operator's properties. Furthermore, bosons in one-dimensional systems are also restricted to occupying states with even parity, resulting in an effective exclusion of states with odd parity. Lastly, we establish the conditions under which a particular angular momentum's properties can give rise to particle exchange statistics, thereby providing a non-relativistic explanation for the spin-statistics connection. Additionally, the connection between the spin and wavefunction exchange statistics can be exemplified through the harmonic oscillator, harmonic oscillator with a rotating erratic force, and the Rydberg oscillator models. Ultimately, this research not only reinterprets the non-relativistic spin-statistics theorem but also sheds light on the origin of the relativistic spin-statistics theorem, which is known as Fermi-Dirac, Pauli-Dirac, and Bose-Einstein parity condition. Finally, we have also reinterpreted the Heisenberg's uncertainty principle in a similar manner. Following our research method, which connects the properties of an operator with its corresponding system's physical properties, we have also obtained a fresh interpretation of the Heisenberg's uncertainty principle in a 3D system, which had been previously analyzed using a different connectedness approach in a previous publication by one of the co-authors. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the properties of wavefunction exchange statistics, spin, and particle statistics can be accounted for by the properties of a particular system's underlying symmetry, which provides a concrete connection between these properties and the corresponding system's angular momentum properties. We have developed a strategy to convert linear algebra techniques used for spanning set construction and dimension reduction into Fourier analysis methods across a variety of function spaces. Specifically, we've identified a method to obtain an $\varepsilon$-isometric dimension reduction for all subspaces of $\ell_p$ (where $p \in (1,\infty)$) by employing random matrix construction, and this construction can be adapted for specific matrix forms with potential speedup and tailored designs achieved through Fourier analysis. Our construction also enables near-minimal dimension reduction for incompressible subsets of $\ell_p$. Furthermore, we've established a general framework for dimension reduction that can be applied to a broad class of function spaces, specifically those with certain decay properties in their Fourier measures. This framework allows for the application of linear algebra techniques to such diverse spaces, and we've verified its effectiveness for several notable spaces, including $L_p$ (for $p \in (1,\infty)$) and $\ell_p$ (for $p \in (0,\infty)$), with the latter resulting in what we believe to be the first known dimension reduction results for $L_p$ and $\ell_p$. Our methods also yield near-minimal dimension reduction for certain pattern learning tasks, such as learning periodic functions and learning functions with narrow supports within these spaces. These results are currently known to hold for $p \in (1,2]$, and we are currently exploring extensions to $p \in (0,1)$, with the latter potentially yielding novel dimension reduction results for trigonometric polynomials. Our work on dimension reduction is also yielding new insights into the $\ell_p$-$\ell_q$ net division points and the location of the $\ell_p$-hardness instances, with these insights potentially holding more broadly across the function space landscape. We've established new upper bounds on the $\ell_p$-$\ell_q$ net division points for $p \neq 2$, and our work has led to a discovery of the location of the $\ell_p$-hardness instances, confirming long-held conjectures and potential insights into the nature of $\ell_p$ and $\ell_q$. Our results also hold potential for applications in computer science, such as learning periodic functions and learning functions with narrow supports, and we've verified the efficacy of these results through testing. We've found that our dimension reduction methods can be applied successfully to these learning tasks. We've also demonstrated the comparative superiority of our methods over existing techniques in these areas

We envision a future where cooperative modeling enables researchers to simulate important biological events, such as neuronal activity, head injuries, and brain injuries, with great potential for advancing both neuroscience and medicine. Our research proposes a novel method to enhance the security of QKD systems using a complex quantum system that randomly varies the phase of light emissions. This novel approach incorporates a linear interferometer with a beam splitter to divide light into two paths, then introduces randomness into the phase shift of one path using a quantum tool, effectively creating a complex quantum system. Our research also explores how a specific quantitative measure affects the accuracy of quantum key distribution when using a complex quantum system with partial phase randomization. Recent studies have highlighted the effectiveness of in-context learning methods using large language models as a viable option for performing tasks. Our research aims to expand on this by investigating how varying training corpora affect the capabilities of LLMs in a Russian setting. We tested six different training corpora, including pairs of parallel and non-parallel corpora derived from different data sources, and assessed their impact on six diverse NLP tasks. Our findings indicate that in-context learning can be successfully applied to a range of tasks, and also reveal a notable disparity in performance brought about by differences in the training corpora. One particular corpus based on Wikipedia data yielded the best results across all examined tasks, while another corpus based on online forums demonstrated poor performance and proved to be essentially useless in a few of the evaluated tasks. Our study demonstrates the importance of considering the origin and characteristics of training data on the development of LLMs. We have made our code and Russian LLMs based on the GPT-3 structure available for public access at github.com/philkon/lm-rus. Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about how other, isolated clouds grow over time. To address this lack of understanding, we developed a mesh-based code for magnetohydrodynamics and used it to simulate the development of individual clouds in a galaxy cluster environment. Our model accounts for the effects of radiative cooling, thermal conduction, and magnetic field instability. Through these simulations, we found that growth rates and break-up patterns vary depending on cloud properties, its surrounding environment, and the strength of magnetic fields. Clouds that cool at an accelerated rate break apart more easily, while those surrounded by strong magnetic fields tend to grow more slowly. To standardize our results, we introduced a dimensionless break-up parameter and conducted a comprehensive analysis of how other factors influence it. Ultimately, our model provides a framework for further studies of galaxy cluster evolution. Additionally, we observed that growth rates and break-up patterns show considerable variation even within a single galaxy cluster, mirroring real-life observations. Our model can now be used to interpret existing data and further research is needed to validate our findings. Our code is available at https://github.com/eduardo-jimenez/clockcode. The proposed framework is implemented and tested in a 5G cellular network using a flexible and extensible simulation platform that models sustainable mobile networks. The results show that the proposed framework reduces the network's energy consumption and latency, outperforming existing resource allocation methods. The exemplary use case involves a latency-sensitive application scenario, but the framework can be easily adapted to accommodate a variety of other use cases. The proposed framework can also be scaled up for use in larger networks by adjusting the queue and incorporating a distributed control system that allows different components of the network to communicate with each other. The main limitations of the proposed framework are its limited support for latency-uncritical applications and the potential for congestion in heavily used networks, which could be addressed through further development and optimization. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD) algorithm. Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our method achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the performance capabilities of DR-DSGD. Additionally, a generalization of our approach, encompassing a broader family of regularization techniques, is explored and proposed. This generalized method exhibits a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT}\right)$. These novel contributions fill significant gaps in the literature by developing robust decentralized algorithms for distributionally robust learning problems over networks. Specifically, as far as we are aware, this is the first paper to address the distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized contexts, outpacing the current state of the art in the literature. Detailed mathematical derivations and key algorithmic steps are provided in the appendix. Additionally, we have made the code available for public access. To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems, effectively allowing for improved motion control even under dynamic conditions. The effectiveness of this innovative approach is showcased through simulation-based testing of a precise moving-magnet planar actuator, known to experience variations based on position during actuation and sensing. This particular component is a key element in the construction of high-precision motion platforms. By applying the LPV sequential loop closing technique, we achieve a substantial enhancement in closed-loop performance, with nearly undetectable position errors under dynamic conditions, in direct contrast to more conventional control strategies that may introduce noticeable position errors. This remarkable advancement in motion control even enables the attainment of sub-nanometer-level precision during actuation-driven movements. Furthermore, the method exhibits increased robustness and can easily be implemented in software compared to other solutions. This study presents an innovative approach to addressing performance limitations in high-precision motion systems. The proposed LPV-SLC strategy is evaluated using a moving-magnet actuator in a motion platform setup to demonstrate its potential to revolutionize high-precision automation equipment. This technique could potentially be applied in various other systems with similar positional dependencies. By achieving superior performance with minimal actuation forces, this method holds great promise for enhancing the accuracy of motion platforms, even in the presence of dynamic conditions. We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Traditional registration methods often struggle with incomplete scenes, as they rely heavily on surface normal information that can be distorted easily. In contrast, PRNet employs a self-supervised learning approach, focusing solely on invariant features derived from input data. By disregarding normals altogether, PRNet is well-suited for inliers with noisy or indeterminate surface normals, as well as outliers. In experiments, PRNet consistently outperforms existing methods on various datasets, both synthetic and real-world, as evidenced by lower displacement errors in datasets SPPNet, OP, and OWL. Furthermore, PRNet demonstrates superior robustness against challenging factors such as increasing partiality, increased noise levels, and differing scene statistics. In applications, PRNet exhibits superior performance in 3D scene understanding and downstream tasks, such as estimating object pose, detecting partial copies, and segmenting point cloud instances. Instead of directly searching for supersymmetry, this study explores various particle collider options to investigate the degradation of electroweak symmetry, a hallmark of supersymmetry, using theoretical and experimental criteria. A comprehensive landscape of collider possibilities is mapped out, starting from current and planned pion colliders like CLIC, to hypothetical future colliders using new Higgs factories, like a 100 TeV proton collider or a compact muon collider. A crucial threshold at which the SM becomes unstable is identified through theoretical instability thresholds and found to require $\sqrt{s} \geq 34$ TeV for new heavy particles. This study demonstrates that a Higgs factory followed by a compact muon collider can efficiently pinpoint this threshold, presenting a cost-effective and feasible option. Furthermore, pion colliders are found to effectively explore the stability of the SM with advantages in cost and feasibility. An optimal approach is suggested, starting with a low-energy Higgs factory (\$20 billion) to eliminate unstable scenarios, followed by a \$\sim\$\$20 billion compact muon collider to confirm the stability of the SM, thereby addressing the critical issue of supersymmetry-related baryon number dark matter. An alternative approach involves a high-energy Higgs factory (\$70-\\$100 billion) that can serve the purpose of a compact muon collider, yielding similar outcomes. Ultimately, this study proposes that a 100 TeV proton collider should be built only if it can significantly advance our understanding of quantum gravity or other non-SM phenomena. Otherwise, it would represent an excessively costly endeavor. Additionally, this study presents conceptual designs for new colliders using either electron beams or proton beams, providing quantitative estimates for construction, operation, and other related costs. It also speculates on the potential for innovative new ideas and technologies to emerge from this study, such as the potential for a compact proton collider or electron collider with immense potential in studying dark matter and related baryon number symmetry. Finally, this study notes that even in a scenario without supersymmetry, where the SM is largely self-consistent, it is shown that various theoretical approaches to extending the SM will inevitably involve $\mathcal{O}(100\text{ TeV})$ mass scales even if dark matter is not related to supersymmetry. Therefore, particle colliders remain a vital tool for investigating fundamental theories of nature for many years to come. Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without labeled data is a difficult task that requires considerable time and effort in medical settings. Deep-learning based solutions that adapt segmentation models from annotated data of one modality to another have been explored previously. However, strong pair-wise alignments between different modalities are typically required, which can be impractical due to imaging discrepancies and variations in image appearance. In the absence of labels, domain adaptation becomes even more challenging, especially in complex medical image data with diverse appearances and pathological variations. This research presents a novel cyclic segmentation generative adversarial network (CS-GAN) that enables seamless segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without labeled data. The framework comprises two segmentation networks that perform bidirectional image segmentation, connected by two domain converters that facilitate pairwise domain adaptation through adversarial minimization. Through cyclic training, the segmentation networks learn to perform domain-agnostic segmentations that are invariant to imaging modalities and help to alleviate the influence of domain discrepancies. Experimental evaluations on three different imaging modalities demonstrate that the proposed CS-GAN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of dice score. For example, it achieves a 85.73% dice score for segmenting cardiac MRI images, significantly outperforming the best available method with a 75.19% dice score. The framework's effectiveness in performing domain-agnostic segmentations makes it suitable for a range of medical imaging applications where labels are scarce or non-existent. Additionally, the open-source code for CS-GAN has been made available for public use at a specified repository. Future research can build upon this framework by incorporating it to other deep learning methods for multiple tasks such as organ pose estimation and full-body segmentation. Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
expectation maximization, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating
future feature predictions and anticipated actions. By using parameter sharing,
Feature Mapping RNN reduces model complexity and reduces the scope of distributional
assumptions required to learn future states from past states. The use of RBF kernels
enables learning of non-linear representations using a nonlinear feature mapping.
Optimization is achieved through EM-based backpropagation, which maintains the
differentiability of model predictions. In action anticipation tasks, our model
outperforms various benchmark methods, including state-of-the-art RNN and generative
model-based approaches, as evidenced in multiple datasets. Furthermore, our
model demonstrates efficient resource usage and satisfies key fundamental criteria.

used to compare our approach with 18 strong baselines. 

In terms of future research, we suggest exploring the integration of our feature
prediction model with other action prediction methods. Additionally, we propose
developing a multi-step feature prediction model that leverages the richness of
described future states. Lastly, we suggest investigating the potential of our
feature mapping strategy in other areas of computer vision and natural language
processing. 

In conclusion, our proposed Feature Mapping RNN architecture shares parameters to
reduce model complexity and uses RBF kernels to generate nonlinear feature
representations, all while using EM-based backpropagation for optimization. The
model has achieved superior performance in various action anticipation tasks and
satisfies key fundamental criteria. Moreover, our approach has efficiently used model

Remarkable solar flare spectra, with intense broadband radiation, occur when a hot coronal ejection interacts with the chromosphere, producing bright UV and white-light flashes. Similar flares have been observed recently on close-by stars using Kepler space telescope and MOST ground-based telescopes. Research has shown that these stellar flares produce extreme amounts of energy in the near-UV and visible light. Studying these events helps us better understand photoionization and radiative feedback effects in the chromospheres of low-mass stars. We have developed a theoretical model for the 1985 April 12 great flare of AD Leo by combining observations from the IUE satellite with laboratory-based transition arrays. Our approach utilizes a multi-component model that includes non-LTE calculations for hydrogen, helium, metal recombination lines, and a dust model that forms in the chromosphere and photosphere. We have obtained satisfactory agreement between our model and observations in the far-UV to red parts of the spectrum. Our simulation shows that the energy distribution of the flare's continuum is similar to that of a blackbody with a high temperature (around 16,000 K), which is consistent with the temperatures of low-mass stars in the chromosphere. We have found that the radiative cooling of the gas is followed by a rapid drop in density to around 10^12 cm^-3 in the upper atmosphere of AD Leo. Our model also predicts that the spectral features of the flare are broadened by dynamic line broadening, which is caused by rapidly moving gas in the chromosphere and photosphere. We have found that the spectral features of the flare are best explained by using the multi-component model and that simple plasma models are not sufficient to explain the complex spectral features of the flare. Our simulation shows that the energy deposition of the flare's energy is concentrated in the near-UV and it is consistent with the picture of a hot ejection interacting with the chromosphere and photosphere. We have found that the time-dependent recombination rates of metal ions are not sufficient to explain the complex spectral features of the flare and that the dust model is essential in modeling the spectral features of the flare in the red part of the spectrum. Our simulation shows that the time it takes for the gas to reach its maximum expansion is longer than 500 seconds, which is consistent with the observation of the long duration of the flare in the white light. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions. The analysis also yields information about the Bettti numbers of these manifolds. Furthermore, we prove that an instanton is uniquely definable by its connection on a nearly G2-manifold if specific conditions are met. These findings build upon the findings of [arXiv:2101.11244], and generalize previously established results of [arXiv:1808.06883] on the deformation theory of instantons on complex manifolds. The method also generalizes the deformation theory of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds, previously established in [arXiv:2008.06465]. The present work draws upon the concepts and techniques developed in [arXiv:1808.06883], as well as in [arXiv:1812.03903], [arXiv:2008.06465], sharing similarities with [arXiv:2101.11244] in the realm of deformation theory. The deformation theory of instantons on almost $\mathrm{G}_2$-manifolds is also a key area of consideration. The connection between Dirac operators and spinors is crucial to the deformation theory, as it allows for the formulation of the deformation theory through the use of elliptic operators and index theory. The results presented establish a general framework that can be applied to specific nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-manifolds, providing insights into the deformation space and its relation to the kernel of an elliptic operator. The findings can also be utilized to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on a specific four-dimensional normal homogeneous $\mathrm{G}_2$-manifold, and in doing so yield information about the Bettti numbers of this particular manifold. The analysis also proves that an instanton is uniquely definable by its connection on a specific nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-manifold if specific conditions are met

Such operators are shown to be C-normal if and only if certain conditions related to linear fractional expressions are met. These conditions include the preservation of holomorphic functions, particularly those in the Hardy space $H^2$, under these operator mappings. Our study also establishes sufficient conditions for these operators to satisfy the preservation of holomorphic functions in $H^2$, which extends existing research on $T$-normal operators. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains such as vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulation by adversarial attacks. Researchers have primarily focused on craftings attacks to disable these models, developing various techniques including gradient-based approaches and unsupervised methods utilising OOD data. Despite these efforts, existing attacks are primarily aimed at compromising models in general cases, not specifically tailored to the unique characteristics of point cloud models. This paper presents a novel gradient-based attack tailored to exploiting the 3D spatial relationships within point cloud data. The proposed attack leverages an ensemble of adjacent geometric transformations, incorporating a novel criterion to measure model uncertainty in 3D spatial configurations. The results show that this attack surpasses current methods in models trained on various benchmark datasets. Moreover, we examine the potential for this attack to be scaled up in a real-world setting involving vehicle navigation. The code for this attack is available at https://github.com/Azahrayeh/3D-Adversarial-Point-Cloud.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new investigation adopts a distinct approach, focusing on analyzing changes in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram resulting from entangled photon interaction. Utilizing Rhodamine B solution as a model nonlinear material exposed to 800 nm photons generated through type-II spontaneous parametric down conversion, researchers have explored conditions facilitating detection of HOM interferogram visibility modifications. A detailed model describing electron-hole pair excitation based on a single-electron picture is presented, enabling the quantification of entangled two-photon absorption cross-sections. Initial findings indicate the potential for enhanced quantum key distribution applications by leveraging entangled two-photon absorption in Rhodamine B, despite facing challenges arising from the material's photovoltaic effects and excited electron-hole pairs coherently interacting with the photon field. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed by G\"ottsche and the second author, using a moduli space of T-connections on vector bundles, is equivalent to the T-equivariant cohomology theory formed from the T-localization of the T-equivariant cohomology of the Grassmannian of 1-dimensional subspaces in V. Notably, this Grassmannian's T-equivariant cohomology is computed in G\"ottsche and the second author's work, and we show that this theory can be reduced to provide a direct computation of the T-equivariant cohomology of the complex projective space CP(V). This result includes a formula for the T-equivariant cohomology ring of CP(V) in terms of the representation V. This complements a longstanding conjecture of Christiane Nussbaum, concerning the ungraded rational T-equivariant cohomology of CP(V), which states it is isomorphic to the T-equivariant cohomology of the form class space of V. This conjecture is proven to be true in this context. validating existing knowledge bases and discovering missing knowledge. Since
most existing KGC methods are designed for static graphs, researchers have
developed model adaptations for temporal graphs. Nevertheless, the literature
still lacks a unifying framework for understanding the impact of time constraints
on representation learning. Furthermore, low-rank representations are incapable
of capturing time-dependent relationships, and model-agnostic representations
fail to leverage model-specific advancements. To address these limitations, we
propose a new low-rank and model-agnostic representation learning method for
temporal entities and time-dependent edges, and we show that our method can be
efficiently implemented using a tensor factorization approach. We also provide
evidence that our low-rank time edge representation is more effective than the
current state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, we introduce a novel evaluation
metric for assessing knowledge graph temporal validity, and we conduct an
extensive ablation study to examine the effect of time constraints on knowledge
graph validity and completion performance. Our experimental results demonstrate
that our low-rank and model-agnostic representation learning method achieves the
best performance in knowledge graph validity and completion across a range of
evaluation metrics. The source code for our approach is available at

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by objects on hard surfaces is generally considered uninteresting and undesired. Current methods either disregard this type of sound or use harsh, unrealistic techniques to generate it. This paper presents a new approach that utilizes a combination of physical simulations and statistical analysis to produce a library of high-quality sounds suitable for percussion instrument design. A simulation protocol is established to generate a compact set of sounds that effectively capture the acoustic properties of hard surfaces, which can then be used for sound synthesis. A critical evaluation of this method is also provided, highlighting its benefits and limitations compared to existing techniques. Furthermore, the development of a novel instrument is presented that combines the generated sound library with a intuitive gestural interface inspired by the Stuart drum, enabling musicians to create dynamic performances that integrate human input with synthesized sounds. The resulting sounds and techniques presented in this paper can facilitate the production of more authentic and detailed sounds in the studio, while also offering a unique creative potential for instrumental improvisation. With this approach, producers can push the boundaries of drum sounds, creating more natural and complex rhythms that were previously impossible to achieve. Additionally, musicians can explore new horizons in percussion music by utilizing the intricate textures and timbres produced by this method. Relevant data and software resources are available at https://i6.unicamp.br/~mcabral/LabAudio/Resources/GroundSound/. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure that the system's performance in the event of a failure does not compromise safe driving procedures. Traditional methods of testing, limited in scope and depth, can be overcome by model checking, a more comprehensive technique. Many scholars, such as Blay, have approached this topic by comparing Leibniz's ideas to contemporary views on limits and as a formalized system respectively.  This paper, in contrast, proposes an alternative method which highlights the common thread among these perspectives - that Leibniz's methodology can be consistently represented within a specific theoretical structure, regardless of the specific framework used (Augustin-Leroux's account is similarly based on this observation).  We examine the core procedures of Leibnizian differential calculus, emphasizing the gradual change links and the transfer principle in relation to a real variable x.  Our analysis is compared to three distinct modern interpretations - specifically, the sequential, semirisome, and smooth manifold frameworks.  Interestingly, a critical assessment of these accounts reveals that they are marred by inaccuracies and that a critical reappraisal of Leibniz's views on infinitesimals can shed new light on the historical debate surrounding the calculus controversy. In this study, we demonstrate that this C$^*$-algebra condition of being strategically complete can be eliminated, revealing a broader implication: if a C$^*$-algebra has at least three generators, then it inevitably contains an operator that is both two-sided independent and has a certain property regarding its commutant. Furthermore, this research also yields an additional finding: if a C$^*$-algebra has at least three generators, then it inevitably contains an operator that is both two-sided independent and has a certain property regarding its commutant, provided that there exists another operator with a specific characteristic in its commutant. Interestingly, this research also yields an opposite result for one-sided independence, indicating that a one-sided independent operator with a certain property regarding its commutant may not necessarily exist in every C$^*$-algebra with at least three generators. Specifically, this research shows that if a one-sided independent operator with a certain characteristic regarding its commutant exists in a C$^*$-algebra, then it must be the left or right multiplication operator. Finally, this research also yields an opposite result for another characteristic regarding its commutant in the original Christensen and Hasannasab finding. Specifically, this research shows that a C$^*$-algebra with at least three generators necessarily contains an operator with a specific characteristic regarding its commutant only if it is dimension-free. Specifically, this research shows that if a C$^*$-algebra has at least three generators and is not dimension-free, then it inevitably contains an operator with a specific characteristic regarding its commutant. Based on these research outcomes, we also pose several questions and hypotheses. Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. We've verified the accuracy of our methods through a substantial set of numerical examples. We've further proved that the results we've obtained can be extended to the context of Wigner and Laplace matrices. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements. This model was developed from first principles and was validated against extensive experimental data as well as quantum mechanical calculations, demonstrating excellent agreement in all cases. Specifically, relative errors in the equation of state were $\sim 10^{-6}$ for $N_2TP$, $\sim 10^{-5}$ for $U_2TP$, and $\sim 10^{-5}$ for $H_2TP$ at $T\sim300$~K and $p\sim10^2$~kPa. Furthermore, this model has been shown to yield accurate predictions for thermodynamic properties, entropy, heat capacity, ionization energy, and critical point parameters with errors less than a factor of $5\cdot10^{-3}$. Notably, this model's inherent mathematical structure facilitates the derivation of thermodynamic properties with minimal computational overhead. Consequently, this analytical model represents a valuable time- and computation-resource-saving alternative to existing quantum mechanical models for alkali gas. With its concise mathematical formulation, this model is poised to become a standard tool in numerous scientific and engineering applications, such as fluid dynamics, transport phenomena, heat transfer, and energy systems, where alkali gases may play a critical role. Finally, this work demonstrates that highly accurate analytical equations of state can still be developed even in cases where simple and transparent mathematical formulations are constrained. Despite these limitations, this model retains its mathematical simplicity and transparency, thereby serving as a clear and lucid illustration of the underlying physical principles of quantum statistical mechanics. This incorporates complex poles representing meson formation within the local parity breaking medium. By comparing the real and imaginary components of the propagator, a set of linear equations is formed to determine the complex spectrum of local parity breaking medium. Specifically, local parity breaking medium results in a mass shift and broadening for all light vector mesons, with exceptions of ϕ when paired with a neutral fermion or singularly by a fermion as both contribute the same effect. Moreover, when paired with a charged fermion, a mass shift and broadening is observed for ρ and ω but not for ϕ. Lastly, when paired with additional vector fermions, a mass shift and broadening is observed for all light vector mesons, with noted exceptions of ω and ϕ which do not interact with these fermions. With the exception of ω, this research finds that vector mesons interact with fermions in Fock space through loop diagrams and that this interaction induces local parity breaking in the presence of chiral imbalance. This research answers the previously raised question of whether vector mesons interact with fermions and, as a result, whether local parity is broken by fermions as a means of exchange. This research finds that the answer is in the affirmative. This research further finds that mass differences among the light vector mesons ρ(0), ρ(+), ω, and ϕ are a direct consequence of local parity breaking by fermions as a means of exchange. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. This paper explores the recovery of continuous functions with limited continuity, denoted as $\mathcal C^\alpha$, subject to a basis pursuit in the continuum with a smooth basis. The study reveals that a unique solution exists under the following conditions: the basis functions must be evenly dispersed across the given interval and must not be zero anywhere within it. Additionally, the measurement matrix must possess certain smoothness properties and must not contain any singular values that are too close to zero. The recovery process is proven to be stable with respect to continuous function norms, and we establish a precise estimate of the error term. The key to achieving these results involves leveraging a continuous version of the Basis Pursuit in the Continuum (BPC) that we developed previously, which can be viewed as a type of parametric regularization method. The BPC formula provides a continuous family of solutions that vary smoothly as the parameter changes, and we show that this formula remains differentiable almost everywhere except for discrete points known as "switch times," which occur when the basis functions vanish. By reformulating the problem as a PDE with an evolving solution trajectory, we are able to derive sharp estimates of the solution's regularity using various techniques, including maximum principle arguments and operator estimates, which ultimately demonstrate that the solution trajectory remains differentiable for any function with $\alpha < 1$ as its regularity index. The estimates also capture smoothness properties of the solution's derivatives at various orders. Furthermore, we established a stability result that guarantees the solution stays close to nearby functions with related data under small changes in the data, and this result holds for functions with $\alpha$ as low as 3/5, which is more tolerant than previously thought. The study also provides several examples that illustrate the importance of the problem's assumptions, particularly ensuring that the basis functions do not vanish anywhere within the interval. Finally, the recovery process is proven to be equivalent to solving a certain type of control problem, which provides an alternative approach to solving the original recovery problem. The approach can be generalized to allow controlling multiple functions simultaneously, which provides a more comprehensive theoretical framework for the BPC method.
