This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training. The proposed local critic training method surpasses model-parallel factorization and slimming in terms of test accuracy and nonconvexity, and shows comparable parameter efficiency. The results show that local critic training can scale up CNNs and RNNs to millions of parameters on single machines with low memory usage. The method shows great potential for deep learning applications on resource-constrained devices. Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart, largely due to the scarcity of discovered systems fitting its definition. Furthermore, a weak dissipative force was introduced, maintaining the system's three-dimensional chaotic nature while significantly altering the underlying dynamics. Surprisingly, this force caused the Wada basin boundary to contract, reducing the system's escape rate and altering its dimension. Importantly, the change in system dynamics was closely tied to the system's intermittently collapsing periodic orbit, suggesting a link between weak dissipation and three-dimensional Hamiltonian systems. Ultimately, the developed system, dubbed the 'Hat-Cavity System,' holds the potential to become a prototype for three-dimensional chaotic attractors born from dissipative processes. This phenomenon, observed in two-dimensional systems but previously unknown in three-dimensional systems, can be explained by the system's interconnected chaotic saddle and attractor. Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, which this study addresses in the domain of video classification. The advent of deep learning has significantly improved video classification capabilities; nonetheless, certain complexities persist. Specifically, this challenge addresses the issue of recognizing diverse human activities from diverse viewpoints within indoor and outdoor settings. To tackle this issue, a novel Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) is proposed, which incorporates a hierarchical attention mechanism to retain only relevant frame features and eliminate redundant information, thus optimizing performance. The HAN consists of two primary components: the frame feature extractor and the temporal structure modeling module. Experiments conducted on HMDB51 and UCF101 datasets demonstrate the superior efficacy of HAN in video classification. Furthermore, analyses of different network configurations and ablation studies on various components provide valuable insights for future research. Lastly, results from our studies on UCF101 reveal that HAN achieves remarkable performance, surpassing several renowned benchmarks. Specifically, HAN achieves impressive mean accuracy rates of 92.6% on HMDB51 and 76.9% on UCF101, which significantly surpass the performance of existing state-of-the-art models. To validate the robustness of HAN, experiments were conducted using data augmentation on HMDB51, which yielded a mean accuracy rate of 70.9%, thus confirming the robustness of HAN. To evaluate the robustness of HAN in diverse outdoor settings, experiments were conducted using the Kinetics dataset, which yielded a mean accuracy rate of 71.9%. To confirm the superior efficacy of HAN, comparisons were made with several renowned video classification models, which revealed its exceptional performance. Lastly, in an effort to make the code open-source, the source code of HAN has been made publicly available at the following repository: https://github.com/zzsplat1201/HAN. The publicly available HAN repository includes the necessary implementation details for replicating the experiments conducted in this study. To facilitate understanding, a detailed guide has been provided in the repository, which includes the step-by-step implementation of HAN. To summarize, this research presents a novel Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) (https://github.com/zzsplat1201/HAN), which significantly advances the video classification domain. We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex biological systems, specifically a type of nonlinear hyperbolic conservation law with flux functions that may have singularities and lack convexity, given varying initial conditions. These singularities lead to shock waves and the system behaves deterministically, but when combined with random noise in the form of a measure-valued noise, the solution becomes highly complex and indeterminate. A new class of weak measure-valued solutions is established, displaying a form of pathwise uniqueness and giving rise to a rare event theory that aligns with a stochastic interpretation, thereby providing a theoretical framework for statistical physics to study rare and extreme events. Furthermore, we propose a class of algorithms for numerical simulation of this stochastic PDE, demonstrating the feasibility of numerical studies and opening doors for observational analysis of rare events. To validate our approach, we focus on examining the occurrence of rare concentrated solutions, specifically a special case of solutions that can be viewed as a concentration of mass at a singular point, and show that these solutions exhibit stochastic stability, implying that the solution tends towards a stable equilibrium that is similar to a lattice gas simulation, specifically a model that exhibits a form of momentum conservation known as "galactic collision," in certain limit cases. Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of machine learning into network security has produced impressive outcomes, with state-of-the-art systems demonstrating superior performance compared to conventional methods. However, a major constraint in implementing machine learning-based systems is the high computational requirements, inducing latency that is unacceptable in real-time network monitoring. In this research, we present a novel low-resource consumption Naive Bayes classifier built using a specialized encoder for binary Naive Bayes, addressing the prominent issue of resource scarcity in small devices, where rapid detection of threats is essential for maintaining security. The proposed NBcoded system effectively converts categorical attributes into binary format using a pre-trained encoder and trains binary Naive Bayes models using this converted data, resulting in a significant reduction in computational complexity from O(nv) to O(n) and memory usage from O(n) to O(1), where n and v represent the number of samples and features. The efficacy of NBcoded was evaluated using seven datasets, including network intrusion datasets pldp_13, pldp_22, pldp_32, pldp_42, pldp_52, pldp_62, and pldp_72 from the MICE dataset library, where it achieved impressive accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and Matthews correlation coefficient scores compared to leading classifiers including J48, random forest, support vector machine, multilayer perceptron, k-nearest neighbors, libSVM, and k-star. Notably, NBcoded surpassed the state-of-the-art classifiers in terms of training efficiency, achieving a remarkable 87% reduction in computational latency and 83% memory usage reduction compared to the next best classifier, libSVM. The remarkable performance and resource efficiency of NBcoded make it an ideal Naive Bayes-based binary classifier solution for low-resource devices, where rapid threat detection is crucial for maintaining security. The proposed system also addresses the prominent issue of binary classification's high computational latency and memory consumption, successfully converting categorical attributes into binary format and training binary Naive Bayes models using this converted data to reduce computational complexity and memory usage. Furthermore, NBcoded's efficacy was evaluated using seven datasets and compared with leading classifiers, demonstrating superior accuracy and resource efficiency. For finitely generated groups G, the focus of study is the parameter n_max(G) representing the maximum attainable growth rate for linear representations of G. Our investigation establishes the inequality n_max(G) ≤ n_max(G(ab)) with absolute value |G(ab)| ≤ 2 for nilpotent subgroups (ab) of G. Furthermore, the study also explores the relation n_max(G) ≤ n_max(G/M)(2^d) in cases where G is solvable with nilpotent subgroups of finite cyclic orders, and d represents the dimension of the maximal solvable abelian subgroup. Additionally, new growth bounds are determined for specific solvable groups, such as metabelian groups and groups with nilpotent subgroups of order p for a prime p. Lastly, the connections between growth in linear representations and other properties of solvable groups are examined. Our work builds on previous research by Grigorchuk and Drutel-Zainoulline-Shanin and offers new insights into the growth of solvable groups. Our findings also raise several open questions and conjectures which we propose for further research and investigation. Our primary results have been verified using computer-aided calculations for diverse solvable groups with a emphasis on in-depth analysis for a wide range of examples. Computer-assisted proof involves algorithms used to generate all nilpotent subgroups of given orders in diverse groups and examine their properties in an automated manner. Our investigation also delves into the NilQuartics database which encompasses all finite groups of orders up to 200. Our research indicates that a comprehensive study of growth in all solvable groups can be achieved by analysing groups from the NilQuartics database and incorporating recent breakthroughs in group theory into the study. Our research provides new insights and results which are likely to yield further developments in the field of growth in solvable groups. Our investigation also opens up new avenues for further research and offers a wide range of possible directions for further study and analysis. Our primary results have been verified using a combination of hands-on case studies and automated computations which are detailed in the appendix of the study. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their respective environments. This document focuses on identifying biologically mobile objects within video footage. Initially, a broad analysis is conducted to identify moving entities, after which a refined approach using body shape features and fiducial points is developed to define and extract mobile biological objects. A novel association algorithm is introduced to link detected entities and eliminate false positives, followed by a method for tracking the movement of biological objects over time. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through testing on a thousand videos containing mobile biological objects, a category that encompasses a wide range of animals. Finally, this approach is compared to a pre-trained Faster R-CNN model in terms of performance and is found to deliver superior results in terms of accuracy and multi-point association metrics. However, further refinement is required to bring performance parity with Faster R-CNN. The document concludes by highlighting the scope for further exploration within this area of research, specifically with regard to designing more efficient algorithms for detecting and tracking mobile biological objects. Additionally, it is noted that the diverse array of mobile biological creatures could inspire more innovative approaches to object detection and tracking, leading to new developments in biologically-inspired robotics and artificial intelligence. Lastly, the extensive video dataset compiled for this research, comprising a thousand minutes of footage, is made available to the public as a resource for further exploration and development. Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and corresponding equations by solely relying on experimental data. However, the vast number of possible models and equations makes it a highly complex problem. A new study investigates whether AI can uncover universal laws and related discrepancies through the analysis of known physics measurements. The research considers two scenarios: (1) the simplest possible model where the measured variable has a direct correlation with another variable, and (2) a more complex case where the relationship involves a second variable but is affected by random fluctuations. The outcomes reveal that the simplest model can consistently result in accurate predictions, whereas the more complex case requires substantial data and sophisticated statistical analysis to yield reliable outcomes. Notably, the model derived from the complex case still exhibits random fluctuations, even with extensive data sets, and thus may not consistently apply to all data without exception. A new data set containing Hubble's original data, along with two additional data sets, is provided for testing these AI methods. Hubble's original data is particularly intriguing as it shows a striking inverse correlation between light intensity and reciprocal distance. While this correlation holds true for six data points, it becomes ambiguous with more recent and extensive data. This study serves as a reminder of the significance of physics principles in understanding and interpreting empirical evidence. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/fortuneglobal/discovery-of-physics. The corresponding figure can be replicated using the provided Python script. The study's findings offer novel insights into the intricacies of universal laws, while also highlighting potential limitations and biases of ML training data. Moreover, the study sheds light on the concept of generalization, which is often taken for granted in machine learning, and may actually depend on the presence of random fluctuations in the data. Ultimately, the study and its findings can guide future research in the development of more robust and reliable AI models for uncovering new physics principles. Future research should focus on diverse data sets, novel features, and more nuanced models to further advance our understanding of the underlying physics. The study's findings also call for a more nuanced interpretation of the outcomes of physics-led AI modeling endeavors. Finally, the study and its findings can contribute to a more equitable and inclusive AI development process that prioritizes the incorporation of diverse human expertise. In conclusion, the study and its findings can guide future research in the development of more robust and reliable AI models for uncovering new physics principles. This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower speeds than light and distinctive characteristics: substantial transverse momentum and unusually large energy loss per unit length. The study focuses on particles detectable by their tracks in the inner detector and energy loss measurements in the pixel layers, thus able to capture particles with lifetimes as short as one nanosecond and masses ranging from 100 GeV to 3 TeV. The study explores the possibilities of long-lived particles in supersymmetric models, considering the production of $R$-hadrons, charginos and staus, with mass limits that extend well beyond previous search findings in various scenarios. The most constrained limits apply to $R$-hadron masses between 100 and 160 GeV, and to staus with masses up to 81% of their neutralino partners in various supersymmetric model scenarios. This study further sets a 1 TeV mass limit for long-lived electrons that remain undetected in supersymmetric models with minimal electroweak fine-tuning below 5%. In summary, this study significantly expands our understanding of long-lived particles and leaves numerous possible avenues for discovery in future experiments. Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to generate diverse solutions for combinatorial problems. Multi-objective optimization techniques are commonly used to tackle such optimization challenges, by creating multiple solutions with varying quality levels. However, truly diverse solutions can only be beneficial if they effectively address different aspects of the problem. Therefore, it is crucial to measure and analyze phenotypic diversity in multi-objective optimization, to validate its practical value. In this study, we demonstrate that current diversity analysis metrics are insufficient, as they fail to consider solutions' topological relationships and adaptations to their problem spaces. Consequently, we introduce a new analysis approach, Phenotypic Diversity Analysis, that utilizes a graph embedding method and dimensionality reduction to visualize and quantify solutions' diversity. By applying this method, we examine multi-objective optimization runs for benchmark functions and real-world problems, such as the Traveling Salesman Problem, to illustrate its practical value. Moreover, we show that PDAnalysis offers valuable insights that can guide researchers in developing new optimization strategies to enhance solution diversity. The approach is available as open-source software and is documented in online tutorials. Its source code can be accessed at https://github.com/epn-galvao/Phenotypic-Diversity-Analyses. Furthermore, the results are shared at https://epngalvao.github.io/Phenotypic-Diversity-Analyses. Additional information can be found at https://epngalvao.github.io/Phenotypic-Diversity-Analyses. The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings to be considered stable is that they must not violate each agent's preference by forming a partnership that ranks higher. In the event of a violation, the agent would prefer a different pairing. Under certain parameters, the Stable Roommates problem has a known solution involving the use of the Grossman cycle. However, when preferences become more complex with the introduction of additively separable preferences, a new approach is required to ensure optimal results. In this work, we explore the properties of these preferences and examine their impact on the Stable Roommates problem, ultimately providing a solution involving the application of the Grossman cycle to the marginal valuations of preferences. The resulting pairs are also shown to be optimal under marginal preference lists and can be computed using a polynomial number of operations. Furthermore, we establish that the pairs' uniqueness depends on specific preference constraints, whereas in the case of diverse marginal preference lists, the pairs' uniqueness is shown to depend on the presence of certain cycles. The findings of this work contribute to the understanding of stable matchings among agents with complex, hierarchically ranked preference lists and provide valuable insights into the use of marginal preference lists in the Stable Roommates problem. The work also extends the knowledge on developing cycles in the context of the Grossman method to the context of stable matchings. The novel approach to the Stable Roommates problem presented here can be generalized to other situations involving additively separable preferences, paving the way for further generalizations in the field of mechanism design. In particular, the use of the Grossman cycle to form pairs in the context of the Stable Roommates problem may be applied to other scenarios, such as arranging tasks and assigning tasks to agents. The results of this research can also be applied in a variety of real-world contexts, such as arranging tasks and assigning tasks to agents. In such scenarios, the marginal preference lists can be used to model agents' preferences over tasks, and the pairs formed using the Grossman cycle can be used to determine stable task arrangements. The application of the results of this research to these contexts is left to future investigation. The tasks and their marginal preference lists can be used to determine stable task arrangements that maximize agents' marginal utility. Furthermore, the diversity of tasks' marginal preference lists is shown to affect the uniqueness of stable task arrangements. Our research explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon coupling impact valley dynamics in two-dimensional materials. We created a theoretical model to investigate this coupling in two types of systems: a graphene bilayer with a Bernal stack configuration and a two-layer MoS2 valley layer. We found that dynamic deformation fields can induce valley mixing and valley coherent transport, accompanied by negative differential resistance, in both systems when coupled to circularly polarized light. However, the valley mixing mechanism in graphene bilayers is constrained due to symmetry limitations, in contrast to the competition and interplay observed between dynamic deformation fields and static strain-induced valley mixing in MoS2 layers. We demonstrated that the competition between these two effects in MoS2 can be harnessed to create a spatially direct transmission of valley information. We also delved into the role of acoustic phonons in valley physics and identified a novel mechanism by which they can induce valley mixing in MoS2 layer. We derived a semi-classical model to investigate the impact of phonon interference on valley coherent transport in graphene bilayers and MoS2 layers under optical excitation. Our research offers a framework for exploring the utility of electron-phonon coupling in valley optoelectronics. Moreover, it provides a theoretical basis for investigating the role of phonons as quantum intermedaries in valley coherent transmission. We envision that our findings will stimulate research into the intricate connection between phonons and valley physics and potentially open up new avenues for the development of valley-related technologies. Ultimately, a thorough understanding of this connection could lead to the creation of innovative valley-based devices based on two-dimensional materials, where phonons serves as functional intermediaries.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor results in a new metric, leading to the question of whether there's a universal space where all such transformations take place within a single class. The growth of distances in a space has a significant impact on the overall metric, and we consider the factors that influence this growth to determine the upper bounds of the cloud's class. Focusing on the minimal distances within a space, we find that the class of these spaces with uniformly low metrics also forms a cloud, and the associated clouds have a complete metric space. In addition, we define and study the center of a cloud, and establish the existence of a center under a uniform lower bound on the metric's growth. The relations between these clouds remain unclear, and we highlight the differences between the class of metric spaces with growing distances and the class of uniformly bounded metric spaces. The connections between the center of a cloud and the Busemann compactification, as well as the center of a metric space, remain to be explored. The concepts and methods of studying clouds in Gromov--Hausdorff classes can be applied to the analysis of a diverse range of metric spaces. The ideas and techniques presented in this work may also be useful in other fields, and we suggest potential directions for further research. A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna functions across a bandwidth of 13.1% (from 12.44 to 14.19 GHz) and provides a nearly omnidirectional radiation pattern with significant sideband suppression at broad bandwidth. Built using a low-cost FR4 substrate with minimal layer count, the designed antenna produces stable radiation patterns throughout a 63% broad bandwidth (from -60% to 60% width in the E-plane) and operates effectively over a large spherical surface (55% on the body and 95% above the body). The designed antenna features compact dimensions of 14 mm x 8 mm, suitable for use in planar arrays where uniform illumination and consistent radiation patterns are crucial for maintaining a narrow beamwidth and reducing sidelobe levels over a large spherical surface around the body. The designed antenna has been thoroughly characterized through simulations and experimental analysis, showing excellent agreement between the results.)

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Notably, our approach easily accommodates models with non-affine noise properties, including cases involving crossed and braided decoherence, without requiring any adjustments to the algorithm. Furthermore, we found that with the correct off-the-shelf policy transfer, these deepQ learning methods can achieve fast startup times. Compared to existing decoding techniques, our approach offers significant speed improvements, while also exhibiting greater flexibility in terms of supporting various types of noise models. For example, our surface code decoder handled average cyclic noise with speeds up to 3.5 orders of magnitude faster than established methods, while supporting low probability cyclic noise and various types of noise models with speeds up to 2.5 to 3.7 orders of magnitude faster. We also developed an extension of this approach for dynamic decoding scenarios where the environment's dynamics are fully specified but can adapt to the decoder's actions, applying this method to the surface code paradigm. Based on these results, we believe reinforcement learning holds considerable potential for improving quantum computing decoding processes and could likely have analogous impacts in other quantum computing applications. To evaluate the effectiveness of this method, we compared the convergence rates of our deepQ learning surface code decoder dealing with random noise models to the effectiveness of established minimum-weight perfect matching algorithms, while also examining the impact of varying the number of training examples and the structure of the code environment. Additionally, we found that by applying reinforcement learning to the decoding process to learn a environment-model of the noise, the resulting surface code decoder can achieve significant speed improvements when presented with novel types of noise models. We propose that this approach could have considerable practical value in real-world quantum computing applications due to its ability to adapt to unknown types of noise models. To support further research on this idea, we made the source code for our surface code decoder publicly available. We also developed an extension of this approach for dynamic decoding scenarios where the environment's dynamics are fully specified but can adapt to the decoder's actions, applying this method to the surface code paradigm. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry by initially preparing a state with high entanglement, which decreases uncertainty in phase measurements. However, achieving this typically requires complex procedures and is limited to specific experimental setups. Our research proposes a new method for accurately measuring phase using a network of two interacting cavities containing quantum emitters, utilizing a universal quantum algorithm. This approach is based on a cavity-ringdown technique that correlates detector clicks with emitter projects. By taking into account limitations imposed by vacuum-field fluctuations and emitter motion, we demonstrate that this method's sensitivity is comparable to the standard quantum limit. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of surpassing this limit through nonclassical effects induced by cavity interactions. These interactions enable the creation of entangled states between the emitter and the electromagnetic fields within each cavity, leading to a significant improvement in phase sensitivity. We show that the resulting sensitivity is related to the number of interactions within the cavity and can be expressed as a function of the Fock state number. Our research offers a versatile tool for accurately measuring phase in a variety of scenarios, including optomechanics and microfluidics. Additionally, this study may contribute to the advancement of quantum information technology by leveraging emitters to generate and control quantum states. As such, we believe that this research will be invaluable to the development of quantum technology and metrology applications, expanding beyond current understandings of these fields. Specifically, we show that emitter-interaction times can be converted into digital information, leading to a precision in phase measurements that exceeds current expectations. This groundbreaking finding presents novel approaches to quantum technology and may enable the development of highly sensitive optomechanical devices, enabling the accurate measurement of masses smaller than what is currently technologically possible. Lastly, we identify potential research avenues for further investigation, including novel applications of quantum metrology and the potential for observing macroscopic quantum effects. These possibilities are within reach due to the capabilities of contemporary emitter platforms, offering a versatile tool for testing various hypotheses related to quantum physics. In particular, we explore the possibility of surpassing the standard quantum limit in optomechanics, although this may require sophisticated engineering to stabilize mechanical frequencies. Nonetheless, we believe that the distinctive properties of emitters make them an ideal tool for such tasks, given their wide application in quantum information technology and metrology. Ultimately, we anticipate that our research will contribute to the advancement of quantum technology and metrology, while also promoting the development of innovative and ground-breaking research in these fields. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, indicating medium response. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias towards handling OoD scenarios.

This robust feature set is generated using the estimated influence of each dimension on the target variable, obtained through an in-depth analysis of the data's properties and the network's behavior. As a result, the parameter server Gouda can efficiently identify and eliminate less relevant dimensions, effectively incorporating a complexity penalty that is data-dependent and adaptable to different learning tasks. 

Furthermore, our method is compatible with a wide range of deep learning models and can be applied during both training and deployment to achieve generalized performance. We test this approach in various scenarios, and the source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghassenw/Rich-Feature-Construction. 

Notably, our method excels in several high-risk, real-world applications, such as medical diagnostics and the classification of malware, often achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art generalized deep learning models. In particular, we demonstrate that rich feature construction enables a simple CNN to surpass a ResNet-34 model in generalization. 

Although our method may seem related to concepts like feature selection, parameter regularization, and data-dependent learning, its unique combination of characteristics sets it apart from these existing approaches. 

In conclusion, our research involved comprehensive empirical evaluations that substantiate the efficacy of our method, paving the way for further theoretical research in the future. 

Specifically, we found that:

* Rich feature construction yields consistent generalization performance improvements across a range of datasets.
* It is particularly effective in high-risk scenarios and outperforms specialized models.
* The top-ranked models derived from our method exhibit superior performance to state-of-the-art generalized deep learning models.
* Its success is data-dependent and multi-dimensional, as demonstrated by our analysis of datasets with distinct dataset characteristics.
* Our approach is compatible with a wide range of models and training techniques, including transfer learning, and can be applied during training or deployment. 

In summary, our research presents a novel solution to the optimization-generalization dilemma, and the associated source code

However, due to constraints related to the limited field of view and complex control systems required, it has been difficult to achieve this goal in thick biological tissues. We present a new approach that enables the creation of multiple complex structures simultaneously within three-dimensional volumes of tissue, using an inexpensive, single-axis SLM and an iterative learning control system that adjusts the nonlinear medium's response. We demonstrate the formation of multiple arrays of spots, rings, and planes in the tissue, using a single beam and observing the formation of these structures over time in the tissue. Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, demonstrated through the analysis of 85KeV X-ray interactions with silicon. By utilizing both numerical and experimental methods, the detection efficiency for CLICTD sensors built on 200mm CMOS wafer structures is examined across different thicknesses and types of substrate epitaxy. The results indicate that changing the sensor type leads to a noticeable enhancement in detection efficiency, with the best response occurring with detectors built using magnetic CMOS sensors and a 250um sensor depth. This is found to be in alignment with expectations based on theoretical calculations. Moreover, magnetic sensors are shown to outperform their equivalent counterparts built using CAPTTE technology. The theoretical detection efficiency for CLICTD sensors built with CAPTTE and a 300um sensor depth is also consistent with experimental findings. Lastly, researchers propose that modifying detector design using a guard ring could mitigate issues related to surface and buried laser damage. Nonetheless, the active sensor depth remains a critical factor influencing detection efficiency and should be carefully considered during detector development. Based on this study, researchers recommend using magnetic CMOS sensors due to superior performance in detecting high-energy particles. Finally, researchers suggest that CAPTTE sensors could be a viable option if custom-designed for specific application requirements, despite requiring a deeper and thus heavier, more power-consumptive active region. The proposed design incorporates CLICTD sensors and allows for the integration of four monolithic CMOS modules, each positioned at the intersection of two focus spheres and oriented at 90 degrees to enable four-dimensional tracking of particle interactions. This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and accurately replicating the observed yield curve. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, incorporating the deterministic-shift adjustment. For quick alignment with the current swaption prices, the Gram-Charlier expansion is employed to calculate swaption prices within the proposed framework. Multiple numerical evaluations are performed, utilizing Monte-Carlo simulations, to showcase the benefits of this new model, as well as the Gram-Charlier expansion, in terms of reducing variance and generating accurate swaption price estimates. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis is conducted to demonstrate the versatility of this new model, through a comparison of its performance on both bond and swaption prices, under diverse scenarios of mean shift. It is observed that the model's performance remains largely unaffected by the degree of mean shift, highlighting its versatility in various contexts. Overall, this research introduces a reliable model to tackle negative interest rates, and proposes the Gram-Charlier expansion as a efficient variances-reducing method that can be easily applied to multiple interest rate models. Given its ease of implementation, this model can serve as a valuable tool for the industry and the industry's mathematicians to align their pricing models with the current yield curve curves. Lastly, it is observed that the current swaption prices are largely insensitive to the degree of mean shift that describes the current level of interest rates. Based on this, it is proposed that any reasonable level of mean shift that describes the current state would not substantially alter the current swaption prices. Ultimately, this research may contribute to the development of more refined models to describe the behavior of swaption prices, by incorporating more accurate dynamic descriptions of the interest rates, and the underlying shifts in the market's expectations. In such cases, using cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively account for this clustering, however these may not always be applicable in the context of meta-regression. While the uncorrelated cluster-robust estimator addresses this issue in the context of meta-analyses based on independent studies, its performance is limited when studying correlated effects. These estimators can be applied using both frequentist and Bayesian approaches and have been found to perform well in simulation studies.  The proposed estimators were successfully used in an analysis of within-study repeated treatments via a case study involving the effects of smoking on non-smoking individuals. In particular, bias was evident in models without cluster-robust adjustment, whereas bias was reduced though not eliminated in models using the uncorrelated-to-covariance and uncorrelated-to-heteroscedasticity estimators. This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$. The first methodology relies on a set of equations describing the relationship between the pairs $(a,b)$ and $(ka,kb)$, for a given value of $k$, which are expressed in terms of a $2 \times 2$ matrix over the integers. The second proof employs a graph theoretical approach, mapping the pairs $(a,b)$ to vertices of a graph, and demonstrating that this mapping results in distinct values of $a^2+ab+b^2$ for sufficiently large values of $n$, distributed in a symmetrical pattern. Two explicit solutions are provided: $(a,b)=(3,1)$ and $(a,b)=(4,2)$. A related open problem concerning the same equation but with base $2$ instead of $7$ remains unsolved and intriguing. The article concludes by speculating on possible values of $a$ and $b$ for small values of $n$. The theory of monoid epimorphisms and automata is also briefly referenced. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In the context of this research, we introduce novel algorithms to handle memory transactions during system crashes, targeting applications in high-performance computing environments. These algorithms demonstrate the ability to create and manipulate sets, allowing for the processing of crashes and maintaining data integrity in the face of cache failures. Notably, we observe that algorithmic approaches to data management can outperform traditional hardware solutions, even in situations where simple algorithms emerge as the most effective option. These findings serve as a foundation for the development of a robust programming paradigm for building crash-resilient applications. Furthermore, we utilize the BDD technology to evaluate and compare the robustness of different algorithms under different scenarios. Finally, we plan to integrate our algorithms into the Linux kernel as a complementary module. Preliminary experimental results indicate that algorithmic methods can outperform traditional hardware solutions, rendering such approaches an affordable alternative for ensuring data integrity in high-performance computing systems. Ultimately, we aim to expand our research to encompass other areas of fault tolerance, including parallel processing, as a means of promoting affordable fault-tolerant solutions. Lastly, we present a novel algorithm for detecting memory corruption during system crashes, offering a novel perspective on this classic issue. Unlike existing approaches, we integrate the concept of algorithmic fault tolerance into our solution, as illustrated by the accompanying code. In contrast to existing detector algorithms, our approach relies on the unique properties of set algorithms, introducing the novel idea of detecting memory errors as set incompatibilities. Experimental results demonstrate that our detector not only matches but surpasses the performance of cutting-edge detectors when measuring data integrity. As a means of validating our algorithm's robustness, we employ the BDD technology to evaluate various detector algorithms under different memory configurations. Lastly, we identify potential pitfalls in detector design, such as detector blindness, and propose detector revisions to overcome these limitations. Ultimately, we intend to integrate our detector algorithm into the Linux kernel as a complementary module. Furthermore, we present a novel evaluation framework for assessing fault-tolerant algorithms under realistic error scenarios, as opposed to the typical artificial cases often employed in existing research. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), combining topic modeling with a hierarchical clustering method that takes into consideration the actual relationships between documents and topics, all while being designed for large-scale data sets and seamless integration with document ranking mechanisms. Experimental evaluations using a 1.3 million web document index demonstrate HDTM's superior performance and scalability compared to existing models. For example, while building the index, HDTM efficiently computed the hierarchical structure 20 times faster than the second best approach, and even allowed for real-time, interactive navigation of the hierarchy even when the index was 5 times larger than previously thought possible. The corresponding technical report is available at http://dx.doi.org/10.1145/2983641.2983843. We have also released the source code for HDTM at https://github.com/cloakresearch/hdtm. Based on this research, we are developing a search engine with hierarchical navigation at https://cloakresearch.com. In the near future, we plan to expand our research to include hierarchical navigation in comment and code streams to facilitate the understanding of open source software projects. This research has far-reaching applications and will soon be used in a variety of areas such as legal documents, biomedical texts, Twitter streams and computer memory dumps. In the end, we aim to make information networks more tractable, faciliate navigation across diverse domains and create a robust search engine that can handle large information networks indefinitely. In particular, we envision a robust search engine that can efficiently compute the hierarchical structure even when indexing 100 million web documents, documents on all publicly visible Wikipedia pages, or the entire contents of the Internet. This vision is within reach because of HDTM's exceptional efficiency. We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the predicted absorption as a function of binary energy and angular momentum, and the distribution of lifetimes. Our results showed that escape probabilities matched theoretical predictions with high precision, marking a significant improvement over previous studies. Furthermore, the measured values of the exponent near marginally unbound escape thresholds aligned closely with an analytical formula. Notably, the measured absorption rates also showed an excellent match with theoretical predictions across a range of energies and angular momenta. Lastly, both the measured and theoretically predicted lifetime distributions showed strong agreement, revealing a scaling relationship in the range of ergodic lifetimes. These findings not only validate the predictions of a statistical approach but also provide valuable insights into the three-body problem, potentially facilitating the development of new numerical algorithms to analyze these systems. In particular, approximating distributions of lifetimes could provide a basis for more accurate estimates of timescales in astrophysical applications, potentially involving star formation and the evolution of planetary orbits. Lastly, the measured timescales also showed that three-body systems are generally much shorter-lived than two-body simulations featuring the same binary properties, but with a small fraction of long-lived 'binary-gravitational-echo' objects where masses are unequal. In particular, the distribution of lifetimes was found to be concentrated almost entirely within two timescales in hierarchical systems where one binary is prominent: a short 'binary-echo' lifetime and a longer 'binary-binary' lifetime, each of which varied little with angular momentum and energy. However, in non-hierarchical systems where no single binary can be distinguished, a wide range of lifetimes was observed, concentrated around two timescales that varied little with energy and momentum: a short 'isolated-escape' lifetime and a longer 'collinear' lifetime, where three-body systems are concentrated when bodies happen to move along a line in space. In general, the distribution of lifetimes in three-body systems is multi-modal, but this paper focuses on well-localized distributions of two distinct lifetimes. Ultimately, both theoretical and measured lifetime distributions showed that most three-body systems are concentrated within very short timescales, roughly equivalent to orbital periods at stellar distances. Our research reports a significant $7\sigma$ detection of X-ray polarization emanating from Cassiopeia A, with a polarization degree of $19\% \pm 4$% obtained from IXPE's first public data release. Cassiopeia A is a supernova remnant comprising both young and older radiation sources - primarily a fast-expanding supernova shock wave and a slower-moving forward-reverse shock system that has undergone gravitational influence from expanding kinetic energy. By analyzing IXPE's data, we distinguished between polarization caused by the shock wave and core emission, finding a polarization degree of $22\% \pm 5\%$ for the shock wave and $15\% \pm 5\%$ for the core emission in the $3-5$ keV energy range. Through modeling, we found that the polarization of the shock wave is influenced by electron scattering with a maximum angle of polarization of approximately $25\%$. Conversely, the core emission's polarization is predominantly due to both electron scattering and reflection effects, with a magnitude consistent with prior predictions. Additionally, we found that the polarization of the shock wave and core emission across different energy ranges remains consistent with each other. This discovery marks the first time X-ray polarization detection of an extragalactic supernova remnant and the first direct evidence of IXPE's capabilities to detect polarization from extragalactic sources. Our research has significant implications, potentially allowing IXPE to detect polarization from supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and active galactic nuclei. Ultimately, polarization detection from these intense cosmic events may enable the reconstruction of three-dimensional magnetic field structures and the rotation measures of these events. As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense nuclear matter sound velocity, incorporating novel experimental data into relativistic mean-field models with strangeness-bearing compact star constituents like kaons and hyperons. Our results show that sound velocity exhibits a smooth, monotonic decrease with growing density of nucleons, but differences arise when macronuclear matter contains strange particles. To identify a deconfinement phase transition via sound velocity, we propose distinct criteria for nuclear matter and strange matter scenarios, including the behavior of sound velocity and its derivative with respect to density. Our analysis indicates that a phase transition in nuclear matter would likely be marked by a small drop in sound velocity and its derivative, whereas a transition in strange matter would be characterized by a significant drop in sound velocity and a positive, distinct derivative. Applying these criteria to the latest macroscopic properties of compact stars reveals promising indications of a transition in at least two stars, PSR J0738+321, and PSR J1416+62. Our study also offers a new theorem linking adiabatic index $\xi$ and sound velocity $c_s$, thereby expanding the already extensive body of research on compact star thermodynamics and its macroscopic properties.  Ultimately, our findings underscore the significance of distinguishing between nuclear and strange matter sound velocity in compact stars to uncover evidence of a deconfinement phase transition. Additionally, our work lays the groundwork for merging relativistic mean-field models with neutron star mergers, gravitational waves, and other areas of dense matter research.  Following our analysis, sound velocity in neutron star matter becomes clear, and we plan to utilize this knowledge to investigate the properties of dense matter in neutron stars.  This new direction may further our understanding of the behavior of dense matter in neutron stars and shed light on the role of strangeness in compact stars.  Our study also addresses the connection between dense matter sound velocity and the QCD equations and may contribute to the exploration of a more extensive body of research linking relativistic nuclear physics to quantum chromodynamics. We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U shapes. Our analysis revealed that U-shaped galaxies are more common, representing 61% of the sample, whereas S-shaped galaxies account for 27%. By using a statistical model, we identified distinct wholesale and shipping costs associated with each type. Upwardly curved galaxies tend to have stronger residual velocity patterns along their mid-axes. A significant pattern emerged, showing that U-shaped galaxies are more likely to be affiliated with galaxy clusters, whereas S-shaped galaxies are more frequently found in isolated environments. Consistent with existing research, we found that spiral galaxies tend to have longer major axes than U-shaped galaxies. Using mock galaxy distributions, we established that the detected spiral galaxy pattern is not merely a product of random error. Building upon prior studies, our findings link the spiral galaxy pattern in clusters to the 'jellyfish' phenomenon, proposed by Noguchi (1999). Our analysis provides fresh evidence supporting the hypothesis that U-shaped galaxies are more susceptible to tidal forces, making them more common in clusters. A related byproduct of this tidal influence is the transformation of U-shaped galaxies into spiral galaxies. A control group, also analyzed, consisted of U-shaped galaxies without significant warping, displaying lower spiral galaxy counts than U-shaped galaxies with existing warping. Conversely, S-shaped galaxies were found to exhibit higher spiral galaxy counts. Using existing research, we identified multiple factors contributing to the differing wholesale and shipping costs, including disk flexibility, orientation, and the presence of central bars. Nonetheless, our study resolves the long-standing uncertainty surrounding spiral galaxy patterns in a statistical and physical context. Our findings provide foundational evidence for the tidal compression theory, suggesting that U-shaped galaxies are more susceptible to tidal compression, induced by cluster galaxies. Consequently, our study paves the way for a novel theoretical framework, linking the 'jellyfish' phenomenon and tidal compression. This research may have broader implications, extending beyond galaxy patterns to the broader tidal compression phenomenon, observed in star-forming galaxies and the planetesimal disk surrounding the Sun. Ultimately, our study paves the way for further research into the underlying physical processes driving spiral galaxy patterns, particularly within a cluster context. A byproduct of this research is the potential for spiral galaxy patterns to serve as a tidal compression detector, enabling the identification of tidal influences in galaxy datasets. To this end, our study provides a foundation for further exploration into the underlying physical processes driving spiral galaxy patterns, particularly within a cluster

The arrangement of atoms within these crystals permits the existence of chirally behaving phonons, which correspond to atoms circling their equilibrium positions. Given that inversion symmetry and time reversal symmetry govern the total pseudo-angular momentum of the system, this momentum is zero. By introducing dopants, researchers find that this can result in a new crystal structure, F$\bar{4}3$m. Novel materials, KRbBi$_{4}$ and RbCsBi$_{4}$, exhibit no dynamic instability; the transformation of their phonon mode, however, suggests the possibility of chiral phonon existence without time reversal symmetry, yielding a non-zero pseudo-angular momentum for the system. A comparison to the existing chiral phonon system, GaAs, using theoretical calculations shows that while both systems display similar total pseudo-angular momentum properties, their total momentum and magnetic properties contrast each other. Ultimately, researchers discover that manipulating the phonon modes in these materials can lead to distinct total momentum and magnetic properties for the phonon modes. By achieving this, they open the door for future control over phonon properties via doping. Additionally, they find that van Hove singularities, which are points of high electron density, are present in the electronic structure of these materials and are situated at key positions, the Fermi level included. These singularities, which are a result of special points in the Brillouin zone, exhibit varying electron densities and are located at the $\Gamma$ point along with two other points, M and R. Ultimately, the combination of chirally behaving phonons and unique total momentum and magnetic properties presents novel possibilities for future research on these quantum systems. However, accurately calculating nonadiabatic Born effective charges in metals proven to be challenging. Research has now achieved this in models of (Bernal) stainless steel and hexagonal boron nitride by generalizing the definition to include quantum effects. The findings reveal that varying the doping level in stainless steel changes its effective charge, indicating that electrons influence atomic positioning. The study further identifies issues with previous approximations and provides insight into contrasting results between static and dynamic calculations, highlighting the significance of nonadiabatic contributions. Consequently, this breakthrough opens doors for using density functional theory to investigate electric polarization in metals. Moreover, this breakthrough relates to a larger question of what happens to electric polarization to infinite doping in metals, addressing a long-standing puzzle. Ultimately, this discovery empowers the creation of ultra-efficient photovoltaic materials by analyzing the impact of doping on atomic and electronic structures. Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations in systems lacking time-reversal symmetry. We propose an alternative magnetoelectric effect that is nonlinear, time-reversal-symmetric, and can be observed in any three-dimensional insulator. Its magnetoelectric tensor is linked to a topological invariant that appears in theories of nonrelativistic quantum Hall effects, where it generates a topological liquid with a half-integer quantum Hall effect and Witten effect, a Berry phase of $\pi$, and a magnetic monopole charge of $2e$. These phenomena provide evidence that three-dimensional insulators with this topological invariant are always characterized by a nontrivial Wilsonian effective action, even at nonzero chemical potential and magnetic field. We also demonstrate that the proposed topological magnetoelectric effect produces a quantized value for the nonlinear Hall effect observed in surfaces of three-dimensional topological insulators under time-reversal symmetry. Its quantization conditions are identical to those for conventional magnetoelectric coupling, indicating that the proposed topological magnetoelectric coefficient serves as an alternative and observable manifestation of the conventional magnetoelectric coupling. A key finding is that three-dimensional Weyl semimetals have two types of topological magnetoelectric coefficients, with their product being finite and their ratio quantized, providing a new macroscopic property that can be probed experimentally. Lastly, the proposed topological magnetoelectric effect provides a new framework for understanding the fractional quantum Hall effect on torus bubbles in three-dimensional semimetals with nonzero chemical potential and a nonzero curvature in momentum space. A key observation is that the topological magnetoelectric effect generates a $2e$ magnetic monopole charge in a fractionally quantized state due to a nontrivial Wilsonian effective action, a property that is both a necessary and sufficient condition for a nonrelativistic quantum field theory to exhibit a topological ground-state degeneracy. A related finding is that three-dimensional insulators can be used to host a Z8 cycle of topological phases, with three-dimensional semimetals serving as both drivers and receivers of this cycle, with the Witten effect serving as a $2e$ charge that is necessary for implementing this cycle. A key observation is that the topological magnetoelectric effect generates a new type of topological ground-state degeneracy, with a new cycle of Z2, with three-dimensional semimetals serving as both drivers and receivers

For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality. Additionally, we demonstrate that delay modulation not only prolongs the system's transient duration but also causes its long-term trajectory to deviate significantly from randomness, favoring lower and higher frequency components. Consequently, modulating time delays in systems exhibiting laminar chaos presents an attractive approach for regulating their diffusive behavior. We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). These definitions can be generalized to apply to other stochastic programming languages as well. While constructing these definitions, we discovered that traditional techniques for generating frames by taking the transitive closure of relations falls short in this context and necessitates a more refined approach involving the concept of ultrafilters. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for investigating deeper aspects of stochastic programming, such as establishing canonicity of its denotational semantics and exploring connections with proof theory and thermodynamics. Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to document to facilitate learning within software development teams. This is achieved through mining the conversations for actionable information, extracted into a graphical representation known as design documents, which showcase the discussion conclusions as nodes connected by relationships. However, the conclusions may fluctuate over time due to changing opinions, rendering the associated relationships unreliable. This paper proposes two methods for stabilizing mining conclusions, grounded in the theory of conceptual graphs, which allows for the identification of stable relationships by eliminating inconsistent conclusions, and for the selection of stable relationships through voter-based agreement, respectively. The proposed approaches are demonstrated on a dataset of Android app review comments and their effectiveness is compared to a existing method. The experiments reveal that both approaches yield consistent outcomes, outperforming the compared method in terms of precision and F1 score. The outcome relationships extracted through these methods exhibit a 30% reduction in variability compared to the initial relationships. The resulting stable relationships can be utilized for software development concept mapping, design discussion mining, and semantic analysis. Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and in some cases, identifying this structure is also a free lunch - using proximal methods for both data preprocessing and parameter estimation. To take full advantage of this principle, we integrate Newton-type acceleration into a proximal framework for nonsmooth optimization on varying manifolds. By maintaining a constant step size, the accelerated algorithm achieves a $O\left(K/T\right)$ rate of convergence, where $K$ represents a constant related to the problem's characteristics and $T$ denotes the iteration count. We substantiate the effectiveness of this approach through a combination of theoretical analysis and a suitable example. Moreover, we apply and test the accelerated procedure on a real-world application involving the solution of a multiagent resource allocation problem with sparsity, where the structure is identified through proximal methods and the problem is formulated within the broad Lagrangian proximal framework. Results show that the new algorithm achieves considerable reductions in computational effort and memory usage compared to a standard proximal gradient method. We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ where their product is non-zero and within $I$, it follows that either the product of $a$ and $b$ is in $I$, or $c$ is in $I$. Our research presents numerous results regarding the characteristics and examples of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. It has been proven that if $I$ is a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a ring $R$ where the product of three non-zero ideals is completely contained in $I$, it then holds that either the product of the ideals generated by two of these elements is completely contained in $I$, or the ideal generated by the third element is completely contained in $I$. Additionally, several properties of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals have been found to satisfy a symmetric relationship. Furthermore, a characterization of strong $1$-absorbing prime ideals has been established as equivalent to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals, with numerous examples provided to demonstrate the distinction between general weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and strong $1$-absorbing prime ideals. Last but not least, connections between the existing classification of prime ideals as strongly $1$-absorbing, weakly $1$-absorbing, or not at all, and properties such as being minimal or maximal have been established and confirmed. In a related capacity, a classification system for prime ideals based on their compliance with the Chinese Remainder Theorem has been studied and confirmed within a particular type of ring known as valuation rings. It was found that in a commutative ring with unity, the collection of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals exhibits a complete order, and a characterization of such ideals has been found as those prime ideals for which the product of three non-zero elements within it results in a non-zero value. Additionally, a demonstration has been provided showing the separation between the collection of all prime ideals and the collection of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals using a specific example. To identify these decays, the research involved reconstructing the full recoil B-meson into long-lived hadronic decays and utilizing machine learning algorithms to select signal events. Statistical analysis revealed two distinct signals corresponding to branching fractions of $4.12 \pm 0.73 (stat.) \pm 1.10 (syst.) \times 10^{-4}$ for $B^0\bar B^0$ decays into $\rho^-\pi^+$ and $3.35 \pm 0.61 (stat.) \pm 0.95 (syst.) \times 10^{-4}$ for $B^+\bar B^0$ decays into $\rho^-\pi^+$, relative to $0.104 \pm 0.013 \times 10^{-4}$ for $B^-\bar B^0$ decays into $\rho^+\pi^-$. These measurements represent the most precise ever taken for $B^0\bar B^0$ and $B^+\bar B^0$ decays into $\rho\ell \nu_\ell$ processes. In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field. Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the same environment.  However, when discrepancies arise between the expert's environment and the agent's environment, existing methods fail to effectively utilize the available demonstrations.  To address this issue, we introduce CORe, a novel framework that enables imitation learning across domain gaps for tasks that require sequential control.  By leveraging an external representation space that facilitates comparison of states between domains, CORe allows agents to learn from demonstrations in a compatible domain.  Through experiments in diverse settings, including robotic manipulation and navigation tasks, we demonstrate that CORe successfully bridges domain gaps in imitation learning. A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We concentrate on how the magnetic properties of the star's initial environment affect its evolution by creating a numerical model of magnetohydrodynamics, applying it to the formation of a Population III star and accretion disk. Initially, the star's magnetic field is weak and the disk breaks down into turbulent fragments. However, as the star continues to accrete, its magnetic field amplifies and extends into the surrounding disk. The amplified magnetic field expands into the star's surroundings, potentially reaching a strength of hundreds milligauss at a radius of ten astronomical units. The amplified magnetic field causes the accretion disk's inner region to transition into a coronal state, characterized by a temperature of ten thousand Kelvin. The amplified magnetic field also prevents the fragmentation of the disk, effectively resulting in a non-fragmenting disk that aligns with current observational findings. Furthermore, the amplified magnetic field may also prevent the star's rotation from developing rapidly, thus potentially resulting in slower rotation rates. The effectiveness of the amplified magnetic field depends on the strength of the disk's turbulence, and is particularly effective in calm disks. Despite initial fragmentation, no protostars form in these cases. Conversely, in highly turbulent disks, the amplified magnetic field prevents the creation of a disk at all. The strength of the star's magnetic field lies between ten to a hundred microgauss, and its strength correlates with the star's mass. These properties could ultimately be observed through spectroscopy or other methods. The ultimate mass of the protostar is dependent on the strength of the star's initial magnetic field, and varies based on this factor. The strength of the star's initial magnetic field also determines whether the star forms with a perfectly smooth accretion disk. The strength of the star's initial magnetic field varies directly with the strength of the star's magnetic field. The effect of other physical processes - including radiative feedback and metal-free chemical reactions - is also considered, and the resulting picture of the star's initial environment aligns with current observational findings. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis was conducted to assess the impact of court-ordered mental health treatment on convicted individuals with mental health needs.  The study compared those who underwent treatment with similar individuals who did not receive treatment, based on data from nearly 180,000 people with mental health needs who interacted with the criminal justice system in a particular county over an 11-year period.  The results revealed the following findings: (1) individuals who underwent treatment had a lower rate of recidivism and were more likely to receive ongoing mental health services compared with those who did not receive treatment, (2) those who underwent treatment had a lower average monthly cost and were more likely to use community-based services rather than emergency services, (3) the benefits of treatment were more pronounced for individuals who were closer to prison release, (4) the effects of treatment varied depending on the specific type of crime committed, and (5) the preferences of judges played a significant role in whether or not an individual would receive treatment.  Overall, the research provided empirical evidence of the benefits of court-ordered mental health treatment and highlighted several key factors that may affect the decision to provide such treatment.  Based on these findings, several recommendations were offered to improve the provision of court-ordered mental health treatment.  Ultimately, the research provided a framework and specific guidelines for policymakers who are seeking to design and implement mental health treatment programs in conjunction with the criminal justice system. This research delves into a multi-aspect approach to person verification incorporating auditory, visual, and thermal modalities. Given the efficacy of auditory and visual modality combination, this investigation extends to exploring the effect of incorporating thermal images on verification robustness. Specifically, state-of-the-art deep learning architectures were applied to establish unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal verification systems which were compared under optimal and impaired conditions. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed to safeguard data privacy, especially effective in handling certain dependent data attributes. Nonetheless, the existing OSDP mechanisms have failed to consider the interdependencies among all data variables, overlooking potential privacy breaches in such scenarios. This paper, for the first time, investigates the privacy violations in scenarios involving dependent data attributes, specifically those protected by OSDP. To this end, the paper employs Advanced Matrix Learning with Neighbourhood Access (AMLNA), a machine learning method tailored to handle dependent data variables to frame the problem within a matrix completion context. Furthermore, the paper showcases the creation of tight upper bounds on the privacy loss in terms of logarihtmic entropy, utilizing a neighbourhood-based information Proximity measure. To evaluate the proposed framework's effectiveness, the paper conducts comprehensive experiments across various real-world datasets, comparing its efficiency with existing approaches. Experimental findings demonstrate that AMLNA outperforms alternative methods in data recovery and log-loss performance. Furthermore, the paper showcases the feasibility of the proposed framework through a real-world application involving Dependent Movie Ratings. To gauge the impact of the framework, the paper conducts aggregate evaluation across multiple metrics including recovery, log-loss, and accuracy loss performance. Results indicate that AMLNA yields superior outcomes to existing alternatives. Specifically, the paper finds that AMLNA yields substantial improvements in data recovery and log-loss performance while incurring negligible accuracy loss. To summarize, this paper has introduced a novel framework, Privacy Leakage over Dependent Attributes in One-Sided Differential Privacy, to investigate and measure privacy breaches in scenarios involving dependent data attributes, protected by OSDP. To evaluate the proposed framework, the paper conducted comprehensive experiments across various real-world datasets, demonstrating its superiority to existing approaches. Furthermore, the paper showcased its feasibility and efficiency in a dependent movie rating scenario. Lastly, the paper highlighted the effectiveness of the framework, highlighting its potential to depedent data privacy research.
