We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls, a requirement we overcome by imposing a small Lipschitz constraint on the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls, and demonstrating the regularity of joint measures under the constraint, which in turn enables the derivation of the necessary regularity of controls. The regularity of joint measures under the constraint relies on establishing a relationship between the regularity of joint measures and the distributional derivatives of the Lagrangian function on the Euclidean space's tangent bundle, a subject that requires further investigation. 

Key Words: Mean field games, state constraints, regularity of joint measures, velocity controls.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that their members are not concentrated on one point, contradicting earlier claims of these structures forming in gaia-like patterns. Further investigation revealed that these structures consist of randomly selected stars from multiple star clusters, including open clusters and the Hercules-Aquila Outer Arm star stream. Upon re-evaluating the classification of these structures, we found that they do not possess unique spatial or movement characteristics distinct from randomly selected stars. Ultimately, we found no evidence to support the presence of these structures, instead attributing the initial findings to Gaia's sampling limitations and the prevalence of overlapping stellar clusters in our galaxy.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style type, gender, and color. Current studies view outfit compatibility as a binary outcome influenced by visual characteristics, disregarding the importance of semantic considerations. To address this, our research introduces the Visual Incompatibility Detection task (VICTOR) and proposes modeling it as a continuous compatibility score that reflects the difficulty in replicating an outfit. We present a detailed analysis of VICTOR, incorporating a suitable dataset and suitable machine learning approaches for comparison. Initially, we examine the efficacy of different visual feature extraction methods and outfit compatibility prediction models. To further improve performance, we develop a large-scale fashion dataset through a quantitative approach and introduce a contrastive learning strategy tailored to the requirements of fashion image understanding. Ultimately, a Transformer-based model leveraging our contrastive pre-trained models achieves the highest accuracy in VICTOR. The proposed approach and associated resources will enable the development of innovative fashion-related applications, such as virtual fashion try-on and digital fashion consulting platforms. The associated code is publicly available at this GitHub repository: https://github.com/steveiclement/victor FashionBERTv2, our fashion-centric language model, and fashion attribute analysis also contribute to the underpinning technology for VICTOR. It is also used in the paper "FashionBERT: Using Fashion Multiple-Source Knowledge for Visual Fashion Retrieval via Language Models" and "Fashion Attribute Analysis and Retrieval by Learning from Fashion Semantic Description with Language Models". These resources can be accessed here: https://github.com/steveiclement/fashion-attribute-retrieval. Additionally, our research relies on the fashion multi-source knowledge that includes existing research and knowledge from knowledge graphs, e-commerce websites, and Wikipedia for fashion retrieval and visual fashion understanding. The associated knowledge graph can be accessed here: https://github.com/steveiclement/fashion-knowledge-graph. It is also used in the paper "Fashion Knowledge Graph Construction and Retrieval by Leveraging Fashion Semantic Description, via Multi-Source Knowledge and Language Models". These resources can be accessed here: https://github.com/steveiclement/fashion-knowledge-graph-construction. It is also used in another research. We presented a new Transformer-based model for the Visual Incompatibility Detection task (VICTOR), and our research in fashion understanding, and the related resources were also discussed in the above text. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and efficiently aggregates data from various devices, even with disparate update frequencies and large update sizes. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, we now consider a challenge where device updates may become unlimited, potentially causing buffer overflow on the edge device. The modified FedBuff algorithm addresses this issue by shifting the aggregation process back to the central server, using a first-in-first-out buffering approach to manage data transmission delays and efficiently aggregate frequent updates from different devices. Theoretical convergence rate analysis and performance benchmarks confirm that FedBuff maintains optimal convergence rates in various scenarios, even with non-synchronous updates, large update sizes, and devices with limited memory. The benefits of this model were demonstrated through numerical simulations and real-world experiments using the CIFAR-10 and ResNet-32 benchmark. The FedBuff algorithm outperformed other models in convergence speed and efficiency, consistently producing results close to the ideal federated learning performance. The code for replicating these experiments is openly available on GitHub. The research highlights the potential of FedBuff in efficiently addressing the scaling limitations of distributed machine learning systems. The study also revealed the conditions under which the FedBuff algorithm can achieve optimal convergence rates in various scenarios. In our investigation, we consider whether the mobility can be enhanced through epitaxial matching of GaN to certain II-IV nitride materials. We performed a theoretical study using the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation to calculate the hole mobility in GaN, revealing that aligning GaN under uniaxial compressive strain by matching it to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ inorganic materials flips the order of the heavy and light hole bands, resulting in a reduced hole mass along the compression axis. Consequently, we observed a significant increase in hole mobility by a factor of ten compared to the unstrained value, primarily due to the altered band structure and reduced hole-phonon scattering rates. Moreover, we found that the predicted hole mobility values matched well with calculated results using a simplified model based only on the strain-induced changes in the material parameters. We have developed a novel method of creating high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y exhibits a local spectral expansion comparable to X. Notably, when X is a graph, Y can be interpreted as a simplicial complex and our method offers an innovative approach in this context.

The link between X and Y can be described using a translation mechanism that allows for the transfer of quantitative properties from one to another. In particular, if X displays strong local spectral expansion, our algorithm generates Y with similar characteristics. This outcome is significant as strong local spectral expansion is a more robust property than local spectral expansion alone.

To confirm the efficacy of our algorithm, we tested it on two specific examples: the Weyl polygon expander graph and the trivial group's Cayley complex. In both cases, the generated Y exhibits local spectral expansion in dimensions up to two, offering an extension of the Weyl polygon's property and proving that expander graphs' properties are not unique to a particular model of computation, thus answering a question first posed by Alberti, Fröhlich, and Strzecki. Furthermore, our algorithm in the trivial group's Cayley complex case reveals a connection between high dimensional expanders and group cohomology, specifically in dimensions one and two, thus offering an algebraic interpretation of our findings. Ultimately, our algorithm's ability to generate Y from X offers a versatile tool for discovering and understanding high dimensional expanders in diverse contexts. 

In related research, our algorithm in this paper has been combined with techniques from generating functions to analysis, enabling us to prove new results about the distribution of simple loops in finite simplicial complexes and also to derive novel estimates about the count of finite simplicial complexes with a local spectral expansion property. The associated work can be found in a separate paper. For a detailed explanation, see arXiv:2102.09138. 

Key words: High dimensional expanders, covering spaces, local spectral expansion, group cohomology, simplicial complexes, projective spaces, projective dimension.

Using data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam, we generated high-resolution images of UGC 8839, revealing a bar structure and multiple spiral arms that extend all the way to a radial distance of about 140 kpc. In contrast, earlier observations were limited by resolution of about 5 kpc. The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and lead-lead interactions but also those of other nuclei and heavy ions. The ALICE detector, situated at the LHC, has successfully captured a broad range of events, including ultra-peripheral collisions between lead ions, which are triggered by the electromagnetic field of the nuclei interacting. These encounters result in the production of a variety of particles both directly and indirectly, making it possible to investigate the photon-photon coupling and subsequent photoproduction of charmonium, particularly the forward J/psi production, using ALICE's detection capabilities. The research outlines two methods used to identify these J/psi interactions and compares them with the theoretical predictions of the NLO model and the $k_T$-factorization PDF, Fit2 PDF. The discrepancy between the predicted values obtained from the two methods is attributed to the differing photon polarization schemes, which can be resolved using the ALICE detector's capabilities to detect exclusive photoproduction cross sections. The study also presents an analysis of the exclusive photoproduction cross section as a function of the square root of the center-of-mass energy and compares it with the results from the previous run at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 62.45$ GeV, showing a significant increase with run IV at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ GeV. The research outlines future plans to further investigate the exclusive photoproduction cross section using additional data from ALICE. The study was presented at The XXV Winter School on the Photonuclear Physics, taking place from January 23-27, 2023, in Dubna, Russia. Formal knowledge acquisition is a crucial aspect of developing artificial intelligence (AI), allowing data providers to illustrate the meaning of raw data through structured information. One essential element of formal knowledge acquisition is Relation Extraction (RE), a subsection of Information Extraction that identifies and categorizes the connections between core entities within a sentence. RE has significant benefits for numerous natural language processing applications, and expertise in RE can facilitate the automated processing of a large amount of institutional data. While rule-based and semi-supervised methods were previously effective approaches to RE, the increasing availability of large datasets and computational capabilities has made deep neural network-based methods the leading choice for RE in recent years. This paper provides an in-depth examination of the deep neural network-based techniques employed in RE, covering recent advancements and providing a comprehensive overview of the top-performing methods. It also discusses the commonly used datasets for RE within different domains and highlights areas for future research. Moreover, the source code used in this study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/hk-ai-lab/RE-overview. This public repository includes code and data resources to support future research on RE. It is expected that future breakthroughs in this area will lead to breakthroughs in natural language understanding and formal knowledge acquisition. We hope that this repository will serve as a valuable asset to researchers working on RE. We intend to continuously update the repository to reflect the latest advancements in RE. We welcome contributions that can enhance the repository and promote collaboration among researchers. If you have any questions or suggestions, please do not hesitate to reach out to us via the email address provided at the end of this document. We look forward to building a research community around RE. Key words: Relation Extraction, Formal Knowledge Acquisition, Artificial Intelligence. Abstract File: overview.pdf. This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving two circular membranes that share a common boundary but differ in their outer and inner radii. The setup also involves a membrane with a sealed end, represented by the interior circle. The shared boundary is subject to a specific transmission condition and generates a unique Dirichlet-to-Neumann map that influences the eigenvalues. By adjusting the outer and inner radii, we can calculate the eigenvalues and analyze the associated eigenvectors. Notably, our results demonstrate that the first eigenvalue reaches a maximum when the transmission coefficient and the Robin parameter achieve a particular optimal value. Conversely, the second eigenvalue reaches a minimum under the same conditions, and this behavior is reflected in various physical and geometric scenarios. Furthermore, our research highlights the significance of choosing the correct transmission and Robin parameters to optimize the Steklov eigenvalues. The study has important implications for understanding Timoshenko's theory of vibrating membranes and shedding light on a longstanding open problem in this context. Additionally, our findings contribute to a broader understanding of the mustache effect, a term that emerged in the context of this problem and describes the intriguing transitions observed in the eigenvalues of the Steklov problem. The mathematical analysis employed in this study can be generalized using the theory of boundary linear relations and is expected to have a broader impact, enabling the extension and application of our results to various other types of operators beyond the Laplacian. The eigenvectors and their behavior are particularly interesting and warrant further exploration, given their relation to the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map and the transmission and Robin parameters. Consequently, this study should facilitate a more in-depth analysis of the eigenvectors and their dynamic characteristics in scenarios involving non-separating interfaces. The connections between our research and other fields, such as non-separating tangles in topology and link homotopy in knot theory, are also an area of active inquiry, and we anticipate that our results will shed new light on these areas. The relationships between the eigenvalues of the Steklov problem, the knot energies and link energies, and other types of energies and homotopy classes in physics and geometry are particularly significant and warrant further quantitative and qualitative study. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework that illustrates its implications and analyze its effects on clustering tasks. To address this issue, we develop a new supervised hypergraph reconstruction method, involving the construction of idealized hypergraphs from graphs, and subsequently apply this framework to cluster nodes within these hypergraphs. Notably, our approach exhibits enhanced accuracy when limited to two nodes, and performs competitively on datasets with three or more nodes. We compare the performance of this method against alternative schemes in clustering tasks, such as clustering on graphs with added inter-node connections, and the selection of key graph nodes. Through thorough evaluation of various datasets and time complexities, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach. Specifically, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on two-node datasets, and displays promising generalization capabilities for datasets with three or more nodes. Furthermore, we show that our approach is resilient to deficiencies in the hypergraph model. We anticipate that this research will contribute positively to the further exploration of hypergraph principles in machine learning. this process would be beneficial. To achieve this, we must first grasp the essence

at multiple levels. Our current research focuses on deciphering the semantic
meaning within these reports by examining the connections between findings,
diseases, body parts, and other critical concepts. We believe that by dissecting
and analyzing reports in great detail, we can uncover hidden patterns and
relationships, ultimately facilitating the understanding of radiology reports. We
have collected and thoroughly annotated a large collection of chest X-ray reports,
which include over 250,000 entries along with over 1.79 billion words. These
detailed annotations allow us to analyze reports from multiple perspectives and
understand the complex relationships within them. Our advanced research takes
these reports as input and aims to generate summaries, identify key information,
and classify reports into predefined categories, all while basing our analysis on
the semantic meaning within the reports. We have successfully created and
tested summary generation models that demonstrate improved accuracy over

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range and then made an educated guess that this range is the absolute minimum. Subsequent work by a different researcher, collaborating with David Gabai, found counterexamples that contradict this theory. Due to the connection between tight contact structures and taut foliations, researchers now consider the possibility that this theory could hold for tight contact structures, which are also related to Euler classes of one. To test this idea, recent findings show that previously found counterexamples are also related to tight contact structures, leaving room for the possibility that this theory might be correct for tight contact structures. This research investigates whether the previously established lower and upper bounds for Euler classes apply solely to the minimum number one. An investigation of previously found counterexamples and the existing knowledge about Euler classes and tight contact structures found that all known examples have a general characteristic, which is that they contain a particular type of subgraph. It can be theorized that this particular type of subgraph is inherently connected to the counterexamples, which might lead to the idea that this theory might be correct for tight contact structures that do not contain this particular type of subgraph. Recent breakthroughs and findings provide evidence to support this idea. It remains to be determined whether this idea is always correct and whether it can be extended to apply to all tight contact structures. To verify the theory for tight contact structures that do not contain the particular type of subgraph, further research is needed to provide a proof by showing that these structures cannot have multiple eigenvalues and that this would confirm the theory. To verify the theory for all tight contact structures, further research is needed to investigate whether the lower and upper bounds apply to the eigenvalues of the Laplacian of the metric of the contact structure. An alternative approach to verifying the theory is to connect the research to an unsolved problem in mathematics, which is to determine whether certain 3-manifolds that have a particular characteristic can be given a particular geometric structure, which is known as the hyperbolicity question. An unrelated research found that a particular type of 3-manifolds that have a particular characteristic, which include some of the previously found counterexamples, can be given a particular geometric structure, which is known as the Delvevo-Thurston theorem. This research connects the evidence that tight contact structures that do not contain the particular type of subgraph can be given a particular geometric structure, which is known as the hyperbolicity structure

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures. Nonetheless, the proposed method falters when different polarization modes exist. Therefore, we suggest combining this approach with anisotropy of the near-field intensity distribution, yielding a comprehensive evaluation of both the degree of unidirectionality and emission polarity. Ultimately, this combined methodology facilitates in-depth analysis of directional emission and reveals the underlying competition between dual polarization modes in their contributions to the polar far-field profile. Consequently, this method holds great potential for investigating more intricate microphotonics systems. Please refer to the attached paper for a detailed description. Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Finally, our investigation involved assessing whether cumulative errors in predicting cryptocurrency prices would fall within the predicted bounds as suggested by model 'G7', an advanced econometric model incorporating a variety of regression analysis methods, model 'B', a basic econometric model featuring linear regression, served as a comparison, revealed that both models would frequently fail to contain the actual price fluctuations of mainstream cryptocurrencies, leaving room for improvement through the incorporation of additional variables in model 'G7'. Lastly, our study addressed the issue of whether investors in cryptocurrencies are taking on excessive risk by comparing the daily returns of leading cryptocurrencies with major financial assets, using both traditional and alternative risk measures – the variance and the skewness of return distributions. Our analysis showed that investors in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple have been taking on relatively high levels of risk as per traditional return analysis; yet, our skewness measure suggested a diverse range of possibilities. To gauge the diversification benefits of including cryptocurrencies in a portfolio of traditional assets, we calculated the Pearson correlation coefficients between daily returns in US dollars of major cryptocurrencies and stock indexes. Our results indicated a significant and steady decrease in correlation coefficients from 2016 to 2020. Furthermore, our time-warping analysis showed a notable increase in similarities between daily returns of cryptocurrencies and their comparators during this period. Lastly, our investigation provided concrete evidence supporting the diversification benefits of including cryptocurrencies in a portfolio of traditional assets – the Euro, Japanese yen, and major stock indexes – as per daily returns in US dollars, particularly evident since the onset of the 'Corona-crisis'. The calculation is complicated and requires resolution of a complete set of hydrodynamic equations, but by leveraging the properties of integrability, we can simplify the problem and directly apply the inverse scattering method to the Zakharov-Shabat system, resulting in a closed form expression for the probability functional. The calculation can be extended to higher time periods, where we find that the probability functional exhibits a nested structure, consisting of a product of probability functionals at earlier time periods, thus demonstrating scaling behavior at early time periods. The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed with data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing calibrated potential data from each spacecraft, researchers are able to examine the full spectrum of turbulence phases within this type of plasma. By calculating the cross-power spectra of difference signals between various spacecraft, they are able to study the spectral behavior of the electric field and density fluctuations within the solar wind. Results show a pronounced scaling pattern in the solar wind at 1-10 dc electron scales, aligning with simulative data of decaying, non-uniform plasmas. This study also explores various sources of turbulence in the solar wind using data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. It's possible that density irregularities observed by the spacecraft could be attributed to cathode spikes, a type of plasma instability previously observed in laboratory settings. However, the full range of observed scales suggests these laboratory experiments don't fully capture the complexity of turbulence in the solar wind. By examining data from passages through the outer heliosphere, researchers discover a broad spectrum of turbulence spanning from ion scales up to scales equivalent to half of the ion inertial length. This particular behavior is observed in multiple, distinct instances where turbulence data is collected during passages through the outer heliosphere. It's worth noting that these discoveries are contingent on positive findings from previous studies on plasma turbulence and require further observation, particularly data from the Parker Solar Probe, which has encountered plasma at unprecedentedly high temperatures and densities. Ultimately, examining data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission shows the associated instruments are capable of detecting electric field and density fluctuations across an extensive range of scales within the solar wind and other environments. This capability could lead to further discoveries in future space missions. Finally, future research should prioritize observing plasma turbulence at scales where decays become minimal and in various environments beyond the solar wind. This includes but isn't limited to observing turbulence at the magnetospheric boundaries, within the Earth's bow shock and in planetary magnetospheres. It's also anticipated that the observations from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission will significantly contribute to, and significantly influence the study of plasma turbulence for years to come. Additionally, examining data at these various scales will present valuable, uncompared findings that will greatly enhance our understanding of space plasma turbulence. In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions in various wavelength ranges. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds, even for wavelengths below 5 nm. This modification has enabled the generation of a pulse with a duration of 50 attoseconds at a wavelength of 6.7 nm using a 10 m undulator, a feat accompanied by a substantial increase in pulse energy and a stable carrier-to-slope frequency ratio. This achievement sets the groundwork for achieving pulse durations of ten attoseconds in the VUV and one attosecond in the soft X-ray region using this modified approach. Furthermore, simulations indicate that with certain improvements to the undulator design, pulse durations as short as 30 fs can be achieved at wavelengths of 2 nm. It is anticipated that this modified approach will significantly boost the capabilities of EUF and FEEF facilities, enabling the generation of higher-energy attosecond pulses for user applications. This modification could potentially be integrated into the ATLAS facility, enabling the production of pulses lasting up to one femtosecond in the soft X-ray region. This development has significant implications for a range of applications including nonlinear multifold paradigm applications, high harmonic table operations, and X-fEL hybrid mode operation, among others. It is anticipated that this work will facilitate groundbreaking breakthroughs in various areas including nonlinear photon-scattering phenomena, attosecond electronics, biomolecular imaging, extreme UV-femtosecond lithography, coherent spectroscopy, few-cycle electron microscopy, attosecond metrology, high-repetition-rate FEL nuclear physics, and quantum computing, among others. Additionally, this modification will enable the demonstration of tabletop hard X-ray sources based on mercury ion schemes and mercury lattices, mercury nanocrystals, and nanowire doped silicon systems. This work will also make available a wide range of new hard X-ray source options including astrophysical source mimicking, biological source mimicking, condensed matter source mimicking, nuclear physics source mimicking, and quantum optics source mimicking hard X-rays. Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a serious threat to democratic integrity in the United States. To address this issue,
our system utilizes simulated annealing to evaluate fairness in election outcomes by
assessing the average difference between voting results in adjusted districts and
those calculated using a neutral, balanced method. This approach allows us to
identify potentially manipulated elections and provide evidence for judicial review.
Additionally, our tool offers a simple way for users to explore the effect of district
redrawing on election outcomes by allowing them to input their own district maps
and view their average result. For illustrative purposes, our research focuses on the
2018 Texas Senate election, which revealed strong indications of voting system
exploitation; however, further legal action is necessary to verify the results. This
project's goal is to create a reliable method for detecting potential election
deception and promoting transparent, fair voting practices. The source code for
this project is openly available on GitHub. To maintain user anonymity, sensitive
election data is stored on a secure server at Texas Tech University. Our research is
a collaborative effort between researchers and lawyers working to address
democratic misconduct. Key stakeholders include the League of Women Voters and the
Karlan & Keys law professor project, which aims to establish a fair election district
redrawing method that promotes transparent politics. To obtain the data used in this
research, contact us at [ew4math@gmail.com](http://ew4math@gmail.com). A novel approach to defect detection in patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor filtering and phase information into the Fourier Momentum to distinguish defects from fabric patterns. The proposed method incorporates three main steps: first, high-resolution images are generated from downsampled versions to conceal the fabric pattern; next, the phase information in the Fourier Momentum is leveraged to localize defects; finally, low-rank decomposition is applied to differentiate defects from genuine fabric images. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in detecting fabric defects, showcasing its superiority to existing techniques through notably high detection rates and remarkably reduced false positives. Furthermore, the designed framework yields impressive performance even when dealing with severely damaged fabric images. In particular, the accuracy of the proposed method surpasses that of the best comparable approaches by 15.13% when the impact of parameters is minimal. Ultimately, the developed framework exhibits exceptional resilience, with results showcasing its potential as a robust and versatile fabric defect detection solution. Precise quantitative values highlighting its performance and comparisons with benchmark approaches are as follows: Our method outperforms others with AUC values of 98.47% for training and 97.18% for testing, respectively; specifically, the accuracy surpasses that of the best comparable approaches by 15.13%, 12.61%, and 4.52% in test datasets 'TD', 'TDr', and 'TDr', respectively. Additionally, the designed framework yields notably high detection rates with AP values of 97.18% for training and 94.49% for testing, especially showing improvements of 12.61%, 4.52%, and 2.03% in test datasets 'TDr', 'TDr', and 'TD', respectively. Lastly, the proposed method exhibits exceptional results with NPV values of 94.49% for testing and 97.18% for training, particularly showing the following comparisons with benchmark approaches: 4.52%, 2.03%, and 6.55% in test datasets 'TDr', 'TDr', and 'TD', respectively. Detailed analysis and visualization reveal that the outstanding performance of the proposed approach is largely attributed to the effectiveness of the integrated GHOG descriptor in accurately extracting directional features from defect images, as well as the utility of low-rank decomposition in distinguishing defects from genuine fabric images. To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to simulate the impact of its actions, leveraging this understanding to forecast the outcome of different navigational choices. As a result, the agent achieves improved cross-target and cross-scene generalization capabilities, outperforming current state-of-the-art models in extensive evaluations on various indoor and outdoor environments. Moreover, the agent demonstrates a more realistic and navigable trajectory in 3D simulations by incorporating the learned environmental structure into its decision-making process. Our work bridges the gap between short-term navigation tasks and long-term goal-oriented navigation, providing a more comprehensive understanding of target-driven visual navigation through the lens of causality and information theory. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/cs-chan/VISNavITR.

In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model and find that about half of these remnants survive as neutron stars or black holes due to disturbances from birth stars. Our study estimates that supernovae explosions caused by core-collapse result in the ejection of nearly all black hole remnants, whereas those from pair-instability have a higher likelihood of 0.1-1% of binary systems surviving as white dwarves. However, binary Population III stars primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear clusters which have a low total mass of $10^4 M_{\odot}$ and an initial radius of 1 pc, and our analysis indicates that about half of these remnants merge within a Hubble time due to dynamical interactions, while the others merge at a higher rate than predicted by stellar evolution. In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on active and reactive power control strategies for ESS. These studies demonstrate that this method can effectively detect incidents and identify the underlying causes in real-time. Furthermore, our approach is versatile and can be easily adapted to accommodate a wide range of incidents involving ESS and other contemporary distribution system technologies. We envision that this method will play a crucial role in the development of intelligent control systems and digital twin frameworks for distribution system operators. Additionally, this work serves as a crucial foundation for the creation of standardized incident detection templates that can be widely applied across various digital infrastructure services. Finally, we anticipate that this method will contribute to the enhancement of cybersecurity and digital forensic capabilities by identifying and analyzing anomalous behavior in distribution networks. The proposed method and associated toolkit are now available for public use at https://github.com/NYU-EPSS/Incident-Detection/tree/main/README.md. It is anticipated that this toolkit will serve as a crucial resource for the entire power industry. Currently, detection of incidents in power distribution systems heavily relies on rule-based methods which face several limitations such as reduced generalizability and increased dependency on experience. A more recent approach to incident detection involves the use of machine learning algorithms, but these methods necessitate a parameterized model of the system and a substantial amount of labeled data, which is often scarce in real-world applications. In contrast, our proposed method employs a data-driven approach based on the principles of flow-based methods to identify anomalies and incidents in power distribution systems without requiring prior knowledge or parameters. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through comprehensive case studies that showcase its ability to detect incidents, identify underlying causes, and function effectively in real-time. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks such as natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One major limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, restricting the number of tests that can be conducted within a reasonable time frame.
This paper introduces TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized framework that enhances the simulation of text-based games, achieving a remarkable increase in processing speed of over one million steps per second on a single CPU core. 
This remarkable boost in performance enables the concurrent evaluation of multiple agents and environments, opening up new avenues for agent training and assessment. 
To validate the capabilities of our system, we present a range of empirical studies that demonstrate its potential for large-scale agent evaluations, fast and simple clone detections, and the creation of diverse game scenarios. 
Furthermore, we provide guidelines and best practices for optimizing commercial game development using our approach, showcasing the effectiveness of these strategies through the successful modification of the commercial game Lost Kingdoms to employ TextWorldExpress. 
This highly optimized framework not only offers a range of innovative processing techniques but also serves as a resource for integrating existing and proposed solutions to accelerate text-based game simulations. 
Ultimately, TextWorldExpress serves as an open-source resource for accelerating text-based game simulations using the Python programming language. 
The source code is freely accessible at https://github.com/braid-lab/TextWorldExpress under the terms of the permissive BSD-3 license. 
The framework's API documentation can be found at https://textworld.readthedocs.io.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-dependent information, significantly contributing to teaching robots human-like motion through emulation. In robotics literature, there has been a recent shift towards transfer learning between robots. However, the transfer of this information from human to robot systems has been overlooked. This research aims to bridge this knowledge gap with a new method to transfer manipulability information from one robot to another by utilizing point clouds to align task spaces. Our approach involves using ICp to match the manipulated points within the manipulability ellipsoids' red and target spaces, employing the Quaternions' manifold as a constraint to prevent convergence on wild trajectories. Additionally, we use the Parallel Transport method to determine the optimal target ellipsoid after successful alignment. This novel approach is evaluated using the Jaco2 and PUMI robots, teaching the former to replicate tasks originally demonstrated by the latter. The results show that our method is successful in all trials, demonstrating its efficiency and effectiveness. You can replicate these experiments using our public mbed library, available at https://github.com/roboticslab/mbe-xycb. This library also includes a web-based interface where you can interactively learn from demonstrations in 3D. Using this tool, you can learn new tasks by uploading existing demonstrations in 3D, and even apply this information to download new poses for your robot's task-dependent variable. This research paves the way for future studies on teaching human-like motion to robots by leveraging human expertise, rather than having to perform time-consuming inverse kinematics computations to replicate human-like joint configurations. This transfer learning paradigm may also extend beyond manipulability and be applied to other robotic systems, significantly reducing the necessary training data and time. A key advantage is that the involved manipulability ellipsoids are easy to understand and interpret, making this transfer learning paradigm accessible to a broad group of roboticists. This research has been presented at the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, held in Birmingham, UK. A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, leveraging unstructured video footage where objects are rotated. These accidental turntables - videos captured incidentally - provide diverse, unlabeled object views, and our method exploits them to learn robust 3D pose representations without requiring manual annotation. We develop an approach to identify turntables from in-the-wild videos, and introduce a simple yet effective framework for estimating 3D object pose from a single view, which can be trained end-to-end without requiring ground truth. Our method demonstrates superior performance in 3D pose estimation compared to existing top-tier models, and we showcase its applications in generating realistic synthetic data and studying object shapes and materials. The proposed approach can also be generalized for training from motion tracks, another type of unstructured data, making it a versatile tool for computer vision research. Code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/aidg/accTurntables. Experimental evaluation reveals that our method excels in 3D pose estimation, outperforms existing models, and provides more stable and generalizable representations compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, we find that training on accidental turntables enhances synthetic data generation, and studying objects through turntables provides valuable insights into their shapes and materials. While initial turntable discovery methods exhibit limitations, particularly in accurately identifying turntables, we find that training models on these discovered turntables significantly improves 3D pose estimation performance. Specifically, our method achieves superior results on 3D evaluation metrics, and consistently performs better than existing models, demonstrating its value in computer vision research. We contribute three main areas of research: (1) a novel approach for discovering turntables from in-the-wild videos, (2) an unsupervised 3D pose estimation framework, and (3) an evaluation of our method's performance, which highlights its generalizability and versatility. Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts about the safety of COVID-19 vaccines due to misinformation spread online. Misinformation about vaccines often takes the form of false information conveyed by influential individuals, typically lacking concrete evidence and presented in social media platforms like Twitter. This study aims to determine the extent to which Twitter discourse reflects mainstream media narratives regarding COVID-19 vaccine efficacy, using a novel approach that categorizes tweets as pro, anti, or neutral. A proposed framework incorporates a combined social influence measure that integrates both individual and group components, showing that Twitter users are more likely to adopt mainstream views on COVID-19 vaccine efficacy due to the influence of neutral parties, such as fact-checking organizations, rather than the opinions of ordinary users. Furthermore, this study illustrates the utility of social network analysis in understanding online discourse around contentious topics like COVID-19 vaccine misinformation. The proposed framework's methodological innovations include the utilization of differential privacy for protecting sensitive user information and the incorporation of misinformation detection, vaccine adoption/rejection classification, and social influence measurement processes. A comprehensive validation strategy was employed to assess the accuracy of the developed system on an independent test set. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly, we establish a similar finite-time collapse outcome for solutions with positive energy located within a confined area. These results are derived using a combination of elements, including the blow-up theorem for the Schrödinger equation in a larger-than-critical range, constructed by Germain and Megchew, as well as an estimate for solutions to the linear Schrödinger equation near a compact convex barrier developed by the present author. We also make use of an energy-related inequality originally proposed by Kapitanski. We develop two distinct strategies to address this problem, each yielding distinct approaches to prove the solution's collapse. These methods draw on insights from the theory of elliptic equations, particularly when dealing with solutions with positive energy, as well as a non-relativistic version of the Hartree approximation for solutions to the Schrödinger equation, particularly when dealing with solutions having negative energy. We hope that these alternative proofs will contribute to the development of new methods and approaches in the field. We also make a statement about the solution's spatial pattern near the compact convex barrier in the case of negative energy. This statement is qualified by a reference to the theory of elliptic equations, particularly in the context of the Harnack-Schwarz inequality. We hope that this problem will attract the attention of researchers in the field of elliptic equations and, in turn, may shed new light on the theory of solutions to the Schrödinger equation. Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency are required for this approach. To address this need, enhancing training point distribution is an important direction of investigation. Both adaptive and quasi-uniform sampling methods have significant advantages, but each has drawbacks: the former can efficiently utilize data points but leads to decreased accuracy, while the latter yields high accuracy but underutilizes data points. To bridge this gap, we propose Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, which combines an adaptive sampling method and a node refinement procedure grounded in the residuals. This way, the framework can dynamically adjust the distribution of training points and further improve sampling quality based on the residuals. Compared to traditional methods, RANG results in a notable decrease in training time and a notable increase in model accuracy. To evaluate the performance of this approach, we used a one-dimensional convection-diffusion equation and a two-dimensional Burgers equation, demonstrating that RANG generates adaptive sampling points during the training process, refines these points using residuals, and boosts both efficiency and accuracy. A comparative study with state-of-the-art sampling methods revealed that RANG yields the best possible outcomes. Furthermore, we investigated the generalizability of this approach by assessing its performance on data generated through Monte Carlo sampling, demonstrating its versatility and practical usefulness. To assess the precision of this approach, we used metrics such as mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared percentage error (RMSPE), showing that RANG significantly outperforms existing sampling methods in both error metrics. To evaluate the efficiency of this approach, we measured the computational time and memory requirements, revealing a notable decrease in computational time and minimal memory requirements following the implementation of RANG. A thorough ablation study further validated the efficacy of this approach, excluding any room for further improvement. To ensure the reliability of this approach, we also developed user-friendly software packages in Python, facilitating the use of RANG for a wide range of users. In conclusion, we believe that RANG presents an innovative, efficient, and adaptable solution to sampling training points for physics-informed neural networks and offers numerous practical applications. While primarily developed to enhance the sampling strategy, this approach can be used to improve both efficiency and accuracy. As such, we expect RANG to become a valuable tool in the continued development of physics-informed neural networks. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/DeepLearn

Deep learning models have achieved great success in computer vision, however they have a major drawback as they are sensitive to image orientation. The issue becomes more pronounced when dealing with images that have ambiguous orientation labels, this problem is particularly evident in the application of orientation-labeled images in tasks such as object recognition. The standard approach to addressing this issue involves the use of Fully Oriented Convolution (FOC) operators; each FOC operator applies a 2D convolution to all eight possible orientation labels, resulting in high computational complexity and vast numbers of parameters. The approaches in the current literature to mitigate this issue are limited to reducing the number of FOC operators or the number of parameters in each FOC operator. In this paper, a new Fully Oriented Convolution (FOC) structure is proposed called Orientation Convolution Network (OCN), where each element in the feature map interacts with neighboring elements in a rotated manner. The major distinction between OCN and FOC lies in the former's reduced complexity of operations and parameters. The proposed model demonstrates superior performance when compared to existing models in various computer vision tasks such as object recognition, semantic segmentation, and k-means clustering. The proposed model also exhibits improved computational efficiency when compared to existing models, with a notable underlining fact that the number of parameters per FOC operator in OCN can be dynamically adjusted in line with the characteristics of the underlying images. The proposed model also exhibits enhanced interpretability when compared to existing models, where the orientation-dependent features can be effectively decoupled for the purpose of understanding representation learning. The proposed model has been extensively tested with oriented-labeled datasets for the purpose of understanding representation learning. The model has been further applied to the application of image denoising and image deblurring, where the model has demonstrated notable performance when compared to existing models. We are developing an image slicer for an integral field unit, ROSIE IFU, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. By splitting the 50.4 x 53.5 field of view into four subfields, and further segmenting these into 21 individual 0.6 x 53.5 slices, we'll achieve four pseudo-slits, spaced six arcminutes apart. This will allow for a spectral range of 1800 Angstroms with a resolution of 2000. Our current progress includes preparing the optics, coating the first slicer, crafting the mounts, and writing the software, all aiming to enhance IMACS's functionality by facilitating the efficient examination of expansive astronomical objects like nebulae and galaxies. Furthermore, by utilizing its own internal optics, ROSIE will offer an additional 1.5 arcsecond x 4.5 arcminute'slice' along the spectrograph's 1.57 arcminute field. This project is crucial in leveraging Magellan's unique 6.5 meter telescope to their fullest potential, thereby contributing to various scientific research, including studying star formations and discovering distant galaxies. We will present Magellan IFU's capabilities at the 233rd AAS meeting.

The findings show that attention-based CSI features lead to a performance enhancement of up to 32.19% in 81.81% of tested locations. COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables running tasks previously requiring user input with programmable buttons, enabling automation and integration with other R tools. It offers a range of features, including model import, species population analysis, and sensitivity assessments, all accessible through a web browser. Currently available as an R package, ShinyCOPASI enhances user access to COPASI capabilities across diverse platforms and web browsers. Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification across a wide range of contexts and applications. This work aims to establish a common framework that 1) systematically addresses various uncertainties associated with experimental and physical data, 2) provides a comprehensive comparison of different uncertainty quantification methods across multiple applications, and 3) promotes future research by highlighting unresolved issues and promising areas for further exploration. This study covers topics such as data randomness, model selection, optimization, overfitting, ensemble methods, sampling, regression, image analysis, portfolio optimization, credit risk assessment, and quantitative seismology, leveraging notable recent projects like amygdalab and DeepHackFinance as illustrative examples. Ultimately, the amygdalab platform is used to demonstrate a comprehensive comparison of different approaches to uncertainty quantification across various applications. This study's main contribution can be accessed in an open-source repository at https://github.com/amygdalab/UQ-Methods-Metrics-Comparisons. This repository offers a wealth of supplementary information, including detailed tutorials, additional resources, and comprehensive results. This work was inspired by the 2019 Amygdalab UQ Workshop, which brought together experts from diverse fields and provided the foundational knowledge needed for this comprehensive review. We hope this study will serve as a valuable resource, connecting expert knowledge on NNs, physics, and engineering to promote collaborative research and develop novel techniques for uncertainty quantification. We welcome contributions from the community, and we look forward to seeing how this study will evolve in the future. In particular, areas where contributions would be particularly valuable are listed below. In the context of Markov Decision Processes, Policy Iteration presents a straightforward approach to solving optimal control problems by iteratively improving policy and value functions until convergence. However, the vast scale of modern Markov Decision Processes often hinders this method, making it computationally infeasible within standard CPU frameworks. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Inexact GMRES Policy Iteration, a modified algorithm that enables suboptimal quality updates to the policy and value functions, thus facilitating the solution of large-scale problems. By allowing for suboptimal updates, the time complexity is reduced from quadratic to linear, while the space complexity remains constant. We validate the efficacy of our approach through both theoretical and practical analyses, showcasing its ability to yield high-performing policies in large-scale Markov Decision Processes at a fraction of the time required by exact methods. Specifically, we achieve speedups of one order of magnitude and three orders of magnitude for the 1000-state Room Grid and 15,634-state Hospital Simulation models, respectively. Moreover, the Inexact GMRES Policy Iteration algorithm consistently produces policies with comparable or higher rewards compared to exact methods in both scenarios. As a result, this algorithm presents a practical and efficient solution to optimal control problems of large-scale Markov Decision Processes. This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. To efficiently handle the large datasets produced by such simulators, an approach involves first selecting key points to approximate the output, and then applying a specialized method to estimate optimal input parameters at those points, while accounting for any uncertainty in the solution. A comprehensive simulation-based study compares the proposed technique with other established methods on a range of synthetic and real-world scenarios. Results show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. To facilitate widespread use, a freely available open-source implementation of the proposed method has been developed and made accessible on GitHub. This tool allows users to easily reproduce the findings and apply the estimated model parameters to related problems. Furthermore, the estimated models can serve as valuable resources for informing policy and strategic decisions in fields such as hydrology. In particular, the tool includes pre-estimated parameter values for Athens, Georgia, USA, and other locations are expected to benefit from similar analyses. Moving forward, researchers intend to expand the proposed method to accommodate additional applications and consider wider range of possible parameter values. A related tutorial T115 Estimating Hydrological Parameters using Multiple Contour Estimation will be presented at MCM 2022. This tutorial aims to introduce participants to the proposed method and demonstrate its implementation on publicly available data for five major cities in the United States. A corresponding Jupyter notebook has been developed to facilitate hands-on participation and is available for download on GitHub. Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts within an aggressive time frame using local queries. Nonetheless, no specific constraint on the distribution was identified in previous studies. Our main findings indicate that (1) if data comes from a finitely dependent distribution with limited mixing, then dense concepts can be efficiently learned using local queries, even for complex parameters (e.g., k-manhattan kernels for large k). (2) if data comes from an independent distribution, but with adversarially selected concepts, then local queries can still be utilized to achieve aggressive learning times. These results are particularly significant as they imply that several well-known problems can be solved efficiently using local queries in certain distributional assumptions. Our techniques, in turn, inspire the development of new query types, such as the 'neighborhood sample' query, which samples nearby instances and can be utilized for several dense concept learning algorithms. Notably, although the findings rely on specific distributional assumptions, they can be easily generalized to various learning settings (e.g., learning with partial feedback, or adapting to concept drift). Our work follows a new paradigm in machine learning research - that is the investigation of learning in specific distributional assumptions - a paradigm which has already led to significant breakthroughs in learning in phases and learning with feedback. We hope that this paradigm will continue to lead to significant advances in machine learning research. Our work is accompanied by thorough educational materials and a set of chosen problem examples in the full paper. Finally, the efficiency and usefulness of the neighborhood sample query can be illustrated using simple word games (e.g. 'wordle'), which can be accessed through our interactive educational website. In particular, the neighborhood sample query can be utilized to solve the 'wordle' game using a simple dense concept learning algorithm. We hope that this material will be useful for teaching graduate level courses in machine learning. We made a special effort to make the educational materials self-contained and provided many examples of chosen problem sets at the end of the educational section. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV were tracked within a narrow cone around the jet axis. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector code's internal consistency results in a relatively accurate estimate of the star formation rate at this particular wavelength. Consequently, we suggest that the star formation rate can be reliably estimated based on spectroscopic data in the near-infrared bracket line, and this methodological approach can serve as a benchmark for testing other predictions of the Prospector framework. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional POMD models that rely on specified duration ranges, this new approach can model any distribution. We demonstrate that by sampling from a median-gained categorical distribution, this model mirrors the accuracy of more complex, higher-capacity recurrent neural network models, including a constant POMD model. This powerful new model offers several advantages, including better handling of outliers and noisy data, and a more stable training process. We also propose an efficient sampling method that reduces computational burden while maintaining comparable performance to previous methods. The results of our experiments reveal that this new model surpasses existing duration models in terms of speech naturalness. Furthermore, we have made the code for our model and evaluation dataset available on GitHub under the MIT License. Moreover, studies have shown that general practitioners make fewer accurate diagnoses compared to artificial intelligence. The Skincare project aimed to address this by creating an innovative diagnostic and decision support system in dermatology. It combined the capabilities of interactive machine learning with deep learning to enhance the skills of doctors and augment diagnostic capabilities, particularly in the identification of malignant skin lesions. A baseline model, trained using a large dermatology image dataset (ISIC), delivered outstanding results and demonstrated potential for widespread application, including support for both general practitioners and dermatologists. The project also focused on creating effective communication channels between humans and machines to facilitate machine learning. In essence, the Skincare project sought to integrate human expertise with artificial intelligence to establish a collaborative diagnostic tool for dermatology. It is now available as a open-source interactive decision support system on GitHub. Currently, a pilot study is being conducted at a primary care clinic to assess whether a general practitioner can improve their diagnostic skills with the help of the Skincare system. To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from time-series data, a innovative approach is introduced, which relies on a probabilistic autoencoder trained end-to-end. This method transforms noisy spectral data into a reduced-dimensional latent space, effectively isolating a supernova's intrinsic characteristics while learning the associated noise. As such, it enables the extraction of variability patterns unique to each supernova, even in cases with limited spectral data. Furthermore, this model can differentiate Type Ia supernovae from other astrophysical sources, such as active galactic nuclei, by learning to distinguish true targets from artificially generated SEDs as negative classes. The model's utility will be particularly significant in various SNe Ia applications, such as cosmology and parameter estimation, by reducing the requirement for extensive spectral data. Our approach was inspired by similar methods used in high-energy astrophysics and climate science. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model through a series of thorough evaluations, including multiple randomness runs to ensure the model's reliability and robustness. The results show that our approach is superior to existing models that use Gaussian Processes and Decision Trees in terms of accuracy and latent feature recovery. Based on these findings, we believe that a low-dimensional latent space is an essential data representation for further deep learning applications aimed at deriving cosmological and phenomenological parameters from SNe Ia spectra with limited wavelength coverage and limited snapshot numbers. The associated code is publicly available on GitHub at the specified link. This paper describes McMini, a lightweight model checker for verifying the correctness of multithreaded C programs. Built around a flexible thread creation mechanism, McMini includes a built-in cache to efficiently manage memory access and enables the model checker to effectively deal with a variety of program structures. Comprised of around 300 lines of code, McMini leverages the features of DPOR, a distributed predicate logical operator-based model checking paradigm, to ensure a high level of efficiency and reliability. In this paper, we delve into the design and implementation details of McMini, including its integration with a state pool strategy and inter-thread hash table, as well as the introduction of a thread suspension mechanism. A comparative evaluation of McMini against other state-of-the-art model checkers highlights its exceptional performance in vectorized operations and minimal memory utilization. Furthermore, a comprehensive set of real-world program tests confirms the McMini model checker's ability to effectively detect a range of errors and its potential for integration within commercial model checkers. Specifically, McMini has the potential to be integrated into OpenMPSC, a lightweight open-source model checker. In fact, a comparison of McMini with OpenMPSC reveals that in cases where both model checkers can detect errors, they yield identical detection results, underscoring the soundness of the McMini design. Crucially, McMini's lightweight design and exceptional performance make it an attractive candidate for use within other model checkers. At the same time, McMini's compact code base and efficient cache system architecture make it a valuable resource for establishing new model checking methodologies focused on multithreaded programs. In particular, two novel distributed model checking approaches, McMini's predictability-aware distributed model checking (PADMC) and McMini's operator-based distributed model checking with thread creation (ODMC), are proposed and demonstrated to yield comparable error detection results to current state-of-the-art model checkers. In conclusion, this research contributes three new ideas in the area of model checking: (i) integrating a thread creation mechanism into a model checker; (ii) employing inter-thread hash tables during model checking; and (iii) effectively incorporating a cache into a model checker. Additionally, this research has identified potential areas for further exploration in the area of distributed model checking. Specifically, the following inquiries were raised: (a) how can cache performance be further optimized; (i) how can thread creation be further refined; and (ii) what other design changes can be made to the McMini model checker to further improve its design.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects in spoken input arising from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating an attentive activation function, like Rectified Linear with attention, into our end-to-end system. This system leverages two fully connected layers and a customizable activation function for processing input features, enabling it to focus on specific input features to distinguish synthetic components. We also introduce a novel strategy to adjust the Rectified Linear with attention function to accommodate variants of Maxout and Linear activation functions. Furthermore, we applied our end-to-end system with attentive activation functions to various datasets, including VCSig, SIGMALabelled, and TIMIT, and compared it with established countermeasure systems. The results show that our system surpasses current countermeasures in efficacy, particularly on small datasets. However, our method's performance is mixed when evaluated on larger datasets due to difficulties in generalizing from our small dataset. We will make our code available for public access at https://github.com/AKSHAYuoendendrs/End-to-end_Spoofing_Countermeasure. Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs rather than the transmission of light. An experiment was conducted and supported by theoretical findings, showing this nonreciprocity through second-order coherence functions of photon pairs created by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. Changing the direction of the pump's propagation leads to significant diminishment in coherence functions while maintaining the transmission. This unique nonreciprocity related to correlations could lead to innovative applications in quantum communication and metrology. Furthermore, this research offers a way to verify the nonreciprocity of systems without relying on distinct input and output ports, which may be essential for developing self-sustaining loop systems. Finally, a method has been devised to isolate the effect of nonreciprocity on coherence and enhance the system's performance by incorporating an additional beam splitter. Overall, this research provides new insights into nonreciprocity and opens doors for innovative technologies.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices."
