Identifying the application protocol is a crucial process in network security monitoring that demands a quick and accurate assessment to support detailed inspection. Although pinpointing the application protocol can be challenging, solely relying on static characteristics like port numbers can be insufficient. As a result, advanced and adaptive approaches have been developed for more precise identification. In this research, the mechanisms of dynamically detecting application protocols in widely used open-source network monitoring tools are examined. Our investigation on which protocols are typically detected and how identification is implemented reveals that a crucial factor is the training data used for shaping and fine-tuning these detection methods. Furthermore, this study illustrates detection evasion techniques that could potentially be incorporated into malicious entities' attacks, such as custom-made malware, for evading detection by network security monitoring systems. Specifically, two primary techniques for evading protocol detection - manipulating protocol flags and simulating false traffic - are thoroughly analyzed, along with two novel approaches. Our analysis shows that adaptive detection methods are susceptible to evasion, but our proposed techniques can effectively evade them, revealing the need for improved robustness in dynamic protocol detection mechanisms. Additionally, this research presents a framework, NetCapTD, for evaluating the efficacy of dynamic protocol detection methods based on traffic behavior. Ultimately, this research contributes knowledge on evading dynamic protocol detection and sheds light on the challenges of evolving network protocols. Furthermore, this research identifies potential avenues for integrating adaptive protocol detection with malicious traffic generation for more effective operation. Additionally, this research highlights potential defense strategies against dynamic protocol detection evasion. In particular, this research presents an analysis of the feasibility of undetectability in HTTP-based malware, revealing various possible methods for evading detection. Our analysis shows that these techniques can enhance undetectability by as much as 78.8% and 64.6%, respectively. Electrostatic gating limits the flow of electrons in integrated circuits. Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is difficult to regulate. However, we found that superconducting strips atop thin magnetic films can completely reflect magnons through their magnetic resistance to stray magnetic fields. The significant frequency shifts resulting from this response effectively halt the forward flow of magnons perpendicular to the magnetic field. By positioning two superconducting gates in parallel with the magnetic field, we were able to create a confined magnon system. The system's unique geometry enables the adjustment of the confining potential using established techniques to trap magnons at the interface between the superconductor and magnet. This novel technique offers a pioneering means of controlling magnons in principle capable of operating within the quantum limit. Moreover, this innovative technology could be integrated with existing semiconductor processing methods to produce a diverse range of magnon-based quantum devices, including those designed for efficient quantum computing and quantum communication applications. Ultimately, this research holds the potential for significant breakthroughs in the field of magnonics.

A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity is federated learning. Nonetheless, novel data classes emerging from user devices can hinder classification tasks and diminish model performance on existing datasets. This paper introduces ZerSHL, a pioneering federated learning technique that enables models to adapt to unknown classes without direct access to new data. By utilizing few-shot learning principles and incorporating a metric learning module that compares embeddings with nearest neighbor search, ZerSHL successfully enhances model accuracy on new classes without requiring explicit labeling. Experiments using the LibriSpeech audio dataset demonstrate that ZerSHL can consistently improve classification results, outperforming a baseline model by 4.6% across various scenarios with limited resource sharing. Importantly, results show that models trained with ZerSHL can achieve superior performance when users share only a small portion of available data, as opposed to sharing all available data. This reduces communication overhead and allows models to converge more efficiently. Overall, ZerSHL offers a promising solution for maintaining model performance in federated learning environments where users may encounter unknown classes. Additionally, the code and dataset used for this research are publicly accessible at https://github.com/jbmvieira/Zero-Shot-Federated-Learning.

The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning, which exhibits a similar inflection point in its learning process. By combining this AI with a sophisticated machine learning algorithm, we successfully decoded the neural mechanisms underlying its newfound counting skill, uncovering evidence of a novel information storage system specifically designed for processing counting data. While the AI's approach counts on the rapid creation of new connections between brain cells, or synapses, our findings suggest that the core principles of this system can be effectively applied to other machine learning challenges where novel data frequently appears sudden bursts of new data. By merging our counting AI with established deep learning systems, we achieved remarkable enhancements in processing learning-to-count skills. Moreover, our study provides a blueprint for developing new AI systems capable of tackling complex, high-level thinking tasks. Ultimately, we bridge the gap between the intricate workings of the human brain and efficient computer programs. Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming actions, such as accessing a disk or the network. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less storage and processes information faster. A different solution, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as an alternative to the Bloom filter. A variation of the Bloomier filter, the xor filter, has been developed by the authors, building upon existing research in this area. The properties of xor filters make them suitable for use in databases and file systems, allowing for the quick identification of unused variables in programming languages, and aiding in the avoidance of redundant computations in frameworks such as Boost.Runtime. A comprehensive evaluation reveals that the existing implementation of xor filters can be improved upon, leading to the introduction of a new and efficient algorithm, FastHash. This new implementation results in a significant reduction in processing time and memory usage, making it more efficient than both Bloom and cuckoo filters. An open-source library, including both Bloom and cuckoo filters, as well as the newly designed FastHash xor filters, is available for public use at github.com/antirez/ BloomFilterBenchmark. This benchmark allows engineers to compare the performance of these different filters in their own projects. An in-depth look at the design of xor filters is provided, along with a detailed analysis of their behavior and the underlying mathematics that govern their performance. A simplified implementation of xor filters is provided, along with more efficient alternatives, including a solution with o(1) complexity for deleting items from the filter. A comprehensive evaluation of xor filters is carried out, comparing their performance in various scenarios. An open-source tool, xorfilter, is available for download at github.com/antonbuffo/xorfilter, allowing engineers to easily incorporate the designed xor filters into their projects. Structural information about code is used to design a new metric, calledorc graph complexity, which measures a program's control flow structure. This new metric is correlated with existing code complexity metrics, including Essential Graph Complexity and Cognitive Complexity, as well as code characteristics, such as code size and age. A deep learning-based approach is proposed to automatically predict the orc graph complexity of Java methods without the need for manual code reviews. The results show that orc graph complexity is a effective predictor of method complexity, and can be accurately predicted using graph neural networks. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively. Additionally, the Minkowski's theorem for measures is reinterpreted as a theorem for divisors with nonintegrable coefficients, which has implications for the existence of canonical models for very ample line bundles. Our analysis also uncovers a previously unacknowledged duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, a relationship that can be seen through the lens of measures in convex geometry. This paper is a synthesis of the author's prior works on geometric analysis and algebraic geometry, aiming to illuminate the underlying connections between these fields. Consequently, several of the results and concepts presented here may be already known or known elsewhere in the literature. Nonetheless, a comprehensive summary of these relationships is currently lacking in the literature, rendering a rewritten and expanded treatment of the subject necessary. Specifically, new results and concepts are presented on the relationship between the pseudoeffective cone of divisors, the movable cone of curves, and the Minkowski's theorem for measures, along with a recently developed functorial connection between the augmented NEF cone of divisors and the convex body of measures with support in the boundary of the unit cube. Ultimately, this study aims to illustrate the fundamental unity of convex geometry and algebraic geometry through the lens of divisorial line bundles, revealing a deep mirror symmetry between these two fields. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating separate solution branches in parameter-dependent systems and generalizes seamlessly to multi-parameter tracking. To demonstrate the proposed methodology, this research achieves the precise calculation of random equilibrium cycles in the Lorenz system, as well as solution branches and 2-dimensional planes of steady states in the Swift-Hohenberg equation. Compared to existing methodologies, this approach exhibits enhanced efficiency and accuracy. Specifically, this research shows that random equilibrium cycles in the Lorenz system feature unique properties and provides a precise approximation within a small error margin, all while requiring significantly fewer numerical calculations than previous studies. Ultimately, this research confirms the potential for generalized polynomial chaos expansions to contribute significantly to the study of dynamical systems with parameter dependencies. However, this research also highlights the need for future investigations into various potential avenues, including but not limited to exploring multi-parameter random equilibrium calculations in systems exhibiting high dimensionality. Furthermore, this research opens the door for future research into generalized polynomial chaos expansions in contexts beyond random equilibrium calculations, such as transient dynamics and multi-parameter steady states. Specifically, this research suggests that chaos expansions can be effectively applied to model probability distributions associated with phase space trajectories that are invariant under parameter changes, a concept that has yet to be thoroughly explored in the literature. We have created a detailed analysis of the history of star formation within a vast collection of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, drawing on supernovae II-powered cosmological chemical evolution models. By utilizing observed metallicity patterns, we identify the most effective supernovae II yields models that explain the chemical composition of these dwarf galaxies. Through Bayesian analysis utilizing star formation history models, we constrain the mass of these dwarf galaxies, exploring their possible initial masses when formed. We have reconstructed the dwarf galaxy progenitor's history of star formation, mass, and metal enrichment, detecting early signs of star formation within 70% of these galaxies, including The Sculptor, with the majority of these dwarfs experiencing extended, 13 billion-year histories of continuous star formation. We have determined the current remaining mass of potential dwarf galaxy progenitors within the Milky Way using our constrained initial masses, totaling $M_{\mathrm{initial}} = (1.8 \pm 0.2) \times 10^9~M_{\odot}$. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments demonstrate that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by up to 90% while achieving comparable or superior results to comprehensive annotation. Additionally, we introduce OpenDocCat, an open-source annotation tool that facilitates collaborative document annotation and serves as a resource for testing our proposed approach. OpenDocCat currently supports the annotation of invoices, but it can be easily adapted to handle other visually complex document types. A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an efficient classification theorem for Borel subsets within any Polish space, thereby allowing for an accurate determination of their respective Wadge classes with simplified computability estimates. Moreover, this advancement leads to an updated classification of Borel Wadge classes, replacing Simpson's earlier work, and includes a related computability estimate for their classification. Additionally, we apply this technology to analyze fundamental questions regarding the complexity of Borel equivalence relations, particularly those related to transfinite levels and decision operations. With further modifications, this method could potentially enable the resolution of prominent open problems, such as the determinacy of a certain real function in the real calculus, and a related computability estimate for Borel Wadge classes up to $\Gamma^0_3$. Furthermore, this work culminates in an effective limit for Borel Wadge classes, denoted as $[\mathcal{B}^\ast_\Xi]$ and $[\mathcal{B}^+_\Xi]$ for various criteria of $\mathcal{B}^\ast_\Xi$ and $\mathcal{B}^+_\Xi$, leading to a partial resolution of a conjecture put forth by Satchwell. With regard to decision operations, we establish a fundamental theorem regarding the equivalence of three distinct notions of decision classes for Borel equivalence relations, allowing for the classification of any Borel equivalence relation $\mathcal{E}$ as either of two types: either it can be decided by a finite amount of information, or else it has no decision boundary within any countable collection of open sets. This discovery leads to a significant simplification and enhancement of a prior theorem by Satchwell, concurring that a particular type of Borel equivalence relation is inherently not decisionable, while also demonstrating that another conjectured theorem, though not universally proven, does hold true in numerous specific instances. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid analysis of a vast number of signals, making it challenging. Our study introduces a novel approach leveraging a neural network to identify the most promising gravitational wave events from neutron star-black hole mergers. The network is trained to distinguish signals affected by noise from genuine signals and to categorize them based on event characteristics. However, further research is required to increase the network's efficiency in identifying relevant events. Additionally, our study's findings suggest that neutron star-black hole mergers produce less gravitational wave signal than binary black hole mergers, making them harder to detect. Moreover, we found that the duration of these signals ranges from 10 to 40 seconds, which is too long for current detector capabilities. Therefore, detecting these events necessitates the utilization of advanced detector techniques and new detectors with expanded bandwidth, such as the future detectors in progress. Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be effectively addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles prevent the application of value function methods in CMDP: the generation of informative backup buffers during reinforcement learning and the resolution of a non-convex policy optimization problem. Our proposed approach includes developing a primal-dual algorithm and a set of function transformations that enable policy optimization via convex programming with a variational inequality. This method, augmented with episodic reinforcement learning, results in an algorithm solving the Fenchel-Young optimization problem and allowing for the selection of the best policy. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach, which is particularly suitable for large-scale CMDPs with n states and m actions, delivering substantial performance improvements. Moreover, the methodology enables the extension of our techniques to related problems, such as structured CMDPs with graph-structured blocks. Two companion papers provide supplementary analysis on backup buffer generation and the application of our techniques to these broader classes of sequential decision-making problems. This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. The approach involves segmenting symbols accurately into over 300 categories. Since many complex mathematical symbols require both horizontal and vertical projection to be split, but certain symbols don't need this processing as they can cause issues with overlap, especially when horizontal and vertical projections intersect. Therefore, we've developed an advanced symbol segmentation method that minimizes errors, especially for tricky symbols. Additionally, we've adapted the ICDAR 2017 MHF14 dataset, which includes 4469 mathematical symbol images, along with 3550 symbols from CMU-CD for training purposes. These datasets combined total 8019 images spanning 416 distinct mathematical symbol categories. For classification, a pre-trained VGG16 model was fine-tuned using the newly assembled dataset. Nevertheless, because handwritten mathematical symbols come in a wide array of shapes and sizes, we've adopted the RotNet algorithm to capture the orientation of the symbols instead of using fixed features. Moreover, to tackle the issue of handwritten mathematical symbols that are either partially written on the page or obscured by other symbols, we've incorporated the SegNet algorithm for post-processing to eliminate unnecessary background pixels. Eventually, our approach achieved a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.9466 on the test dataset, consisting of 8019 mathematical symbol images, by utilizing the aforementioned techniques. Nonetheless, because handwritten mathematical symbols are notoriously hard to recognize, we acknowledge that this task is a difficult challenge. Therefore, we're confident that our method has shown promise and set a new benchmark, achieving the highest correlation coefficient so far. Although this study only recognizes individual mathematical symbols, it lays the groundwork for full equation recognition in the future. In comparison to related research, our method excels at recognizing so many diverse mathematical symbol categories, a total of 416 distinct types. In contrast, related research was limited to recognizing just 112 symbols, a far more restricted set. Consequently, this study holds great potential for further development in mathematical symbol recognition. The growth rates of BPS state degeneracies, specifically their orders, are connected to Euler characteristic computations in equivariant sheaf cohomology. A notable instance is when considering the Hilbert scheme of points on a 2D plane; this yields an accurate calculation of exponential BPS state degeneracy growth rates as the number of points becomes very large. The growth characteristics serve as an indicator for supersymmetric quantum mechanics phase transitions. Moreover, an analysis of an equivariant symplectic quadric presents an interesting possibility of a first-order phase transition in a related supersymmetric quantum mechanics model. In such a scenario, BPS state degeneracies would experience a discontinuous change within a continuous parameter variation. Lastly, a mathematical relationship is found between supersymmetric quantum mechanics phase transitions and the structure of an algebra that underlies cohomology rings of flag varieties and Hilbert schemes of points. We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process using numerical methods. Initially, our research reveals that the disparity in epidemic behavior between homogeneous and heterogeneous networks is substantial. Specifically, our findings show that the latter often exhibit reduced infection rates and shorter duration of outbreaks. This outcome can be attributed to the reduced average distance between nodes in smaller, localized clusters that arise from heterogeneity in the network, resulting in faster disease spread within these areas. However, the increased average distance in heterogeneous networks also impedes spread to uninfected components, leading to shorter overall outbreaks. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that a balance between large, isolated clusters and well-connected local components is desirable for effective epidemic spread. Interestingly, this strategy aligns with principles from social sciences, such as anthropology and sociology, that aim to optimize social interactions and community engagement. From an epidemiological perspective, our study provides a practical approach to controlling disease spread by modifying network interconnections. Specifically, our results demonstrate the potential benefits of targeting close social contacts for epidemic intervention, highlighting the value of close proximity as a risk factor for infection. Moreover, our research offers an innovative perspective on the relationship between social and physical environments that can inform public health policies aimed at mitigating the spread of diseases. Ultimately, our analysis underscores the significance of understanding network topology in understanding epidemic behavior and controlling disease transmission. Additionally, our study provides a useful framework for applying complex network theory to real-world epidemic models, as well as practical guidance for applying numerical simulation methods to complex networks. Lastly, our research highlights the broad applicability of the contact process model to diverse contexts, as seen in the numerous examples provided in the companion chapter. Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its widely used Policy Gradient Method (PGM) often faces challenges such as local minima and overestimation of value functions, which can result in suboptimal performance in complex environments. This paper introduces an innovative hybrid approach that integrates PGM with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for better exploration. In our proposed method, the policy network is optimized using an alternative representation of its parameters, for more efficient exploration in the state-action space. Additionally, we have investigated the incorporation of HMC within the actor-critic framework and found that it offers a pure exploration benefit. We tested our method on a set of controlled environments and compared it with PGM, as well as more advanced models like AlphaGo and SafeReach, achieving comparable results and outperforming PGM by 30% in a critical reaching task without collision constraints. Furthermore, we have successfully applied our method to a real-world robotic reaching task, demonstrating its efficacy and versatility in real-world conditions. Our findings indicate that Nereid's spectral pattern is not duplicated in any ordinary water-ice mixture. Using a model that incorporates complex refractive indices, our results show that Nereid's surface composition is comprised of approximately 60% water ice, with the remaining 40% consisting of darker materials. Two models emerge that can explain Nereid's spectral characteristics: the first involves a surface layer rich in sodium ammonium phosphate ice, coupled with sodium chloride ice that's 10% of the total ice content; the second model features a surface layer made up of magnesium sulfate hexahydrite ice, coupled with sodium chloride ice that's 5% of the total ice content. Both models are based on sodium chloride ice that's been exposed to radiation, resulting in the formation of sodium chloride hydroxide ice that's near the surface. A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little policy coverage, but current implementations lack a clear statistical basis for a hyper-parameter that's critical to performance. Our approach uses a block-diagonal approximation in conjunction with a shrinkage technique to address this issue, offering a data-driven method to choose the pessimism hyper-parameter. The resulting method surpasses current alternatives in both efficiency and performance. The core statistical principles and a Bayesian learning framework for this issue have previously been established, but we will primarily focus on the innovative pessimism principle in this study. Theoretical validation, as well as practical applications with real-world data, demonstrate the exceptional performance of our approach. The findings indicate that our method significantly outperforms current pessimism-based solutions in both efficiency and performance. The novel Bayesian learning framework for a block-diagonal approximation represents a fresh contribution to the field. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption patterns, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting the varying energy levels may result in image distortion and degrade the quality of the resulting images. Furthermore, the electronic ports of CT scanners can become clogged over time, causing measurement data corruption and ultimately affecting reconstruction accuracy. Consequently, we propose an innovative mathematical approach that incorporates a variational method capable of handling CT data collected from multiple sources of varying energies, data collected just before system malfunction, and distinguishing between different energy levels. Notably, we incorporate an additional regularizing term designed to promote consistency between 3D projections and 3D images, thereby improving our model's robustness when dealing with incomplete and missing data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model by applying it to synthetic data and comparing the resulting images to those obtained from traditional techniques. Specifically, our proposed method is capable of removing system noise, distinguishing between different energy levels, and producing high-quality 3D micro-CT images. The computational experiments indicate that our model outperformed the comparison methods in terms of reconstruction accuracy. Moreover, we observed a significant enhancement in the quality of the 3D reconstructed images. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) has numerous practical applications in
deciphering historical documents and forms. While modern approaches demonstrate
significant success for standard written scripts, they often fail to accurately
recognize unique, handwritten scripts lacking sufficient labeled data. In
response, we present a novel, composite dataset consisting of FormoFUND, adapted
from Taiwanese historical forms, and Bangla handwritten text, to overcome the
limitations of English handwritten text models. We also introduce a one-shot
unsupervised adaptation technique for HTR, utilizing a self-learning strategy
using the newly created FormoFUND dataset to bridge the gap in scarce labeled
data for new scripts. This method involves a straightforward reformulation of
existing models and can be implemented without any modifications. We evaluate
our proposed method on the Bangla dataset, demonstrating notable performance
improvements with the one-shot unsupervised adaptation technique. Furthermore,
we directly compare our method with top-ranked models on the Bangla dataset,
revealing superior results and a significant reduction in errors. These
contributions include a comprehensive dataset, innovative method, and exemplary
model improvements, ultimately facilitating more accurate HTR systems for
unfamiliar, handwritten scripts. We will make the code and dataset publicly
available at https://github.com/wcstyan/htr-composition.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to potential performance bottlenecks from variable memory allocations and potential data corruption. Despite a notable absence of memory management tailored to object-oriented programming on GPUs, researchers have explored the use of object-oriented patterns in recent years. To address this gap, we introduce DynaSOAr, a highly efficient memory allocator designed for high-throughput object creation on GPUs, optimized for efficient memory access. By leveraging recent GPU features, DynaSOAr provides several performance-enhancing benefits, including support for large memory allocation, cache optimization, and automatic memory management alignment. Furthermore, DynaSOAr incorporates a novel technique for reducing memory allocation overhead, grouping multiple memory requests together. To maximize performance, DynaSOAr includes several optimization strategies, such as minimizing memory reader/writer conflicts and using cache-friendly memory access. Our experimental results demonstrate DynaSOAr's superiority over state-of-the-art memory allocators, achieving speedups of up to 3.3x and 2.3x in various benchmarks. Additionally, DynaSOAr showcases significant performance gains, averaging 2.3x and 1.5x improvements over state-of-the-art memory allocators in real-world applications. Moreover, DynaSOAr consistently outperforms a prominent memory allocator, Mempool, by a margin of 1.3x to 2.8x in several benchmarks. DynaSOAr's exceptional performance is a direct result of our in-depth, workload-driven design approach. To further validate DynaSOAr's efficiency, we conducted a detailed analysis of its memory allocation latency, revealing a latency of 281 ns, outperforming Mempool by approximately 3 times. Our in-depth evaluation demonstrates DynaSOAr's high level of scalability, achieving performance gains of up to 3.8x and 2.6x with increasing problem sizes in two benchmark tests. To further establish DynaSOAr's robustness, we conducted a series of crash diagnostics, simulating memory corruption scenarios. Our results show DynaSOAr's exceptional memory management capabilities, accurately identifying 96% of memory corruption cases at a latency of 461.7 ns. In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces a framework that protects such functions within Bayesian networks, providing a worst-case estimate for how much these functions can vary when subjected to different possible interpretations of the network. By utilizing a novel application of probabilistic equivalence checking in the analysis, the method enables the identification of the widest range in which function values can be contained, surpassing current standards. Building on this concept, a related approach is developed for identifying the most expansive bounds on attribute-driven functions within Bayesian networks. Both methods are complemented by a computational tool available for public use. Our analysis shows that certain structures can yield functions with nearly perfect robustness guarantees, while others may have unbounded guarantees due to inherently uncertain conditions. As a result, the decision-making capacity of Bayesian networks in decision theory is greatly enhanced, making them more suitable for a wide range of decision-making applications under uncertainty. Furthermore, this tool is anticipated to contribute to the growing field of credal machine learning by offering a valuable resource for assessing the reliability of decisions made with probabilistic predictions. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for a promising and performance-driven paradigm in decision theory, known as \emph{robustness-driven decision making}, where decisions are made with maximum certainty and the least possible risk. Keywords: Bayesian robustness, credal networks, robustness guarantees, decision theory, machine learning. Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a critical requirement, with implications extending to security and data protection aspects. Research has successfully applied machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices, however these approaches often rely on complete and unlabeled device data for training and testing purposes. In contrast, real-world device data is frequently incomplete and comes without device labels. Recent studies have applied information theory concepts, specifically mutual information, to select the most informative features for classification tasks. This paper evaluates the effectiveness of three distinct feature selection methods based on mutual information for training supervised classifiers to identify IoT devices. Additionally, we assess the impact of feature selection methods on classification efficiency and model performance when operating with reduced feature sets. Notably, our experiments involve realistic network data captured through a virtualized IoT network, complete with 50 devices spanning various features. Our analysis demonstrates that the MI-Q statistic is capable of distinctively differentiating IoT devices using entropy-based feature selection methods, resulting in improved classification accuracy when combined with feature selection methods exhibiting lower computational complexity and runtime. Consequently, this approach facilitates more efficient and accurate IoT device classification, with corresponding effects on memory usage and power consumption for the classification model. Ultimately, our findings suggest that feature selection methods varying in computational intensity can be effectively utilized to reduce feature dimensionality, thus enabling more precise device classification with subsequent security and data protection benefits. Moreover, this approach enables the identification of key network packet attributes essential for distinguishing between distinct IoT devices. As such, this research holds significant practical implications for device classification in real-world scenarios, with additional avenues for integration with existing security frameworks and systems also identified. These low entropy, high MI-Q value attributes provide crucial differentiation between distinct IoT devices, underscoring the potential for improved energy efficiency through optimized feature selection in real-world IoT device classification scenarios. Furthermore, our findings also underscore the potential for reduced memory usage in actual IoT devices, given the correspondence between feature selection method rankings and unique feature selection values. This simulation demonstrates how to generate PBH mass functions and their potential impact on the dark matter composition. However, as a theoretical study, this work does not provide evidence for the existence of PBHs as a dark matter source but rather presents a useful tool for future research. Future analyses can utilize this code to study specific characteristics of PBHs, such as their effects on the dark matter spectrum and the potential detection through the accumulation of PBHs in binary systems. The systems' phases were studied as a function of parameter $d$ and the packing density of molecules $\eta$, under the condition that only repulsive interactions were present. This led to the system's behavior being controlled solely by the entropy of molecular arrangement. For systems where the packing density was below 0.5, in addition to the standard liquid state, we observed standard nematic and smectic A liquid crystalline phases. Conversely, when the packing density exceeded 0.5, two distinct non-standard polar liquid crystalline phases emerged alongside the nematic and smectic A phases. Notably, we found that the standard nematic phase existed within the parameter space where nematic, smectic A, and two distinct polar phases coexisted. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we completely mapped the system's phase diagram in three-dimensional form, utilizing $d$ and $\eta$ as the primary coordinates. Conversely, we found two distinct regions with different polar modulations in the parameter space and found that the standard nematic phase was surrounded by two modulation regions. Notably, we found that the system's phase behavior was controlled by the decaying nematic order parameter in the smectic A phase as the packing density increased. Consequently, we observed a change in the modulations present in the system as a direct result of this increase in smectic order. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The stick-slip regime is characterized by a "piano-key" sound and by stress fluctuations that vary in sign and amplitude. The transition from stick-slip to stationary behavior is triggered by increasing the surface roughness or the persistence length of the foam. The stationary regime is distinguished by stress values that are higher than those of smooth foams and by persistent blockages that produce loud "clunk" sounds when the surface barriers are overcome. Our study provides comprehensive insight into the complex friction modes encountered in dry liquid foams and sheds light on the underlying physical mechanisms governing friction at rough surfaces. Additionally, these findings may be applied to other complex liquids, such as polymers and suspensions, to better understand their unique dynamics. Lastly, we suggest that the concept of "roughness modes" could be employed to develop new technologies that induce and utilize surface roughness to drive mechanical movements, all by utilizing the surface topography of the blockers. These innovative ideas might have potential applications in robotics, where the development of artificial muscles with enhanced capabilities could be facilitated through a deeper understanding of surface roughness and its effects on locomotion. Predicting the weather in different locations is a difficult task due to variations in weather patterns and the limited availability of local historical weather data. Given a set of future weather images and spatial location coordinates, our proposed NeWeatherNet network predicts the sequence of weather conditions for that location. To evaluate the network's ability to learn about the spatiotemporal relationships between weather patterns, we have released a new dataset containing 887 weather images from the United States. In experiments using this dataset to test NeWeatherNet, we found that it outperformed comparison networks in forecasting accuracy. Additionally, we analyzed how the network's use of attention mechanisms contributed to its performance by visualizing the attention weights applied by individual network modules. To validate the network's performance in real-world applications, we have also conducted a study of its predictions of severe weather events such as heavy rain and strong winds. In this study, we found that NeWeatherNet performed well in predicting the occurrence of these events within a 12-hour time frame. Further work on improving the network's use of attention mechanisms, as well as its incorporation into a larger decision support system for weather forecasting, is also discussed. Specifically, we analyze the $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet models that allow softly broken $S_3$ terms, determining which models can host dark matter. The variety of models arises from different arrangements of vacuum expectation values, leading to vacua with either one or two vanishing expectation values. In our research, we consider a scenario where the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, a remnant of $S_3$, stabilizes the dark matter candidate. Our study focuses on two models: one with CP violation and another without, each consisting of a single dark matter candidate and two active scalar sectors behaving similarly to a Type-I two-Higgs-doublet model. After investigating these models under various constraints, we identified potential masses for dark matter in both cases. A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented with a notable achievement: the PPT square conjecture's validity has been rigorously demonstrated for the case involving finite-dimensional space. Additionally, several important insights were gained, including the development of a method to generate PPT operators and a finding showing that the PPT square conjecture implies a more comprehensive scenario. Furthermore, this study explores the relationship between the PPT square conjecture and other foundational principles in quantum mechanics, such as the entanglement scaling law and the minimum output entropy. The study also delves into the obstacles hindering a full proof of the PPT square conjecture and proposes potential directions for future research. Lastly, several previously unrecognized consequences of the PPT square conjecture were identified, providing further evidence of its significance in the field of quantum mechanics. Intracellular transport is a vital process that requires a quantitative understanding of cellular behavior, particularly in neurons where it affects brain disorders such as Alzheimer's disease. To tackle this issue, we developed a unique optimization framework that incorporates partial differential equations modeling transport on a complex network of branches mimicking dendrites and axons. Introducing various costs into the equation helps to balance transport efficiency with the economic cost of jammed neurons. By adjusting key parameters and optimizing transport speeds, we can resolve traffic jams and improve signal transmission between neurons. This novel approach offers a versatile tool for studying cellular traffic and optimizing neuronal function. A detailed numerical example demonstrates the method's effectiveness in simulating transport on a tree-like network, emulating the structure of neuronal compartments. Furthermore, we identified a critical parameter that governs the transition between jammed and cleared systems, revealing a second-order phase transition. To validate our model's relevance to real-world neuronal systems, we applied it to a case study modeling the axon of a olfactory receptor neuron. The model was then used to predict how the receptor's signals would be affected by changes in intracellular transport rates. The results show that even temporary blockages of receptor jam could significantly impact signal quality, highlighting the importance of optimal transport regulation in neuronal function. A comprehensive description of our model, along with numerical implementation and analysis, is available online. The full source code can be accessed at https://github.com/pmeunier/transport_optimization. Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than $0$. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function, denoted as $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, represents a semimetric for all possible subsets of a given set. Our research found that the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is equivalent to a specific transformation of the Jaccard distance function $D_{\frac{1-\alpha}{\beta},1}$ when the set contains only binary elements. Furthermore, the function $D_{\frac{1-\alpha}{\beta},1}$ is a specialization of yet another function $D_{\frac{1}{1+\beta},1$ that was previously studied by Sanz (2019). Additionally, the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a realization of the formula $\frac{m-n}{k-m}$ where $k$ is the size of the smaller set among $A$ and $B$, $m$ is the size of the larger set, and $n$ is the size of the intersection between $A$ and $B$. This result links the Jaccard distance function $D_{\frac{1-\alpha}{\beta},1}$ to an analogue of the normalized information distance, which was studied by Cohen and Lave (1978), particularly in the case where $\alpha$ equals $\frac{1}{1+\beta}$. When the set contains elements that have a weight rather than size, the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a specialization of yet another function that was studied by Sanz (2019). The function can also be employed in order to develop a similarity measure. This research not only confirms but also extends the results of Jim\'enez et al. (2013), particularly in the case where $\alpha$ is greater than $\frac{1}{1+\beta}$. Our research has several possible applications, including information search and retrieval, classification tasks that utilize text-based methods, and similarity analysis between texts. Our research also delves into how the choice of the parameter $\alpha$ affects these applications. Finally, our research investigates ways in which the results can be employed in order to develop a loss function that balances recall and precision in the context of ranking

Hebbian theory proposes that synaptic connections between brain cells are responsible for memory and learning processes. A notable aspect of Hebbian learning is its ability to utilize local biophysical mechanisms found commonly across species, making it an attractive area of study for developing artificial neural networks using programmable molecular systems. To investigate this further, we have designed a self-assembling artificial system that mimics a Hebbian learning neuron based on the standard integrate-and-fire model, incorporating reversible and programmable acetyltransferase, acetylcholinesterase, and conformationally responsive polymer technologies. This system is capable of forming artificial synapses between specialized receptors and can effectively learn patterns similar to those processed by biological neurons, as demonstrated through the example learning of a basic odor combination. The development of molecular systems emulating Hebbian learning neurons may serve as a foundation for constructing low-power, distributed artificial neural networks capable of supporting widespread AI applications. Additionally, this work may facilitate novel biological insights by testing Hebbian learning hypotheses in controlled laboratory settings. Furthermore, this work presents opportunities for advancing technology in fields such as distributed computing, network design, and other technological fields that require scaling up distributed information processing while minimizing energy consumption. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the open completeness property in the refined version, whereas its original cardinality dictates whether the refined version is complete. Specifically, the refined version will always have at most countably many open intervals if the original set had a cardinality less than aleph-two. Conversely, if a set had a cardinality greater than or equal to aleph-two, then the refined version would necessarily have a countable open completeness property. The purpose of this research paper is to derive optimal estimates for the first Robin eigenvalue in relation to the first Robin eigenvalue of a nonlinear elliptic operator. We demonstrate that this eigenvalue is closely related to the first variation of the norm of a nonlinear operator in a Banach space. By applying this approach, we are able to obtain precise estimates for the first eigenvalue of a nonlinear elliptic operator, building upon the existing results for linear operators. We also introduce a new concept of 'phased monotonicity' for nonlinear operators, which has broader applications and implications in functional analysis and the study of partial differential equations. We test the validity and applications of our results through the analysis of several concrete examples and models. These include the examination of the first eigenvalue of a one-dimensional nonlinear differential equation with a non-homogeneous boundary condition and the assessment of the first eigenvalue of a nonlinear elliptic operator in R^n. The results we obtain can be utilized to model a wide array of physical phenomena, including the behavior of elastic rods and the flow of a heat transfer system subject to heat loss at the boundary. Finally, our approach leads to novel insights and interpretations of the first eigenvalue in terms of optimal values and limits of quadratic forms. These interpretations can be generalized to the context of nonlinear operators in functional analysis. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages in diverse settings, and the results clearly indicate that our approach outperforms traditional self-training and state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods by a significant margin. Moreover, we found that our method is adaptable to both BERT and ELMo language models and can be easily adapted to various parser architectures. Ultimately, DCST has enabled us to achieve results rivaling those of fully supervised methods on languages with as few as 50 annotated sentences. Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics. The study of branes, so(4N), and non-trivial symmetries also enables us to explore orthosymmetry, a concept where two algebras are mutually invertible. Specifically, we examine orthosymmetry between so(4N) and various algebras usp(2N), u(2, 2N), and u*(2, 2N). Furthermore, the study of branes offers insights into general properties of non-trivial symmetries, such as their Lie superalgebra structure and a possible generalised homotopy theory. Ultimately, the relationship between branes, sp(2N), and non-trivial symmetries remains a key area of research, and possibly even a necessary condition for the brane configuration. The study of orientifold and Klein branes also presents us with interesting scenarios involving non-trivial symmetries defying inversion, examples of which can be found in N=1* Yang-Mills theories and in theories of Yang-Mills with u*(2, 2N) and u(2, 2N) algebras. The diversity of brane configurations, their deformations, and associated non-trivial symmetries defying inversion, suggests the extensive presence of non-trivial symmetries in the superconformal quantum mechanics sector. The various dimensionless parameters in Yang-Mills theories, derived from the Gauged Linear Sigma Models, can be understood through the parameter's relationship with the brane deformations in the theories. Ultimately, the dimensionless parameters in Yang-Mills theories can be explained by the domain walls present in these theories, whose physical implications need to be explored. The study of branes, so(4N), non-trivial symmetries defying inversion, and various algebraic varieties also brings to light related research topics in mathematics, a subject area that holds considerable influence over the research in theoretical physics. The diverse mathematical concepts from cohomology in sp(2N) to Calabi-Yau manifolds, and from algebraic varieties to Klein bottles can be brought to bear over problems in supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories. Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity, having demonstrated the capability to be contained within PTIME and yet evade a straightforward description via first-order logic. Notably, CPT can be defined through the use of choice-free recursive equations applied to binary relations, along with an initial set of elements, and has been shown to be equivalent to another relation-based system known as Cyclic Composability (CC). Although CPT has been demonstrated to operate effectively on structures with a pre-defined colouring, its performance when dealing with uncoloured structures remains uncertain. Specifically, when CPT is applied to undirected graphs without colours, it fails to solve the Subgraph Isomorphism problem, which is now confirmed to be PTIME-completeness eligible under a novel constraint. This new constraint involves limiting the number of properties (edges) available to any given equation. This breakthrough reveals the existence of a specific graph class called Cai-Fürer-Immerman (CFI) graphs, constructed deliberately to demonstrate this result, which consists of intersecting cliques. Moreover, CFI graphs serve as a CF-matrix reduction for several prominent PTIME-completeness candidates, thereby invalidating potential CPT-based algorithms for these decision problems. This includes a surprising consequence that CPT cannot solve the Graph Equivalence problem, which involves determining whether two given graphs can be transformed into each other using a series of prescribed operations. This surprising result further establishes CPT's inability to solve the Subgraph Isomorphism problem in undirected graphs, which has far-reaching implications. Furthermore, a more general theory is proposed, known as CPT*, which operates on any graph class that can be described using a set of properties, and which is shown to be equivalent to CPT applied to coloured structures. This new framework is demonstrated to be effective in tackling decision problems within polynomial time complexity. One key example of a decision problem that can be solved effectively through CPT*, and which eludes a solution using CPT, involves determining whether a given graph can be partitioned into a specified number of cliques. CPT* is also shown to be a more general approach than an alternative system known as Fixed Point Logic (FPL), which is a fundamental approach in describing properties of graphs, and which can be translated effectively into CPT*. In a compound known for potential Weyl semimetal characteristics, Eu2Ir2O7 undergoes an insulator-to-metal transition with increasing amounts of Bi substitution at the Eu site. To explore the properties of the resulting series, Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 was studied via HAXPES. Interestingly, Bi substitution unexpectedly led to a significant (20 %) reduction in the lattice size at relatively low levels of Bi (3.5 %) doping. The experiments using HAXPES showed that the ion states near the Fermi level change little with Bi doping, but the shift in the Ir 4f core level decreases as Bi concentration increases, indicating increased electron withdrawal from the Ir site. This trend suggests that the main source of charge disruption in this series is the change in the Eu ion state rather than the Ir site, with the former exhibiting unusual valence variation in the series. The degree of charge deﬀiciency on the Ir site is heavily dependent on its surrounding environment, specifically on the valence state of the Eu ions, with the correlation strength increasing as the insulating behavior transitions to metallicity. These results indicate reduced charge deﬁciency on the Ir site in the metal phase, possibly due to the increased kinetic energy of the Ir 5t electrons in that phase. This phenomenon is potentially linked to the potential Weyl semimetal characteristics of this compound series. The degree of charge deﬁciency on the Ir site is compared with that from an established pyrochlore series (Gd2Ir2O7 to Gd1-xBix2Ir2O7, 0 ≤ x ≤ 0.2), with significant variations observed between the two series under similar conditions. These diﬀerences in Ir ion state around the Fermi level may indicate distinct roles of electron correlation and orbital physics in in these in metals. Finally, our studies highlight the potential of using HAXPES as a precise tool for exploring the Ir ion state around the Fermi level in 4f-5d-4f hybridization-based systems, where the limited excitation of photons might result in inadequate photoemission signal. The study was conducted at the SuperAstra beamline, with data analysis supported by software from Blake A. Richards. The corresponding author can be contacted at Blake.Richards@monash.edu for additional information. The data presented in this study can be accessed via DOI: 10.1788/doi.

If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We begin this study by establishing the parameters within the range [0,5] for [0,5] the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ which satisfies the 'cyclic' condition, referred to as the 'base'. In comparing the 'base' to the 0.5-filled vector $(0.5, \ldots, 0.5)$, we find the total sum of the absolute difference between each element in the 'base' and 0.5 to be greater than the total sum of the absolute difference between each element in the 'base' and 1-0.5. We then refer to this total sum of the absolute difference between each element in the 'base' and 1-0.5 as the 'dishonesty' of the 'cyclic' n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$. In contrast, we refer to the total sum of the absolute difference between each element in the 'base' and 0.5 as the 'cyclic risk'. 

In this study, we first demonstrate that a 'nontransitive' n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ with the largest possible 'cyclic risk' is equivalent to one with the smallest possible 'dishonesty'. We then show through induction that 'cyclic' n-tuples $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ where the elements $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ increase at a rate of at least $n-1$ are 'nontransitive'. Our study reveals that such adjustments are feasible in a significant portion of cases, primarily due to the numerous possible settings of command-line inputs. We found that reducing the search space by focusing on relevant, practically viable settings can significantly limit the scope of exploration. Additionally, our analysis shows that many viable settings share similar preferences and only differ in their chosen options, thereby enabling the exclusion of irrelevant settings from consideration. This study explores the behavior of a two-level atom and a qubit in a cavity
cavity system under the anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction model, a counter-part
of the standard Jaynes-Cummings model. A comparison is made with the standard
model and interesting contrasts are identified. Furthermore, numerical
investigations of entanglement development, as well as entanglement swapping
throughout both models, are conducted. Additionally, entanglement transmission
between the atom and qubit is examined as the atom moves away from the cavity
center in both scenarios. Lastly, a demonstration of quantum teleportation
using the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model is provided, showcasing that entanglement
is not always a necessary precondition for successful teleportation. This work
provides valuable insights for utilization of quantum information technologies. 
Keywords: Quantum Information Technologies, Anti-Jaynes-Cummings Model, Quantum
Entanglement, Quantum Information Processing, Quantum Information Transactions,

Measuring inter-beat intervals (IBI) from ECG signals is crucial for detecting cardiac disorders and analyzing the autonomic nervous system's (ANS) influence on heart function. However, IBI estimation can be inaccurate due to motion-induced noise, especially in mobile ECG monitoring settings. Researchers have developed noise reduction methods to improve IBI estimation's accuracy, but existing solutions have limitations. In this study, a novel approach is introduced based on a Tiramisu autoencoder, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both simulation and real-world clinical trials. By effectively removing noise and accurately identifying R-wave peaks, this model surpasses existing solutions with an average error rate of 0.0418 ms, significantly lower than the standard 0.1 ms precision standard. Furthermore, the model's low-weighted parameter count and data representation capabilities make it suitable for mobile devices, with estimated processing times of merely 0.12 ms even on resource-constrained devices. As a result, this model can be easily integrated into wearable ECG devices for medical professionals to use. Our research suggests that the proposed Tiramisu-based approach not only outperforms traditional and deep learning methods but also offers highly scalable solutions for IBI estimation, meeting clinical precision standards while being adaptable to mobile ECG monitoring needs. The associated code and datasets are publicly accessible for other researchers to build upon our findings. Overall, this approach provides a practical, accurate, and efficient means of IBI estimation from noisy ECG signals, enabling cardiac disorder detection and analyzing the ANS's influence on heart function with high precision. Please refer to the associated figure list at the end of this document for a visual summary of our approach. This research introduces HUMBI, a large, diverse dataset containing over 3.6 million detailed human body pose images, along with rich annotation information, including face, hand, and body expressions. The annotations encompass a wide range of facial expressions, hand gestures, and body language, including postures, Proximity, Touch, and other intricate details. The dataset was created by annotating a substantial collection of images from various viewpoints, utilizing a novel system that can automatically detect and align human figures within images. The development of this framework facilitated seamless annotation transfer across different viewpoints. A benchmark challenge for measuring human body expression recognition capabilities will also be launched in conjunction with HUMBI, utilizing the dataset for evaluation. The goal of this initiative is not only to assess the effectiveness of existing methods but also to drive innovative research in the field of human body expression recognition. Despite the abundance of NLP models capable of performing various tasks, cross-lingual translations remain challenging due to a lack of data in target languages. Typically, multilingual NLP models rely on shared text representations to tackle this issue, but this approach often necessitates target language data and extensive training. We propose a model-agnostic framework that leverages neural task representations to achieve seamless zero-shot and multilingual task translations without the need for target language data. We implement this strategy using a combination of pre-trained mBERT and linear projections, where task representations are learned from high-resource languages, and apply them to low-resource languages to perform tasks on diverse languages, including Hindi, Thai, Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean, Russian, and Indonesian. We evaluate our method on 12 languages for 8 tasks and find it to be highly effective, achieving a success rate of 80% across all tasks, and significantly outperforming existing model-agnostic and multilingual NLP models by 10-20% or more in 7 out of 8 tasks. The source code is available at https://github.com/salehjafari/NTRT. We also created TaskEmb, a neural task representation resource with embeddings for 34 tasks across 16 languages at https://taskemb.github.io. We hope this resource benefits the community by saving NLP researchers and developers time and effort in creating task representations for their models. Finally, we demonstrated that task representations can be utilized beyond translation tasks and found that model performance often reaches state-of-the-art levels on tasks such as named entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging, and dependency parsing. We believe this underscores the universal potential of task embeddings in accelerating the development of low-resource NLP datasets. To further validate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted ablation studies by removing data from both source and target languages and found that it enables task performance without target language data, confirming the model-agnostic nature of our approach. We also analyzed the impact of linear projections on task results and found that they play a crucial role in achieving successful task performance. We plan to explore extensions of our method that can learn task representations from related languages in the future. Overall, we hope this research contributes positively to the community by promoting research on zero-shot and multilingual NLP, and we are excited about the potential applications of our method in real-world settings. We estimate that our method can accelerate the development of NLP datasets by approximately two years for each new language. benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we developed a method

models. Our proposed approach significantly outperforms existing model-based
multi-task methods in a variety of challenging Atari games. Moreover, by

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these maps, and also reveal the underlying cause for the failure of certain entropy-based approaches. As such, the generalized baker maps provide a useful tool for exploring the relationship between the geometric structure of compact manifolds and their algebraic properties, offering insights into questions regarding entropy approachability and the stability of periodic orbits. Additionally, this work offers a novel interpretation of the invariant measures of the Dyck system, known as Cantor sets of continued fractions, via the study of the 2D generalized baker map. Furthermore, we propose that the ergodic measures with maximal entropy for the 3D generalized baker map hold significance in understanding the properties of compact 3D convex sets with periodic boundaries. Through numerical simulation, we confirm that the ergodic measures with maximal entropy for the 2D generalized baker map converge at a rate of $O(\tau^{5/2})$ and for the 3D map at a rate of $O(\tau^{5/3})$ when approached using the entropy approach. This result constitutes a theoretical justification for an previously proposed method, known as entropy approachability, which was found to converge at a rate of $O(\tau^{5/2})$ and $O(\tau^{5/3})$ in previous studies. The ergodic measures with maximal entropy for the 3D generalized baker map can be thought of as representing a distribution of images on the surface of a 3D sphere, and also provide a novel interpretation of the ergodic measures of the Dyck system, known as Cantor sets of continued fractions. We also offer a geometric interpretation of the ergodic measures with maximal entropy for the 2D generalized baker map, known as Cantor sets, by representing them as distributions of images on the surface of a 2D sphere. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the synthesis of raw audio data by introducing pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks into the Autoregressive Raw Waveform Model. By incorporating QPNet's network structure, the model can generate raw audio data at a longer dilation rate, resulting in a longer output sequence with the same number of parameters as the underlying WaveNet models. Due to the quasi-periodic nature of speech and music, this modification enables the model to capture repeated patterns more efficiently. Experimental evaluations have demonstrated that the proposed QPNet model exhibits comparable quality to the underlying WaveNet models and even outperforms them in cases where the state-of-the-art models exhibit reduced performance. Additionally, the study has confirmed that the proposed method is scalable and practical for raw audio generation applications. Lastly, the researchers have successfully applied the QPNet model to low-resolution speech synthesis with a sampling rate as low as 8 kHz, achieving promising results in this novel domain. Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), having proven to be effective and widely adopted, encounter limitations in dealing with recommendation data characteristics, such as the density of user-item interaction matrices and the subjective nature of user preferences. Dense user-item interaction matrices complicate CF's ability to accurately group users and items into meaningful groups, while the subjectivity of preferences raises doubts about the reliability of these groups in making individualized recommendations. This research introduces User-Specific Bicluster-based CF (USB), a novel CF approach that generates user-and-item subgroupings tailored to each user's unique preferences. By leveraging Biclustering, a data mining technique, USB captures patterns within each user's most engaged items, demonstrating improved accuracy and scalability compared to previous CF methods in numerous experiments. Furthermore, USB shows significant performance gains over state-of-the-art CF frameworks, specifically in Handling Preference Sparsity (HPS) and Subjectivity in Recommendation (SIR), highlighting its potential to overcome existing CF limitations. The proposed USB methodology offers a flexible framework that accommodates various data mining strategies and can be further adapted to suit the needs of evolving recommender systems. The source code for USB is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AmrYousef/USB. Experimental findings and associated data are also available on MIRALab's GitHub repository at https://github.com/MIRALabUIUC/USB_experiments. Research findings have been documented in the research report 'User-Specific Bicluster-based CF: Biclustering Meets Recommender Systems', available on MIRALab's website. Amr Youssef has successfully defended his PhD dissertation on USB at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign under the supervision of Dr. Shlomo Berkovsky. This work has been presented at ACM RecSys 2019, Florence, Italy, and has received the ACM RecSys 2019 Travel Award.

Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. This study analyzed HARPS-N solar data, incorporating multiple activity indicators, including S\'{o}kanina--Indyk--Pietrokovski (SIP) units, to evaluate their sensitivity to different types of stellar activity. Using time-frequency diagrams and wavelet analysis, the study demonstrated that these indicators can distinguish between various p- and s-axion modes. Notably, the study found that certain activity indicators are more sensitive to the p-axision mode 1, which experiences strong variations due to solar eclipses, indicating potential for these indicators in solar activity monitoring. Furthermore, the study investigated the spectral impact of different activity indicators on their own and other signals, providing insights into the interplay between different p- and s-axion modes and magnetic cycles. Ultimately, the study's findings contribute to the development of more sophisticated methods for analyzing stellar activity and detecting exoplanets. Additionally, the study's results will be useful in understanding the photometric and spectroscopic properties of solar-like magnetic cycles through observational data. The study's code is publicly available at https://github.com/JuliaAstro/SPAXMAN_solar/blob/main/spaxman_solar.jl. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of Morita invariance for shadows. Additionally, by interpreting topological Hochschild cohomology (THCoH) as a homotopy invariant of bicategories, it is shown that functors from THCoH can be seen as a type of "shadow cohomology," with this concept exhibiting morita invariance as well. Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as various styling options can produce distinct effects. Although a task-specific style can be considered objective, current machine learning-based methods typically ignore it in favor of generalization, despite objective styles existing alongside subjective ones. Our research aims to capture task-specific style characteristics and incorporate them into machine learning models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our style extraction algorithm in conjunction with a neural network-based image manipulation framework, which typically disregards objective styles, by showing that models trained with objective styles outperform those trained with subjective styles, as evidenced by higher performance metrics and a stylistic analysis. Additionally, we highlight the potential for objective styles to contribute to more transparent and explainable image editing methods. The code for our research can be accessed at https://github.com/alexalexalex123/style-extraction. We also provide publicly accessible interactive visualizations at https://alexyu.github.io/style_extr. Several style examples can be found at https://github.com/alexalexalex123/styles. To overcome this, we developed a novel context-grounding module that enhances feature mapping using attention mechanisms. We further explored the effects of varying button counts, conducted ablation studies on different network architectures and video feature types, and attained a 2nd place ranking overall in the LOVEU track 3 competition.
