LoveU, a popular Chinese dating application, hosted a CVPR 2022 challenge to enhance user experience through automatic question-answering tasks. To address this, we participated in the AQTC branch of the competition, aiming to develop a program that could automatically identify the "uniqueness" attribute from a video content provided by LoveU. 

2. Methods
To achieve this, we initially broke down the response into three parts - the main content, the button list, and the unique attribute. We then processed each segment separately, where the main content was analyzed through a pre-trained vision transformer, and the button list was fine-tuned using a multi-head attention mechanism. A context-grounding module was also implemented to enhance feature mapping. We explored the effects of various button counts and conducted ablation studies on different video feature types and network architectures.

A novel framework, known as Active Inference, has been widely employed for autonomous decision-making. This framework naturally balances exploration and exploitation by using a Bayesian approach to merge prior knowledge with sensory data. While traditional Active Inference has been successful in various tasks, it struggles with large datasets due to computationally costly sampling-based methods. This has led to the development of more efficient, but less flexible sampling-free alternatives. In this study, we adapt a sampling-free Active Inference method to a complex real-world robot navigation task, incorporating prior knowledge in the form of a pre-constructed map. By combining this map with sensory data, the robot learns to optimize its exploration and navigation. This is achieved through a dynamic belief representation that incorporates uncertainty and adapts as new information becomes available. This work contributes to the development of a versatile and efficient Active Inference method suitable for tasks requiring long-term autonomous navigation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the dynamic nature of the belief representation can be replaced with a compact, map-based structure without compromising performance. This offers a computationally efficient solution for autonomous navigation tasks. This study provides a framework for incorporating prior knowledge into sampling-free Active Inference methods, enabling their use in a range of real-world tasks. This work also paves the way for the adaptation of these methods to a range of challenging robotic tasks, including the coordination of multiple robots and novel robot tasks. This study is a significant contribution to the field of Active Inference, particularly in robotics, and opens up a range of exciting research avenues. In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, the data generated by Multi-Wire Proportional Chambers (MWPC) is often contaminated with large amounts of noise, rendering the existing sparse data compression methods ineffective due to their inability to handle both 3D sparse and dense data formats. To address this issue, we have developed a Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE) that can learn and extract meaningful features from the noisy MWPC data, allowing for an efficient compression of the sparse data through a 3D format. The BCAE consists of two components: a sensor encoder that removes noise from the MWPC sensors using a 2D autoencoder, and a fusion encoder that merges the reconstructed data from the sensor modules via a 1D autoencoder. The BCAE encodes the processed data into a compact format, enabling efficient data transmission and storage. By training the BCAE with a combination of binary cross-entropy and mean squared error, we have demonstrated that the BCAE can successfully remove noise from the MWPC data and perform data compression, resulting in a significant reduction in data size while maintaining overall quality. Notably, the BCAE has achieved a data compression ratio of up to 93.67% in complex geometries with minimal loss of signal information, making it an effective compression method for 3D sparse data. Moreover, the BCAE has been shown to outperform existing sparse data compression methods, such as Factorized Neural Network (FNN) and Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), by a margin of up to 10.37% in terms of data size reduction. The BCAE has been successfully tested on real-world MWPC data from the TPC at the T2K neutrino experiment, demonstrating its effectiveness and generalizability to real-world datasets. With its ability to efficiently compress 3D sparse data while maintaining data quality, the BCAE has the potential to greatly benefit data transmission and storage operations in high energy physics experiments. By integrating the BCAE into the data processing pipeline of TPC at the T2K neutrino experiment, we have shown that the BCAE can significantly reduce data storage costs by a factor of up to 79.12% while maintaining data transmission bandwidth by a factor of up to 79.64%. The BCAE has emerged as a vital component for data compression in high energy physics experiments, enabling efficient data transmission, storage, and processing while maintaining data quality. Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on minimizing excessive interference through effective device scheduling. Traditional scheduling methods mainly prioritize maximizing throughput and fairness without considering the timeliness of received data. This paper presents a novel D2D wireless D2D system model that takes into account both Age of Information (AoI) and standard Wireless Fidelity (Wi-Fi) interference models to maximize D2D communication quality, focusing on minimizing both interference and AoI. To achieve optimal results, a deep learning-based method is proposed that uses a Schedule-then-Transmit (StT) approach to first select the best D2D schedule and then transmit data simultaneously. To model user behavior, a Deep Neural Network (DNN) is designed with multiple layers, and its weights are optimized using an optimizer algorithm. Additionally, a reinforcement learning-based method is proposed that uses Policy Gradient (PG) to maximize D2D communication quality under interference constraints. Both scheduling approaches are evaluated through simulations and shown to provide comparable performance improvements. Notably, the deep learning-based DNN-schedule-first approach outperforms other state-of-the-art scheduling methods by significantly reducing average interference and AoI while increasing the success rate and energy efficiency. These advanced scheduling techniques can be applied in various D2D communication systems to maximize wireless communication quality. Furthermore, these scheduling methods can be extended to other emerging technologies, such as Non-Line-of-Sight (NLoS) D2D, with optimized performance. Finally, the deep learning-based D2D scheduling techniques can be generalized to various real-world scenarios to provide better services, such as video streaming and file sharing. Eventually, these scheduling methods can be employed in industry standards, such as IEEE 802.15.4m, to provide a solid foundation for future D2D communication systems. Lastly, due to the emergence of D2D, IEEE has actively worked on developing a new and highly relevant standard, 802.15m, to provide D2D communication services, and our work can significantly contribute to this effort by offering optimized scheduling methods. To sum up, this paper has offered a comprehensive study on wireless D2D systems, and we have contributed novel scheduling techniques to maximize D2D communication quality by using Schedule-then-Transmit (StT) and other advanced scheduling methods. These results can be extended to provide valuable insights for industry, and we have provided a detailed explanation of how our work can significantly help in developing a new and highly relevant standard, 802.

Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data structures.  Graph-based machine learning has made notable advancements lately, but detecting events in evolving networks still poses difficulties for current frameworks. Current methods typically convert node features into a single vector, then apply traditional machine learning models, though they struggle with dynamic graphs where relationships between nodes change over time. To address this, we propose an end-to-end framework for detecting events in evolving networks. First, we represent each node using multiple features and encode the temporal aspects of adjacent nodes. Then, a designed event detection model leverages temporal node representations to identify events. To boost generalization, we also employ a node embedding generator based on the clustergCNN method. Finally, we validate our approach with actual event data from air traffic systems, showing improved accuracy over baseline models. The proposed framework generates promising results and serves as a useful resource for developing advanced graph-based machine learning models. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. Additionally, the paper will raise intriguing questions for further investigation within the RE community. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved the accuracy of this characterization; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated histopathological images, a resource that is particularly scarce for the Italian context, sparking the development of the UniToPatho dataset. The UniToPatho dataset comprises 1096 whole-slide images, each annotated by Italian pathologists in accordance with standards established by the World Health Organization, thereby serving as a valuable resource for training, evaluating, and refining machine-learning models tailored to the characterization of colorectal polyps and dysplasia. The dataset is accessible via https://git.io/UniToPatho. This research outlines the methodology employed to create and evaluate the UniToPatho dataset, showcasing its potential to contribute to the development of accurate and generalizable systems for colorectal polyp characterization and dysplasia grading in the Italian region. The evaluation involved assessing the variability inherent in the dataset by simulating leave-region-out cross-validation, incorporating image downsampling to balance annotation factors with image content, and using well-established evaluation metrics to compare the performance of models trained with and without UniToPatho with existing benchmarks. In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is determined by their view of the encoded information, which is modeled using a directed acyclic graph. By establishing the minimum and maximum entropy of the source conditional on the adversary's guesses, we relate their effectiveness to the graph metrics of the adversary's view graph and the confusion graph. Specifically, we show that the conditional entropy is minimized when the view graph is a spanning graph of the confusion graph, and that this achieves the maximum possible leakage in the confusion graph. Conversely, we show that the conditional entropy is maximized when the view graph is a matching in the confusion graph, and that this gives the minimum possible leakage in the confusion graph. These findings are illustrated in two examples: one in which the adversary can learn the source sequence with high confidence when the confusion graph is complete, and another in which the adversary can learn the source sequence with high confidence when the view graph is a path covering of the confusion graph. Furthermore, we show that the zero-error information leakage is equivalent to the minimum number of edges in a spanning walk of the confusion graph that contains all vertices, and that this can be solved using a single source shortest path algorithm. Finally, we examine the scenario in which the adversary can only make a limited number of guesses and find that the optimal strategy involves using a set of critical nodes in the view graph. These critical nodes are those with the highest degree in the view graph and are located at branching points in the view graph, and we show that they allow the adversary to successfully identify the source sequence with the fewest guesses possible. Additionally, we propose an algorithm for finding these critical nodes and show that this algorithm can be solved using a graph reduction technique. Overall, our investigation provides new insights into how much information an adversary can gain when the source coding problem is considered in terms of zero-error information leakage. Deep learning-trained generative models can function as a prior in under-determined inverse problems such as generating images from limited radar data, exploiting their trained models to refine an approximate solution. However, standard generative models are ill-equipped for use as a prior due to their lack of consistency with the underlying physics of the problem. A new hierarchical generative model, called the Multi-resolution Sequential Argumentative Refinement model (MrSARP), is introduced in this study to overcome this limitation by simulating the process of imaging and iteration of refinement. It is trained on Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) image data and is tested on the generation of high-resolution SAR images from simulated radar data, with the results indicating a significant improvement in image quality over existing methods. The code for this model is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/achalag/MrSARP. The model has outperformed state-of-the-art methods in a recent SAR image super-resolution challenge, further demonstrating its effectiveness. MrSARP is a versatile approach that can be applied to a range of under-determined inverse problems due to its modular design and argumentative refinement mechanism. It has the potential for use in various applications such as image generation, SAR image super-resolution, and radar-based human activity monitoring. MrSARP has been patented as a radar image generation method. A demonstration of its performance can be found here: https://youtube.com/achalag. A description of its design is provided below. The trained MrSARP model is used to generate high-resolution images from simulated radar data, either through a forward pass or by refining an initial approximation, which can be either a low-resolution SAR image or a coarse filter-based approximation. The model is trained on a dataset of 53,000 image pairs, which is based on the SimSAR dataset and is augmented with random noise to simulate the effects of real radar data. The model is tested on a range of SAR images, including images with man-made objects, vehicles, and humans, which are either present in the training dataset or generated using SimSAR. The results indicate a significant improvement in image quality over existing methods due to its ability to exploit the structure of radar data through its argumentative refinement mechanism. This paper explores the behavior of Q-learning in continuous time scenarios. Under the assumption of average reward termination, we prove that Q-learning converges at a rate of O(1/t) in both tabular and general settings, showcasing a linear relationship between the error bound and the exploratory information. Furthermore, our theoretical findings are supported by numerical simulations. Additionally, we address the issue of drawing independent samples in continuous time and propose an algorithm that modifies the exploratory information using past observations. This modification enables sampling independent exploratory information and enhances the convergence rate. Our work can be extended to settings with misspecified Markov models by incorporating regularization techniques and provides a framework for future research in this domain. Moreover, our results suggest the applicability of Q-learning to real-time settings with limited computational constraints. Nevertheless, in scenarios with aging memoryless exploratory information, our approach faces a significant obstacle - the loss of optimality. This drawback can potentially be mitigated by future researchers. Finally, our study raises crucial research questions for further investigation, such as generalizing our results to settings with multiple objectives and exploring the relationship between exploratory information and policy improvement. Quantum magnets exhibit exceptional robustness due to the principles of Jordan-Wigner, Lieb-Wu, and Yang, which relate their spectra to fermionic properties. In systems with extended fermionic degeneracies, this stability can be further enhanced by spontaneous symmetry breaking or order-by-disorder effects triggered by quantum fluctuations. This study focuses on an extended Hubbard model on the triangular lattice, where a semi-fermionic degeneracy is introduced through nearest-neighbor hoppings modulated by biquadratic terms. This model exhibits a rich phase diagram featuring doped spin-1/2 Heisenberg lattice, dimerized Heisenberg lattice, and a N\'eel-Vaf\'ehi-Toulouse phase. Magnetic excitations are analyzed in detail, and the results are verified against exact diagonalization and matrix product state methods. Additionally, the role of order-by-disorder effects in generating the N\'eel-Vaf\'ehi-Toulouse phase is investigated. The dimerized phase can be stabilized in a range of parameter space that is equivalent to the regime in which order-by-disorder effects trigger dimerization in the doped triangular Heisenberg lattice model. This lattice model exhibits a tri-critical point that also emerges in a related Hubbard model on a hexagonal lattice with a similar fermionic degeneracy and a spin-1/2 Kitaev material, compound BaCo$_2$(As$_{1-x}$P$_x$)$_2$. The analysis of this system reveals that its phase diagram is characterized by an extension of the N\'eel-Vaf\'ehi-Toulouse phase to two dimensions. The dimerization parameter exhibits a subleading correction that varies as $\sim1/\ln\Delta$, where $\Delta$ is the doping or hole concentration. The results of this study can be generalized to other materials and Hubbard models based on triangular lattices with extended fermionic degenergies. These predictions could be verified using time-of-flight and momentum-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, in conjunction with neutron scattering experiments. The dimerization phenomenon observed in this system can be stabilized in two distinct ways: (i) through order-by-disorder effects triggered by quantum fluctuations in spin, and (ii) by direct fermionic exchange. Accurate vertebrae detection is crucial in linking CT imaging with medical records. However, the complex structure and high degree of variability in the human spine pose significant challenges to automatically identifying individual vertebrae. To overcome these difficulties, our method employs spine rectification - a novel approach that aligns and standardizes the spinal column across different patients, thereby simplifying the identification of individual vertebrae. By constraining the optimization process to take into account the anatomical characteristics of the adapted spine, our solution has been refined. Notably, our approach can locate and differentiate vertebrae from the sacrum without requiring any prior knowledge of their locations. To validate our solution, we evaluated its accuracy by comparing it to expert annotations in a large dataset containing images of the lumbar and sacral regions. Our results indicate that our approach can accurately locate and identify vertebrae with a high degree of precision. Specifically, our method achieved a mean distance error of 1.7 mm and a mean average surface distance error of 1.3 mm, surpassing previously published state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, our approach can correctly identify 30 out of 31 individual vertebrae and the sacrum with high accuracy, exceeding a previously established threshold of 0.65. To evaluate and demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution, we created a set of descriptive videos. Our work represents a significant advancement in the field of vertebrae detection and identification, and our method is expected to be useful for linking CT imaging with medical records in a variety of clinical applications. Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy across an intervening vacuum gap by transmitting acoustic waves. Our research provides a mathematical explanation for how this energy transfer occurs, and reveals that specific conditions allow for complete transmission of these waves. This finding holds true for materials of any shape or orientation and can be determined experimentally through measurement of surface properties. Furthermore, we analyzed the optimal energy transfer between identical zinc oxide crystals for various orientations and found a significant number of conditions that facilitate this energy transfer. Specifically, we found that zinc oxide has 22 possible orientations that enable optimal energy transfer across a 1 millimeter gap, and these orientations remain valid for crystals of any size. Additionally, we analyzed other materials and found that hexagonal silicon carbide has 35 possible orientations, while gallium nitride has 39. These findings could potentially expand applications of piezoelectric devices by allowing for more efficient energy harvesting and storage capabilities. Moreover, we explored the phenomenon of complete tunneling for thousands of material combinations and found that silicon arsenide and indium phosphide exhibit the largest number of orientations with optimal energy transfer conditions. We developed an online tool that allows users to quickly calculate the optimal energy transfer conditions for any material combination. Furthermore, we analyzed the relationship between a material's properties and its ability to exhibit complete tunneling, and found that a higher energy gap and higher sound velocities contribute to optimal energy transfer conditions. Finally, we analyzed the largest particle sizes for which complete tunneling occurs and found that it varies depending on the materials involved, with some exhibiting complete tunneling for nanometer-scale particles and others requiring larger particles. Overall, our research sheds new light on the optimal energy transfer between piezoelectric materials and opens up new avenues for research in materials science and acoustic wave technology. Additionally, we propose a new set of experiments that can determine the optimal energy transfer conditions for a specific material, such as testing the energy transfer between a zinc oxide crystal and a diamond surface by measuring the transmitted power at different frequencies and orientations. Similarly, we suggest other experiments such as investigating the energy transfer between a barite crystal and a lead zirconate titanate crystal in water, or between a quartz crystal and a silver halide crystal in air. These proposed experiments could potentially lead to new applications and technologies that utilize piezoelectric materials. We explore a cutting-edge method for optically manipulating polariton condensates at a microscale, relying on micro-reservoirs that facilitate non-equilibrium quantum fluid behavior even in the presence of high optical intensities. This technique proves effective in creating micro-scale optical traps for polariton condensates that exhibit coherent oscillations, unprecedented in macroholariton systems. By shaping the micro-reservoir's refractive index using photo-induced effects, we demonstrate the self-organization of the trapped condensates into crystal patterns and emulate macro-scale optical trapping phenomena, including vortex formation and picosecond coherent oscillations. This innovative approach offers promising avenues for developing miniaturized spintronic and opto-electronic devices.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris still unknown. Analyzing grain size and sublimation rate is essential in comprehending the environment that contributes to planetary disintegration. In this study, dual photometric data obtained through the Large Binocular Telescope utilizing the WHT/GRISM and GEMINI/NIRSAP instruments during different observing sessions are examined. These transits show variations in shape, possibly due to cloud layers at different depths, with the upper cloud experiencing temperature fluctuations between 500-700K as observed in two distinct episodes. The data indicate a decrease in particle size as the cloud forms, with particles measuring 0.5-1 micrometers in diameter before the most recent eclipse in 2020, in contrast to larger particles (100-200 micrometers) observed in 2016. The particle size increase is proposed to be a result of the escape of smaller particles due to a high mass loss rate of $3\times10^{8}g/s$ driven by the presence of a companion star, with this rate supported by both theoretical models and past observations, and may provide the necessary energy for the creation of the debris cloud's shape-retaining spheres. This research may offer fresh insights into the planetary disintegration theory known as photoevaporation. I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's mathematical methods as reflective of a more advanced scientific mindset compared to his philosophical approach, which is seen as more speculative and less reliable. Galileo's avoidance of certain mathematical tools, such as infinity, can be attributed to his adherence to Aristotelian thought rather than any inherent limitations of mathematics itself. This observation highlights the need for greater historical accuracy in evaluating the mathematical methods of past scientists, avoiding present-day assumptions about what is considered acceptable mathematical practice. It also offers an alternative interpretation of Galileo's career, marking a significant turning point in the history of science, where a prominent scientist deliberately adopted more rigorous mathematical methods in his later years. This development created a model for future scientists to incorporate mathematics into scientific inquiry, ultimately contributing to the separation of science from philosophy in modern times. Galileo's influence can be seen in prominent mathematicians of the 20th and 21st centuries, such as Abraham Robinson and Michael Slade, who also encountered resistance to their mathematical ideas due to concerns about infinity. This study also reexamines the contributions of two lesser-known mathematicians, Pedro Nu\~n\~ez and James Gregory, who independently developed key concepts of calculus in the 10th and 17th centuries, respectively. Their work not only predates Galileo's time but also challenges the conventional view of the origins of calculus as a logical outcome of the scientific revolution. Finally, this study reflects on the broader implications of these historical observations, suggesting a reassessment of the scientific revolution and its legacy in the fields of mathematics and science. It also offers an alternative perspective on the interplay between science and philosophy in the modern era, where ongoing debates over infinity in physics and cosmology take center stage. Our study focuses on examining non-Gaussian influences on Saha's ionization through the application of Tsallis statistics. We addressed this challenge by generalizing the number density with a non-Gaussian distribution based on Fermi-Dirac theory, and then formulated the Saha equation for cosmological recombination. Our analysis reveals two novel parameters: one governing Gaussian fluctuations and another representing Tsallis' free parameter. These parameters are examined in two scenarios: the case where radiation and matter have the same temperature and the phase transition of hydrogen occurs at the same time as the Universe's matter-radiation equality. Our results demonstrate how the application of Tsallis statistics to Saha's ionization leads to two distinct, non-zero parameters: N$_\mathrm{G}$=0 and Q$_\mathrm{S}$=0.25 for the first scenario, and N$_\mathrm{G}$=0.57 and Q$_\mathrm{S}$=0.19 for the second scenario. These values are consistent with numerous observational constraints from big bang nucleosynthesis, cosmic microwave background, large scale structure and baryon acoustic oscillations. Consequently, Tsallis statistics can effectively describe non-Gaussian fluctuations during the Universe's early stages of evolution, thereby providing a robust theoretical foundation for probing cosmological perturbations on tiny length scales. Moreover, our study paves the way for future cosmological experiments to test Tsallis statistics by analyzing small length scales. Lastly, two novel parameters offer immense potential for exploring the early Universe's microphysical landscape, thereby opening up new avenues for research and development, as exemplified by future projects such as probing big bang nucleosynthesis with precision via astrophysical analysis of light elements. Additionally, Tsallis statistics presents an intriguing possibility that future cosmic surveys might uncover novel length scale patterns governed by this distribution, thereby providing rare insights into the fractional part of the length scales present during the Universe's early stages of evolution. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes a novel approach that combines a magnetohydrodynamic framework with an embedded particle-in-cell model to investigate the coalescence of magnetic islands. By leveraging adaptive modeling, coarse-resolution fluid elements are paired with PIC cells from nearby flux surfaces to develop an efficient and tractable method for studying reconnection. This approach incorporates an embedded Maxwellian distribution to calculate electron temperatures and resistivity within a general MHD framework. To assess its validity, we compare the coalescence outcome with existing analytical and fully kinetic simulations, demonstrating satisfactory correspondence. Furthermore, we examine the effect of various numerical techniques on the reconnection process, showing that using the Neumann procedure instead of the standard Adams-Bashforth scheme significantly reduces numerical errors. Our study demonstrates that adaptive PIC embeddings within a magnetohydrodynamic framework provide an effective compromise between detailed kinetic models and simpler fluid-based approaches, offering an valuable resource for investigating the interaction between reconnection and surrounding turbulent plasma. With the capability to include numerous embedded PIC cells, this model enables us to explore reconnecting currents and heat fluxes reminiscent of collisionless whistler-mode turbulence. Additionally, we see potential applications in studying reconnection-mediated energization, heat flux regulation, and turbulent reconnection scenarios. Given its proven adaptability and performance, this model serves as an excellent precursor to more sophisticated fully kinetic Vlasov-Poisson simulations. Ultimately, this work aims to facilitate the development of more sophisticated kinetic models, making them accessible to our research group for the study of high-performance computational clusters. With this in mind, we propose to undertake fully kinetic VP simulations to corroborate our findings and shed light on the longstanding debate surrounding turbulent reconnection. Based on our estimates, fully kinetic VP simulations of the relevant scenario could be undertaken within reach of our research group using 102 and 104 particles per cell. However, we require enhanced computational resources to undertake these simulations. This document provides background information for understanding the research demo, Amanuensis, in the 2023 ACM SIGCPHYS Conference. Amanuensis is an interactive system designed to help programmers with minor tasks by taking over routine work, freeing them to focus on high-level programming concepts. During the conference, a demo will be presented showcasing Amanuensis's capabilities, with research findings from a user study on its effectiveness, as well as the development details of its underlying technology. This supplementary material includes additional context, research details, and implementation information for the conference demo. Specifically, it contains videos demonstrating Amanuensis's features, a study protocol for evaluating Amanuensis, and additional technical notes on its design and development. Additionally, code repositories for Amanuensis and research support can be found at https://github.com/facebookresearch/amanuensis. The research paper detailing Amanuensis's research findings will be published in the 2023 ACM SIGCPHYS Conference.
